Mapping near-daily large lake water surface topography by integrating SWOT swath observations with multi-mission satellite radar altimetry
abstract: Large lakes exhibit spatial variations in water levels, leading to distinct lake surface topography. Accurate characterization of this topography enables an improved understanding of lake dynamics, hydrological exchanges and water balance assessments. While satellite radar altimetry is widely used to monitor lake water, most missions utilize nadir-looking profiling altimeters that measure water levels only along fixed ground tracks, leaving significant data gaps in between. The recently launched Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission provides wide-swath 2D elevation measurements at high spatial resolution over the water bodies on a global scale. However, its 21-day repeat cycle limits the temporal frequency of observations. In this study, we present a framework capable of mapping lake water surface topography on a near-daily basis by integrating 2D SWOT observations with 1D radar altimetry. The method consists of three components: first, inter-mission biases between SWOT and four operational radar altimetry missions (Jason-3, Sentinel-3A, −3B, and Sentinel-6) are estimated using concurrent and co-located overpasses. Second, the stable and average intra-lake spatial pattern of water surface topography is derived by applying an Empirical Orthogonal Function (EOF) to the SWOT time series wide-swath measurements. Third, the SWOT-calibrated profiling altimetry measurements from the four radar altimetry mission were propagated to the entire lake based on that stable spatial pattern. This method has been successfully applied to Lake Ontario by using SWOT Calibration/Validation data, generating a near-daily time series of water surface topography maps with Root Mean Square Error ( RMSE ) for spatial and temporal water level variations below 4 cm and 5 cm, respectively.

title: N2O emissions and driving factors of coastal agricultural drainage ditches: implications for the nitrogen cycle
Applicability of an analytical probabilistic stormwater management model for large rural watersheds
abstract: Accurate peak flow predictions are critical for effective stormwater management. A wide range of techniques has been developed to estimate peak flows at pour points of interest. In many cases, the suitability of a model for a given watershed depends on numerous factors such as climate, catchment characteristics, data availability, and project objectives. This study focuses on extending the applicability of the Analytical Probabilistic Stormwater Management Model (APSWM), which was developed for small urban catchments. The APSWM peak flow model was recently enhanced to incorporate trapezoidal hydrograph shapes, referred to as APSWM(Tra), beyond the original triangular assumption. The model’s performance was investigated in a relatively large rural watershed within the Upper Thames River Basin in southwestern Ontario, Canada. APSWM(Tra) predicted peak flows within 14% of observed rates for return periods of 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, and 100 years and had a percent bias (PBIAS) of 13%. However, 2- and 5-year peak flows were underestimated. The study results suggest that APSWM(Tra) shows good potential as a tool for further development and use in large rural watersheds but further investigations and validations would be required before broader application.

title: Refining image-based approaches for river monitoring: a focus on graphical enhancement and software parameter sensitivity
abstract: Image-based techniques for estimating river surface velocity include traditional Large-Scale Particle Image Velocimetry (LSPIV) methods based on cross-correlation of tracer displacements and alternative optical flow approaches that infer motion from image intensity gradients. The accuracy of both is contingent on the quality of the input images and the configuration of the processing algorithms. This study presents a sensitivity analysis evaluating the impact of different combinations of graphical enhancement filters and software parameterizations on performance under varying environmental conditions. Image-based measurements were performed in two field case studies in Sicily (Italy): the Oreto and Platani rivers. Acquired videos were pre-processed applying enhancement filters and testing multiple parameter configurations. Analyses were carried out using PIVlab and SSIMS-Flow, each tested with distinct processing setups. Overall, 1296 surface velocity fields were derived and compared to ADCP reference data. To objectively characterize water clarity and the background conditions, the Normalized Difference Turbidity Index (NDTI) was used for the acquired sequences. The findings of the study demonstrate that both filter selection and software settings significantly influence image velocimetry accuracy. PIVlab, relying on cross-correlation, showed greater robustness in visually complex scenarios, while SSIMS-Flow, based on intensity gradients, achieved higher accuracy in uniform and turbid conditions. Poor performance was generally associated with unsuitable filter or parameter combinations. These findings underscore the necessity of adapting image processing workflows to specific environmental contexts. The proposed evaluation framework offers a replicable approach for optimizing LSPIV and optical flow accuracy and supports the development of adaptive monitoring solutions for hydrological applications.

abstract: • We estimated canal evaporation in an arid urban area with an isotope enrichment model. • Annual evaporative losses of 5.2 ± 2.3% and 3.3 ± 1.5% were obtained in open canals. • High seasonality was noted in canal evaporation, which a maximum value of 8.5%. • Isotope-based evaporation estimates were consistent with pan evaporation measurements.

title: Process-informed feature engineering for explainable optimization-driven AI in groundwater-level prediction
abstract: Accurate prediction of groundwater levels is crucial for sustainable water management, yet most machine-learning approaches remain black boxes that overlook delayed recharge and cumulative hydroclimatic effects. To address this gap, this study developed and evaluated an explainable, optimization-driven artificial intelligence framework integrating Bayesian optimization with XGBoost to capture temporal dependencies, improve interpretability, and identify dominant hydroclimatic controls on groundwater in the Bécancour River Basin, Québec, Canada.The framework combines automatic hyperparameter tuning with process-informed feature engineering, incorporating lagged discharge, temperature, and precipitation, plus rolling and antecedent indices representing cumulative hydrological effects. Using a 12-year daily hydro-meteorological dataset (2010–2022), the baseline BOXGBoost model captured the overall groundwater dynamics but exhibited spatial inconsistencies in upland regions. Incorporating process-informed engineered features markedly improved performance, achieving mean Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) and coefficient of determination (R2) values of ~0.92 and a Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) level ~0.90, and reduced Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of ~0.14 m and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of ~0.10 m across all wells. The SHAP analysis revealed that lagged discharge, water temperature, and rolling precipitation explained ~70% of the predictive importance, confirming that delayed recharge and cumulative hydrological responses dominate groundwater behavior. The BOXGBoost framework achieved its aim by delivering accurate and interpretable groundwater-level predictions, revealing the dominant hydroclimatic controls, and outperforming conventional models while maintaining hydrological consistency.This outcome demonstrates that explainable, physically consistent AI models can support groundwater monitoring, drought forecasting, and sustainable water management under variable hydroclimatic conditions.

High-resolution study of pollutant mobility in an acid mine drainage-impacted estuary under changing tidal and river contributions
abstract: The present study investigates the behaviour of acid mine drainage (AMD)-derived contaminants in the Tinto River estuary (SW Spain) using five high-resolution (hourly) fixed-point sampling campaigns conducted under contrasting hydrological and tidal regimes: low-riverflow neap and spring tides, and high-riverflow events following rainfall across different tidal coefficients. The results indicate that Mn, Zn, Co, Ni and Cd exhibit a quasi-conservative behavior, with low partition coefficients (Kd) and predominance in the dissolved phase. Contrary, Fe and Al undergo mineral precipitation, as schwertmannite and basaluminite, respectively, dominating the suspended particulate matter (SPM) composition and acting as sink of other metal(oid)s (As, Pb and Cu) through sorption processes. Arsenic is initially removed from solution under acidic conditions and returns when pH exceeds 6 by desorption from schwertmannite. Lead exhibited a singular response likely driven by sulfate-mineral solubility control and the wash-out of evaporitic salts recording significant high dissolved concentrations in one of the high-flow samplings (> 400µg/L). Low-flow conditions—especially during spring tide—and high-flow events with strong rainfall dilution reduce metal mobility by enhancing their partitioning into SPM and subsequent sedimentation in the upper estuary (except for As). In contrast, high-flow conditions with weaker dilution can increase metal transport toward downstream estuarine areas and ultimately the Atlantic Ocean. This work provides the first systematic, tide-resolved and hydrologically contrasted assessment of contaminant dynamics in an AMD-impacted estuarine system, revealing that both tidal phases and hydrological regime must be jointly considered to understand and predict the net flux of AMD-derived contaminants to the ocean.

title: An efficient fracture network reduction method for characterizing flow and mass transport in three-dimensional fracture networks
Long-term and interannual variability of African terrestrial water storage revealed by GRACE/GRACE-FO and models
abstract: Climate change is intensifying the hydrologic cycle, and terrestrial water storage (TWS) provides an integrated indicator of these shifts. In this study, we analyzed long-term and interannual TWS variations across Africa over April 2002-December 2024 using GRACE/GRACE Follow-On (GRACE/-FO) satellite gravimetry, together with land surface models (LSMs) and satellite altimetry derived lake storage. GRACE/-FO revealed a continental TWS increase of 96.1 ± 13.4 Gt yr −1 (2σ), with an acceleration of 11.6 ± 3.83 Gt yr −2 . Basin-scale attribution exhibited that large lakes/reservoirs storage increases largely contributed to the observed TWS gains, whereas model predicted soil moisture showed a general declining trend, likely indicating the limitations of LSMs in this region. The long-term TWS increase was further quantitatively supported by a rising water balance. Interannual variability was structured by large-scale climate modes: El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) paced continental and tripole-like responses, respectively, as identified by empirical orthogonal function (EOF) analysis. Our results elucidated new observational constraints on the drivers of African TWS dynamics and their responses to a changing climate.

title: Fire can explain rainfall-runoff shifts during and after drought
abstract: State shifts in rainfall-runoff relationships, driven by disturbances such as droughts and bushfires, can persist long after the disturbance, resulting in reduced streamflow per unit rainfall. However, droughts and fires are highly correlated, and fires can also affect runoff patterns. In this study, we investigated the joint influence of fires and prolonged drought on rainfall-runoff relationships in the Australian Capital Territory (ACT) and neighbouring Queanbeyan catchments. State shifts in rainfall-runoff relationships were detected using Hidden Markov Modelling (HMM) of runoff, incorporating Kuczera fire parameters that characterise the duration and magnitude of streamflow reduction following fire. Hidden Markov Models avoid the need for a priori definition of drought periods and provide a flexible framework to identify the state changes in the rainfall-runoff relationship. We found that: (1) Fire can explain apparent state shifts in rainfall-runoff relationships during and after drought. Based on previous literature, we hypothesised the existence of multiple hydrological states in the western forested region, however the inclusion of fire as a factor removed most of the two-state behaviour (3 of 6 gauges); (2) State shifts, in this study, were more common in non-urban non-forested catchments (4 gauges) rather than the forested ones (1 of 7 gauges), contrary to expectation; (3) Moreover, almost all gauges (13 of 16) did not display a long-term rainfall-runoff state shift following drought, suggesting that the study catchments are resilient to drought. The catchments exhibited recovery behaviour even when fire events that occurred amid prolonged drought were considered for the analysis. These findings underscore the importance of integrating both fire and drought in hydrological modelling to better understand their combined effects on catchment behaviour.

title: Precision mapping of evapotranspiration in arid basins: Spatiotemporal optimization and sensitivity to extreme climate conditions based on multi-mechanism model fusion

Performance-based assessment of tropical cyclone parametric precipitation models for flood simulation applications
abstract: Tropical cyclone (TC) rainfall is one of the primary drivers of flooding in coastal watersheds; therefore, accurate rainfall estimation is essential for reliable hydrologic and hydraulic (H&H) modeling. In TC-prone regions like the Caribbean Islands, which are also topographically complex, the wide range of models available for estimating TC rainfall presents a challenge in identifying the most suitable Parametric Precipitation Models (PPMs) for flood modeling applications. Thus, this study proposes a dual-component framework for benchmarking PPM-derived rainfall: (i) a rainfall-level comparison of PPMs and (ii) a performance-based assessment of the rainfall fields produced by PPMs for flood simulations applications. The proposed framework was applied to a watershed in Puerto Rico and tested under three historical hurricanes using five PPMs and Stage IV radar-based rainfall as a benchmark. The rainfall-level analysis assessed precipitation accumulation distribution, patterns, and cumulative totals, while the performance-based assessment examined the impacts on riverine flow timing, peak discharge, and overland flood levels in the selected watershed. Results show that the Parametric Hurricane Rainfall Model (PHRaM) and its shear-excluded variant performed most consistently across all metrics. However, PPM-derived rainfall fields are unreliable for real-time forecasting in their current state. Importantly, simulated peak flows were more affected by the rainfall uncertainty than flood extents. Thus, this study highlights the need to select an appropriate tool for assessing flood risk, particularly in steep, complex terrain. Although PPMs are efficient in data-scarce regions, their inherent structural limitations must be carefully evaluated to ensure reliable flood hazard predictions.

title: Multivariate design storms using vine copulas and Gaussian process regression
abstract: Multivariate design storms represent events associated with a defined Joint Return Period (JRP) while preserving observed spatial dependence. They enable the synthetic generation of storms that have not yet been observed but are plausibly likely, thereby expanding the scenario space for design and risk assessment. Two practical challenges persist: (i) embedding JRPs within storm-generation procedures beyond three dimensions, which is computationally demanding; and (ii) representing spatial intermittency, which has so far been treated only with a bivariate Multivariate Mixture Model (MMM). We present a method that addresses both challenges concurrently. We compare five copula-based approaches for high-dimensional dependence, employ Gaussian process regression (GPR) to accelerate JRP estimation, and extend the MMM to represent intermittency in multiple dimensions. The framework is applied to the Besaya River basin (northern Spain). Results show that GPR reduces computational cost by an order of magnitude while maintaining approximation errors on the order of 10 − 3 , and that the MMM captures intermittency in multidimensional settings. Flexible vine copula–based approaches best preserve spatial and multidimensional dependence in multivariate storm generation, whereas Gaussian-based and univariate benchmarks systematically underestimate storm totals. • Multivariate design storms preserve spatial dependence to explore plausible unobserved extremes for a given return period. • Gaussian process regression cuts joint return period computation by 10 × in high dimensions, with approximation errors near 10 − 3 . • Multivariate Mixture Models capture spatial intermittency patterns in multidimensional precipitation scenarios. • Flexible vine copulas outperform Gaussian methods in preserving spatial dependence and estimating compound storm magnitudes.

Temporal evolution of stormwater basin soil properties and infiltration rates
abstract: Infiltration-based green stormwater infrastructure (GSI) practices are widely used to mitigate the hydrologic impacts of urbanization. However, how GSI performance evolves over time remains poorly understood. In particular, there is little consensus among published studies on whether GSI infiltration rates increase, decrease, or remain constant as GSI practices age. To address this gap, we hypothesized that GSI soil properties change with age and these changes drive corresponding changes in the infiltration rate. Soil properties and infiltration rates were measured in 28 stormwater infiltration basins along a chronosequence ranging in age from 2 to 20 years. Clay, silt, and organic matter contents increased with age while bulk density decreased with age, suggesting that vegetation and soil biota activity as well as fine sediment accumulation contributed to soil profile evolution. Age, clay, silt, and organic matter correlated with infiltration rate, whereas bulk density and porosity did not. Percent silt content was the best predictor of infiltration rate (R2 = 0.46–0.65, p < 0.001); however, age alone provided moderate predictive power (R2 = 0.16–0.45, p = 0.035–0.001). The best performing single and multiple regression models of infiltration rate used age, organic matter, and silt as predictors (R2 = 0.61–0.65, p < 0.001). These data and models revealed that infiltration rate decreased with basin age and silt content, and increased with organic matter, providing a quantitative link between soil properties and infiltration rate evolution with basin age.

FlowGATFormer: A streamflow prediction model based on spatiotemporal dual attention
abstract: Achieving high accuracy in long-term river streamflow prediction is essential for simulating the terrestrial hydrological cycle and managing water resources. However, traditional hydrological models are often computationally expensive and require complex parameter estimation and calibration. Deep learning models, particularly long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, have shown promise in streamflow forecasting, but their predictive accuracy tends to decrease at longer forecast horizons. To address these issues, this study proposes FlowGATFormer, a streamflow forecasting model that integrates a graph attention network (GAT) with the Informer architecture. The model introduces a dual spatiotemporal attention to capture spatial dependencies and temporal dynamics in river systems. FlowGATFormer is applied to predict streamflow at five forecast horizons including 1, 6, 12, 16, and 24 days ahead. Specifically, the GAT models spatial dependencies among hydrological stations located upstream and downstream of a river network, while the Informer captures temporal dependencies within long-term streamflow series derived from the same hydrological station. Based on data from 11 stations in the CAMELS-CH dataset (1999–2020), FlowGATFormer significantly outperforms baseline models by achieving a Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) of 0.5616 (NSE > 0.5) for the 12-day-ahead prediction. Compared to the LSTM baseline, the NSE improvement gradually increases with the prediction horizon, rising from 3.09% for the 6-day-ahead prediction to 10.98% for the 24-day-ahead prediction. We believe that the FlowGATFormer has the potential to be a robust data-driven approach for high-accuracy, long-term river streamflow prediction.

AI-assisted framework using physically informed rainfall–drainage features for real-time urban flood risk forecasting
abstract: Urban flash flooding is becoming more severe as urban population density increases, and severe and frequent floods occur. As a result, early warning systems are required that translate raw sensor data into clear and actionable hazard situations, rather than simply providing ongoing forecasts. For this purpose, this study develops a hydrological- and hydraulics-informed framework for real-time multi-class AI-based flood warning across evaporation (low risk), drained (medium risk), and flooding (high risk) states. The methodology firstly derives physically guided rainfall features using a rule-based back-propagation neural network to estimate return-period signals alongside seasonality and antecedent-rainfall cues, while hydraulics-informed “water-level memory” (current class and class duration) captures system dynamics. These inputs feed seven weak-learner families whose outputs are fused by a time-series mixture-of-experts. The model performance is evaluated for lead times of up to 5 h using both multi-step metrics and event-based analyses. The framework is applied to the Ruislip urban drainage system, UK, using long-term IoT rainfall and water-level records (2011–2024). The results show discrimination improved compared with voting and averaging ensembles. It also increases hit rates for flood and non-flood decisions at 1–3 h. At 4–5 h, it reduces false alarms and late detections. Event-based results show more on-time hits and shorter timing lags. Feature analysis shows that rainfall intensity and duration are the main drivers. Seasonal effects and antecedent occurrence also provide added value. Residual errors concentrate at longer horizons e.g. 5 h later where transitions between adjacent states are intrinsically difficult.

title: Molecular responses of dissolved organic matter to surface water–groundwater interactions in the Tibetan Plateau
Soil moisture thresholds for runoff generation: depth sensitivity and mechanistic controls
abstract: A compound wetness index combining antecedent soil moisture and event rainfall (S 0 = ASI 0 + P) is commonly used to analyze threshold-based runoff responses. However, it remains unclear how the depth of soil moisture integration affects threshold detection and predictive performance. Here, we examined the relationship between runoff thresholds and maximum integration depth (MID) across four experimental catchments spanning diverse climates and runoff generation mechanisms. Using segmented regression across multiple MIDs and monitoring sites, we identified runoff thresholds and evaluated the explanatory power of S 0 for stormflow using post-threshold coefficients of determination (R h 2 ). Thresholds were consistently detected across integration depths, but explanatory power varies strongly among catchments. In storage-controlled systems, R h 2 increased with depth, indicating that deeper soil moisture integration better captured subsurface storage controls on stormflow initiation. In contrast, in connectivity-limited or shallow flow-dominated systems, shallow integration depths performed better because near-surface wetting controlled preferential flow or infiltration-excess runoff, whereas deeper integration included hydrologically inactive storage. These results show that the optimal integration depth is catchment dependent and closely linked to dominant runoff generation processes. Accounting for this depth dependence can improve threshold-based runoff analysis and support more process-consistent soil moisture monitoring and hydrological modeling

Laboratory investigation of anchor ice evolution under steady and varying heat fluxes
abstract: Anchor ice formation, growth, and release in rivers impact flooding risk, sediment transport, and aquatic habitats in winter. The heat flux is known to significantly affect the growth of anchor ice, but there have been no studies on how the anchor ice growth rate is affected by variations in the heat flux. This study investigated anchor ice evolution under steady and varying heat flux conditions in the laboratory. Anchor ice images were captured using a high-resolution camera, and air and water temperatures measurements were collected. Four steady cases with constant heat flux and six varying heat flux cases, in which the heat flux was increased by either decreasing the air temperature or applying wind at three different times during a supercooling event, were examined. Results showed that anchor ice growth during steady heat flux cases experienced initial, transitional, and final growth stages in sequence. An additional heat change stage, which was defined as the time period of increased anchor ice growth following an increase in heat flux, always occurred prior to the final stage in varying heat flux cases. The anchor ice growth rate (i.e., the rate of change of anchor ice thickness) during the heat change stage was 150% and 80% larger on average compared to the transitional and final stages, respectively. The peak anchor ice growth rate reached an upper limit of ∼9 cm/h when the heat flux exceeded ∼300 W/m 2 , and the growth rate during the transitional and final stages increased approximately linearly with the heat flux.

HydroCraft: an efficient online platform for hydrological modeling integrated with a large language model agent
abstract: Hydrological modeling is essential for water resources management but often requires specialized expertise, creating a significant barrier to its broad application. To address this challenge, we developed HydroCraft, a web-based platform designed to democratize the modeling process. HydroCraft provides a comprehensive and integrated workflow for basin extraction, driving data generation, parameter calibration, and result visualization, enabling rapid modeling for any watershed globally. Key features of the platform include: an adaptive watershed delineation method that optimizes the distribution of computational units based on user-defined sub-basin area thresholds; the integration of three hydrological models (THREW, Xin’anjiang, and Miyun Hydrological Model) suitable for diverse climatic and geological conditions; and the incorporation of a Large Language Model (LLM) agent, which serves as a robust assistant to provide guidance and automated task execution. Users only need a device with a web browser and an internet connection to perform advanced hydrologic simulations. Two case studies (user-driven vs. LLM-agent-assisted) demonstrated the platform’s efficiency and intelligence. The platform advances hydrological modeling toward greater intelligence and accessibility, providing support for applications such as water resource management and flood forecasting

title: Disentangling hydroclimatic controls on drought-induced vegetation productivity loss at the basin scale across China
An analysis of direct and indirect methods of estimating evaporation from a water supply reservoir
Modeling the impact of nature-based solutions on dry season water availability: exploration of spatio-temporal configurations
abstract: Nature-based Solutions (NbS) and other small-scale, decentralized infrastructure elements are increasingly recognized for their potential to reduce flood and drought impacts. Systematic evaluation approaches are now needed to identify effective spatial configurations and temporal staging for the implementation of NbS. This study develops and applies a hydrologic modeling framework to evaluate five NbS pathways combining alien invasive vegetation removal and replacement by indigenous grasslands or forest, and targeted soil conductivity modification to enhance infiltration. Pathways were assessed using multi-criteria metrics including hydrologic performance, feasibility, cost, and co-benefits for enhancing dry season flows. The five adaptation pathways were developed as representative combinations of short-, mid-, and long-term NbS interventions selected based on modeled hydrologic performance, feasibility, and stakeholder-identified implementation priorities and constraints. Pathway 1 and Pathway 2 emphasize the alien invasive vegetation removal and replacement with indigenous grasslands in different spatial sequences; Pathway 3 combines the alien invasive vegetation replacement with grasslands and soil modification; Pathway 4 combines the alien invasive vegetation replacement with grasslands and indigenous forest in different locations; and Pathway 5 combines the alien invasive vegetation replacement with indigenous grasslands and forest with soil modification at high-performing locations. Results show that each of the five adaptation pathways improves water availability relative to the baseline, with variations in their performance, feasibility, cost, and co-benefits. Across pathways, modeled average daily flow at the outlet increased from 6.0 m 3 /s (baseline) to 6.8–7.4 m 3 /s (+0.8–1.4 m 3 /s; ∼13–23%) under full-year conditions. Improvements were more pronounced during water-stressed periods: dry-season flow increased from 3.2 m 3 /s to 3.8–4.0 m 3 /s (∼19–25%), and flow in the driest year increased from 0.6 m 3 /s to 1.0–2.9. Pathway 5 enhanced the dry season flows the most while mitigating peak flows and providing ecosystem benefits. This research advances the integration of hydrologic modeling of decentralized land use changes and water system infrastructure elements with stakeholder-driven decision-making, thereby contributing to the adaptation planning and Adaptative Pathways Planning literature.

title: A localisation strategy for scalable and efficient multi-source precipitation blending at high resolutions over large domains
abstract: Driven by growing demands for higher resolution and quality in hydrometeorological applications, precipitation products are increasingly being developed at sub-daily and kilometre-scale resolutions by blending information from multiple data sources. However, these developments face substantial modelling complexity, as the integration of multiple heterogeneous sources expands the inter- and intra-source error relationships that need to be represented, particularly when applied across large spatial domains. To address this challenge, this study presents the theoretical formulation and scalable implementation strategies for generalised multi-source precipitation blending within a statistical interpolation framework. We use an error-informed localisation concept, which formalises the insight that, in most blending scenarios, only observations that are both spatially representative and characterised by relatively low errors exert meaningful influence on blended precipitation field. Motivated by this concept, we develop a highly efficient implementation that approximates source influence by selecting only the nearest grid cell from each additional spatial input, enabling a substantial reduction in covariance modelling while preserving the essential blending characteristics. The framework is demonstrated in a three-source blending experiment integrating satellite, radar, and gauge data to produce 2-km and hourly rainfall fields over two radar domains in Australia. Qualitative assessment of precipitation and error spatial structures during extreme events, together with quantitative evaluation using the fractions skill score (FSS), show that the simplified implementation retains blending performance comparable to a comprehensive scheme, while requiring only a fraction of the computational cost. This work provides both conceptual understanding and practical implementation strategies to support large-scale, high-resolution, multi-source precipitation product development.

title: Seasonal and interannual dynamics of non-rainfall water inputs in a coastal mediterranean dune ecosystem
abstract: Non-rainfall water inputs (NRWI)—including dew, fog deposition, frost, and water-vapour adsorption (WVA)—can provide ecologically relevant moisture in water-limited environments, yet their long-term magnitude and partitioning remain poorly constrained. We present a three-year (2021–2024) assessment of NRWI in a Mediterranean coastal dune ecosystem in Doñana National Park (SW Spain), based on two large, high-precision weighing lysimeters under bare-soil and shrub-covered conditions. Hourly lysimeter mass changes during rain-free periods were combined with meteorological data to identify and classify NRWI components. Water-vapour adsorption dominated NRWI across all seasons and years, accounting for most events and cumulative inputs, while dew produced larger per-event gains but occurred less frequently. Fog deposition was negligible under conservative detection criteria. Bare soil consistently accumulated more NRWI than shrub-covered surfaces, reflecting stronger nocturnal cooling and greater coupling to near-surface humidity. Dew showed pronounced interannual variability and was strongly reduced during the anomalously warm and dry hydrological year 2022, whereas WVA proved comparatively climate-resilient.

title: Spatiotemporal evolution, physical drivers, and future prediction of global terrestrial moisture imbalance: a multi-expert AI-agent approach based on SVBI
Non-stationary framework of quantifying heat-driven drought propagation mechanisms in the Yellow River Basin of China

title: Advancing the calibration of macroscale hydrological models by integrating sensitivity analysis, adaptive pseudo-modeling optimization and multi-site calibration
abstract: Accurate estimation of parameters in macroscale, complex hydrological models (HMs) using effective calibration procedures can improve the characterization of real-world phenomena of hydrological fluxes. This study presents a novel, model-agnostic calibration framework that integrates global sensitivity analysis (SA) with an adaptive pseudo-modelling optimization strategy. The framework is designed to overcome key limitations of conventional calibration methods, such as reliance on exhaustive one-shot sampling, absence of formal parameter screening, and restriction to single site calibration. To demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework, catchment-specific sensitive parameters of the variable infiltration capacity model (VIC) with a 0.15° spatial resolution were calibrated for streamflow simulations over the Godavari River basin in India using both single- and multi-site calibration. An ensemble of pseudo models, including Gaussian process regression, kriging, and artificial neural networks, was employed to enhance robustness and generalization. Although the performance indicators (NSE, KGE ≥ 0.8 and PBIAS ≤ 15) in both scenarios demonstrated similar model performance at the catchment outlet, scenario 2 outperformed single-site calibration in terms of equifinality reduction, less parameter uncertainty and improved computational efficiency. By combining Sobol SA, ensemble pseudo modelling, and multi-site calibration, the framework efficiently explored hydrologically relevant regions of the parameter space, reduced dimensionality by excluding non-influential parameters, and lowered overall computational burden. The proposed framework is a robust method for improving the simulation capability of macroscale HMs under diverse hydroclimatic conditions. Plain language summary Hydrological models, such as the VIC model, are powerful computer-based tools used to study and understand water movement on a local to large scale, particularly at the river basin scale. The calibration process involves adjusting the model’s parameters to ensure that the model outputs align with real-world observations. Improving the calibration of hydrological models, like VIC, enhances their ability to make reliable predictions, which is vital for effective water resource management and decision-making. This paper presents a novel hybrid modelling framework combining sensitivity analysis and an adaptive optimization algorithm to calibrate complex hydrological models automatically. The proposed approach can be a robust and time-efficient method for improving large-scale hydrological models, enabling decision-makers to make informed choices and develop effective strategies for addressing water-related challenges.

title: Spatiotemporal quantification of relative contributions of compound flood drivers using Shapley value-based approach
The localized sediment resuspension (LSR) model: demonstrating the importance of spatial heterogeneity for improved TSS predictions in combined sewer systems
abstract: This study introduces the Localized Sediment Resuspension (LSR) model, which considers spatial heterogeneity in sediment accumulation and resuspension processes across sewer networks to improve predictions of total suspended solids (TSS) fluxes in Combined Sewer Overflows (CSOs). The LSR model involves identifying areas prone to sediment accumulation (virtual hotspots), simulating sediment release based on local hydraulic variables, and routing resuspended sediments along the network. The LSR model results are superimposed on TSS predictions from a detailed hydrodynamic model, improving the representation of TSS peaks during CSO events. To evaluate performance improvements, the newly developed Peak-Weighted Dynamic Time Warping (PW-DTW) metric, which emphasizes peak matching, was employed. The LSR performance was evaluated for different levels of parameter heterogeneity and model complexity. Better TSS predictions were obtained with the model structure that balances uniform sediment accumulation characteristics with spatial heterogeneity in resuspension processes, achieving a 40.1% median improvement in PW-DTW across verification events, with performance improvements observed in all 17 events classified as resuspension-dominated. The performance of the LSR model did not degrade when parameters were estimated using low-temporal-resolution data (composite samples) instead of high-resolution turbidity measurements. Under this low-resolution scenario, a 40.6% median PW-DTW improvement was obtained, again improving all 17 resuspension-dominated events. Overall, the LSR model demonstrates that explicitly considering spatial heterogeneity is essential for improving the modelling of TSS discharges during CSO events, ultimately supporting more effective pollution control strategies.

title: Model-based disaggregation of satellite-based total water storage anomalies for the Upper Colorado River Basin
abstract: This study demonstrates the capability of an integrated hydrologic model of the Upper Colorado River Basin to disaggregate total water storage anomalies into constituent parts over a 44-year period. The Upper Colorado River Basin is a critical transboundary water source in that supports tens of millions of people in North America. Groundwater plays an important role in basin hydrology, but few methods explicitly measure or simulate groundwater at the basin scale. Here, we developed a physically based groundwater-surface water-land surface model and decomposed basin-wide water storage trends into constituent parts. We evaluated model output (i.e. streamflow, water table depth, snow, evapotranspiration, and water storage) against a suite of observations. The simulated data match observations well, particularly at monthly timescales—which is the temporal resolution of GRACE. Simulated trends in subsurface water storage are very sensitive to the initial condition, which required careful attention to the model’s transient initialization process to ensure that residual trends from spinup did not obscure the total water storage signal. Each component of total water storage contributes uniquely to sub-annual and inter-annual trends in basin hydrology. Here, we demonstrate that the integrated hydrologic model presented in this work explicitly partitions water storage trends into soil moisture and groundwater components, enabling improved water management strategies for the Upper Colorado River Basin.

title: Spatial-heterogeneity-aware deep learning for water quality prediction: a case study in Hong Kong
An end-to-end framework for semi-automated and cost-effective urban drainage system design: integrating deep learning, topology generation, and multi-objective optimization
Offshore wind farms' impact on phytoplankton carbon and water quality: A multimethod analysis

Interconnected groundwater–surface water interactions and carbon transport across a subarctic river valley
abstract: Groundwater–surface water (GW-SW) interactions play an important role in subsurface carbon transport and transformation but remain understudied. This study investigates the aquifer-river system of the Oulankajoki River Valley in northeastern Finland to evaluate how hydrostratigraphy and recharge pathways regulate groundwater hydrogeochemistry and carbon transformations during 2022–2025, using a combination of a 3D geological model, multivariate analyses (PCA, HCA), and stable isotope analysis. Results reveal three major findings. First, carbon dynamics within the aquifer are primarily governed by hydrostratigraphy, recharge connectivity, and groundwater residence time, while redox evolution regulates transformations between organic and inorganic carbon species. Second, groundwater is DOC-poor (1.2 ± 0.6 mg L −1 ) and DIC-rich (20.3 ± 6.7 mg L −1 ) relative to surface water (DOC = 8.3 ± 1.9 mg L −1 ; DIC = 4.5 ± 0.2 mg L −1 ), indicating efficient organic carbon processing and carbonate buffering. Third, multivariate analyses identify a clear hydrogeochemical separation between shallow, recharge-dominated groundwater characterized by transient DOC transport and deeper, carbonate-buffered groundwater associated with progressive DIC accumulation under longer residence times. The conceptual model developed in this study integrates recharge pathways, carbonate weathering, and redox evolution, and carbon transformation within a unified framework. These findings underscore the importance of hydrogeological heterogeneity and groundwater evolution in regulating carbon coupling within boreal aquifer systems.

title: Geochemical footprints of climate-driven increases in groundwater contributions in a Canadian Rocky mountain watershed
Variability of discharge response from tile drains in a small agricultural catchment
abstract: Understanding the discharge response of tile drains is essential to better manage water resources in agricultural areas. The aim of this study was to compare two tile-drainage systems in an agricultural catchment, the Hydrological Open Air Laboratory in Austria in May-October, using six years of high-frequency hydrometric and isotopic observations, to determine whether new or old water contributes more to their discharge and whether new-water contributions correlate with hydrograph flashiness or time to peak flow. The results showed clear differences between the discharge responses and new water fractions of the two tile drainage systems. Sys4 inlet represented a perennial system with larger drainage area, larger pipes and simpler topology, that responded rapidly to even small amounts of rainfall. The response was mainly independent from the soil moisture state and the groundwater level. The second drainage system, Frau2 was an ephemeral system with smaller drainage area, smaller pipes and complex topology that exhibited the flashiest behavior. Larger discharge peaks at Frau2 occurred above a certain soil moisture (0.35 m 3 /m 3 ) and groundwater level threshold (0.3 m below ground surface). Sys4 had the largest average peak flow new water fractions (0.54 with δ 18 O), higher than Frau2 (0.47) and the catchment outlet (0.41). The differences in the hydrometric and isotopic characteristics of the drains could be explained by differences in their construction properties. Discharge from the drainage system draining larger area and with simpler topology and pipes with larger diameter had faster response to rainfall and larger new water fractions.

title: Radial flow in an anisotropic aperture field in a rough-walled fracture
abstract: Preferential flow channels with low hydraulic resistance in a single fracture can transmit large fluid volumes in fractured rock. Characterizing these channels and the associated flow channeling at the field scale, however, remains challenging. In this study, a hybrid iterative computational workflow was used to generate a field-scale (30 m diameter) synthetic fracture with self-affine surfaces and a high-resolution (2 mm spatial resolution) aperture field. We investigate the effects of anisotropic surface roughness, shearing displacement, and closure ratio on flow channeling in a radial flow system using advective Lagrangian particle tracking and advection–dispersion numerical simulations. Results show a transition from local microscale channeling effects to a homogenous flow pattern at the field-scale within rough-walled fractures. The transition is enhanced by the increasing microscale channels which occur via surface roughness anisotropy. Surface shearing displacement and anisotropic surface roughness control the fracture closure area and principal orientations, aligning with the tortuosity and direction of preferential flow pathways. The solute peak arrival times in synthetic fractures are similar to those in smooth fractures with an equivalent Cubic Law aperture. This demonstrates the applicability of the Cubic Law aperture in predicting bulk arrival times, even in the presence of flow channeling within sheared synthetic fractures. The strong flow channeling behavior observed in some field studies is therefore likely related to local geological conditions (stress included) and post-fracturing processes, underscoring the need to integrate initial fracturing and subsequent weathering history obtained using rock sample properties and outcrop analysis when investigating channeling effects.

title: Simulation of pollutant transport and identification of longitudinal dispersion coefficient in vegetated channels based on a vegetation-constrained physics-informed neural network
Progressive scale convolutional network for spatio-temporal downscaling of soil moisture: A case study over the Tibetan Plateau
abstract: Soil moisture (SM) plays a critical role in hydrological and meteorological processes. High-resolution SM can be obtained by combining coarse passive microwave data with fine-scale auxiliary variables. However, the inversion of SM at the temporal scale is hindered by the incompleteness of surface auxiliary factors. To address this issue, first, we introduce validated high temporal resolution ERA5-Land variables into the downscaling process of the low-resolution SMAP SM product. Subsequently, we design a progressive scale convolutional network (PSCNet), at the core of which are two innovative components: a multi-frequency temporal fusion module (MFTF) for capturing temporal dynamics, and a bespoke squeeze-and-excitation (SE) block designed to preserve fine-grained spatial details. Using this approach, we obtained seamless SM products for the Tibetan Plateau (TP) from 2016 to 2018 at 10-km spatial and 3-hour temporal resolution. The experimental results on the TP demonstrated the following: 1) In the satellite product validation, the PSCNet exhibited comparable accuracy and lower error, with a mean R value of 0.881, outperforming other methods. 2) In the in-situ site validation, PSCNet consistently ranked among the top three models for the R metric across all sites, while also showing superior performance in overall error reduction. 3) In the temporal generalization validation, the feasibility of using high-temporal resolution ERA5-Land variables for downscaling was confirmed, as all methods maintained an average relative error within 6\% for the R metric and 2\% for the ubRMSE metric. 4) In the temporal dynamics and visualization validation, PSCNet demonstrated excellent temporal sensitivity and vivid spatial details. Overall, PSCNet provides a promising solution for spatio-temporal downscaling by effectively modeling the intricate spatio-temporal relationships in SM data.

title: Efficacy of evapotranspiration products on improving streamflow prediction in ungauged catchments under various hydrological models and climates
Reducing dependence on GRACE mascon datasets: bayesian‑TCH fusion for robust groundwater storage anomaly diagnoses in the U‑shaped meander region of the Yellow River basin
abstract: Groundwater storage changes in regions with scarce observations are increasingly being inferred from satellite gravimetry, but different institutional datasets can lead to inconsistent conclusions. Focusing on the U-shaped Meander Region of the Yellow River Basin, we examine how groundwater storage trends depend on the choice of satellite gravimetry datasets and develop a Bayesian three‑cornered hat groundwater storage anomaly (GWSA) fusion framework to alleviate this problem. The proposed fusion framework estimates institution specific noise levels relative to a potential truth and uses them for Bayesian weighted fusion of three institutional datasets. The results show that the five GWSA datasets give different conclusions about groundwater changes when trends are segmented around 2007. The Bayesian-TCH GWSA dataset reduces regional mean uncertainty by about 50–80 % and raises the signal-to-noise ratio above 20 dB. The Bayesian-TCH time series shows a near steady declining trend before 2007 and, afterward, weakened seasonal coherence and a stronger role of human activities. This pattern is more consistent with independent understanding that the region is shifting from mainly climate driven variability to increasing impacts of sustained groundwater pumping and coal mining dewatering, whereas some GWSA datasets show stable recovery before the breakpoint and others still display climate dominated variability after the breakpoint.

title: Distinguishing drought and flash drought: definitions, processes, and consequences
Seasonal hydrochemical variations of a regulated river in the North China Plain: mechanisms and implications for chemical weathering
Wavelet-Kalman-LSTM fusion: enhancing meteorological drought prediction with robust feature selection and uncertainty quantification
abstract: Accurate drought forecasting is essential for minimizing socio-economic and environmental impacts but remains challenging due to climatic variability and complexity of droughts. This study presents the Wavelet-Kalman-LSTM (WKLSTM), a new hybrid deep learning framework that combines wavelet decomposition, Kalman filtering, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), improving multi-timescale drought predictions (SPI3, SPI6, SPI9, SPI12) across various regions of Australia. The WKLSTM addresses non-stationarity by decomposing signals into hierarchical subseries using discrete wavelet transforms, denoising coefficients with Kalman filtering, and utilizing LSTM’s temporal modeling. Advanced feature selection techniques such as Boruta, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), and LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) are integrated with eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) to identify critical lagged predictors. The WKLSTM model is assessed against both standalone and hybrid benchmark models, including LSTM, Feedforward Neural Networks (FNN), attention-based LSTM (attLSTM), Convolutional Neural Network combined with Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (CNN-BiGRU), and WLSTM. The results show that the WKLSTM outperforms by achieving R 2 values from 0.51 to 0.99 and lowered RMSE by 7% to 33% compared to benchmark models. Monte Carlo simulations quantify uncertainty with 95PPU bounds covering 50–81% of observations, indicating that although WKLSTM performs well across various regions and timescales, high predictive uncertainty persists due to the nonlinear and stochastic nature of droughts. The framework integrates noise reduction, dynamic feature selection, and probabilistic forecasting, enhancing drought prediction, aiding water resource management and climate resilience strategies. This study highlights the effectiveness of WKLSTM in addressing climatic non-linearity and offers practical insights into drought mitigation.

title: Reconciling model simulated and GRACE observed groundwater storage changes in Africa through coordinated forward modelling
Effects of the spatial distribution of internal water storage on soil–plant hydraulic function
Identification of extreme socioeconomic droughts considering heavy tailed distribution
Intercomparison of gridded hydroclimate reconstruction datasets in Asia and evaluation of regional hydroclimate changes
Pore evolution and infiltration mechanisms under freezing saline water irrigation: Cross-scale evidence from X-ray CT and stable isotopes
abstract: Freezing saline water irrigation (FSWI) is an important strategy for developing unconventional water resources in cold and arid regions. However, the evolution of soil micropores under freeze–thaw conditions and the mechanisms by which they regulate infiltration remain unclear, limiting precise application. To clarify these processes, this study established a cross-scale framework of “microstructural characterization–macro-scale process tracing–physical mechanism simulation”. A field experiment was conducted with an irrigation gradient of 0–270 mm, and X-ray CT, stable isotopes, and interpretable machine learning (XGBoost–SHAP) were jointly applied to resolve the “structure–process–function” linkage. The results showed a nonlinear threshold in structural improvement: 180 mm was identified as the optimal critical point, forming during the thawing period a transport skeleton with the highest connectivity and the lowest tortuosity. Isotope data consistently supported this finding, demonstrating efficient displacement of deep soil water. Attribution analysis further proposed criteria for functional enhancement (tortuosity < 2.5 and global connectivity > 0.5), confirming that pore-topology quality plays a much stronger role in water-conducting function than pore quantity. These findings provide a scientific basis for the efficient and safe use of unconventional water resources and offer important guidance for alleviating agricultural water supply–demand conflicts in cold and arid regions.

title: Calibrated uncertainty for continental design flood estimation using conformal probabilistic machine learning
Impact of sand mining on groundwater-surface water interactions in the Vietnamese Mekong Delta
Assessing the impact of process simulation order in hydrological modeling
A self-reinforcing feedback loop exacerbates groundwater depletion in semiarid aquifers
abstract: Groundwater depletion is a growing concern in semiarid regions, where aquifer sustainability is increasingly threatened by intensive irrigation. This study investigates the hydrological impacts of depletion on groundwater recharge processes. A multi-faceted approach combining long-term groundwater level analysis, remote sensing-based irrigation water requirements, drought indices, and isotopes (δ18O, 3H) was applied to an alluvial aquifer in central Morocco. Results show a marked acceleration of groundwater depletion post-2000, with decline rates reaching up to 5.8 m/yr in certain sectors, amid expanding irrigation water requirements and droughts. Tritium data reveal a significant reduction in modern recharge in depleted areas where groundwater depths have declined below 50 m, suggesting reduced aquifer renewal. Concurrently, the δ18O values show a transition in the recharge origin from low-altitude local precipitation to high-altitude mountain-derived sources in more depleted zones. A three-component isotopic mixing model confirms that depletion leads to vertical stratification in renewal times and recharge sources, with deeper groundwater that is extensively exploited for irrigation exhibiting older, higher-altitude signatures. The findings indicate that the large thickening of the unsaturated zone, driven by depletion-induced groundwater decline, leads to diminished recharge, creating a reinforcing feedback loop that exacerbates groundwater depletion and complicates aquifer recovery. The results presented here affirm that continued groundwater over-abstraction not only diminishes aquifer storage but also undermines aquifer renewability. Mitigating this unsustainable cycle necessitates immediate interventions to reduce groundwater withdrawals and enhance recharge. Groundwater should be managed as a strategic resource for both human and environmental needs, against climate change impacts, and as a legacy to future generations.

title: A multi-catchment evaluation of hydrological model transferability and ensemble averaging under contrasting hydroclimatic conditions in Iran
abstract: Robust hydrological projections under climate change depend on model performance under conditions outside those used for calibration. This study presents a large-sample evaluation across 37 Iranian catchments to evaluate the transferability of six hydrological models using Differential Split-Sample Testing (DSST). Four ensemble-averaging approaches were also evaluated to determine whether under contrasting hydroclimatic conditions. DSST experiments were based on non-sequential 2–3-year periods selected according to (i) annual wettest and driest years and (ii) contrasting seasonal precipitation regimes. Model transferability varied substantially with the transfer setting, catchment attributes, and performance criterion. Ensemble averaging generally outperformed most individual models, although performance depended on the averaging method. Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA) and Granger-Ramanathan Averaging (GRA) consistently outperformed the Simple Arithmetic Mean (SAM) and Akaike Information Criterion Averaging (AICA). Based on the Nah-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) metric, GRA exceeded the performance of the best individual model in 50–87% of transfer cases. This study provides a coordinated DSST-based evaluation of conceptual rainfall-runoff models and ensemble-averaging approaches across a large set of Iranian catchments. The results demonstrate how these established methods can be combined into a practical framework for climate-impact assessment in semi-arid, strongly seasonal regions. Based on this large-sample Iranian case study, we recommend DSST-based evaluation using climatically relevant analogues, multiple performance metrics, and advanced ensemble-averaging methods. Among the evaluated approaches, GRA emerged as the most practical compromise between predictive performance and computational efficiency. However, the relative ranking of models and averaging methods may differ under other climatic, hydrological, or data conditions

title: Flood frequency analysis combining observed streamflows with simulations from a continental hydrological model
abstract: Despite considerable effort to improve flood frequency analysis (FFA) models, FFA remains a highly uncertain endeavour for sites with limited streamflow records. This paper introduces the Covariate-based Flood Frequency Inference (CoFFI), where a censored bivariate flood probability distribution is fitted jointly to two annual maximum series, one from a short available observation record and the other from a long simulation generated by a continental hydrological model. CoFFI combines two General Extreme Value (GEV) marginals and a Gumbel-Hougaard copula, with all parameters estimated within a Bayesian inference scheme. The method is applied to 39 stations across Australia with observation records exceeding 70 years in length. Performance is assessed by applying both CoFFI and a univariate model to 10 years of randomly selected observed data, and comparing the results against a reference distribution fitted to all observed data. CoFFI is found to reduce the discrepancy against the reference by 10% compared to the univariate model. CoFFI performance is equivalent to that of the univariate model using 20 years of data, hence doubling the equivalent record length. CoFFI yields its maximum benefit when observed record lengths range from 5 to 30 years, with equivalent record lengths of 10 to 15 years longer than those of the univariate model. Finally, a simple criterion is developed to anticipate performance gains from CoFFI in a particular catchment. The criterion is based on the Kendall-Tau correlation coefficient between observed and simulated annual maximums. CoFFI is likely to outperform a univariate model when this coefficient exceeds 0.5.

title: Tracing water use sources in rubber monoculture and rubber-Alpinia oxyphylla agroforestry systems using hydrogen and oxygen isotopes
Mapping the past: identifying analog precipitation years with reference rainfall metrics
abstract: Stormwater control measures (SCMs) are important for urban climate adaptation and mitigation strategies. Current design approaches use historical rainfall estimates to determine the design case; however these historical rainfall records do not adequately capture the observed nonstationarity resulting from climate change. While there are climate change projections, these have not easily or consistently been brought into practice. There is an opportunity to simulate climate change impacts analytically through analogous observations of other climate regions or past observations, as well as provide a method to express hydrologic observations and model predictions. This study aims to identify past years of rainfall in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA that are analogous to projected precipitation under various climate change scenarios (three socioeconomic pathways projecting three future 25-year periods). Analogous rainfall years were identified using a novel metric that has previously been used to identify reference years of rainfall The analogous years and future projections both indicate the same precipitation risks in the form of larger, extreme events (approximately 10 mm of additional rainfall for the region’s 2-year, 24-hour event on average and preferential selection of the wettest years on record with climate change intensification). However, future temperature projections remain unprecedented in comparison to observations from the analogous precipitation years, where climate change projections consistently indicate a + 2–6 °C anomaly in monthly maximum air temperature from the baseline of 1950–2000 but the analogous years show little to no difference. In all, this work provides the two-fold outcome of a practical means for communicating the risks of climate change with recallable observations, and the potential to indicate observations that could be used in hydrological simulations to model the risks of climate change to water resources systems.

title: Assessment of Sentinel-1 C-band SAR snow depth assimilation in operational hydrological modeling of high-alpine catchments
abstract: Monitoring and forecasting mountainous runoff is essential, as snowmelt provides vital freshwater resources while also posing flood and drought risks to downstream regions. However, spatiotemporal modeling of the high-alpine snowpack remains challenging, due to shortcomings in their process-based descriptions and substantial deficits in input data of operational hydrological models. To address this issue, we evaluate the potential of assimilating 500~m resolution Sentinel-1 C-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) snow depth retrievals in operational hydrological modeling of several high-alpine catchments in Austria.We first evaluated the Sentinel-1 snow depth product with ground-based measurements from 27 AWS (automatic weather stations) in Austria (r=0.88, MAE=20\,cm) and annual photogrammetric snow depth surveys in the Dischma catchment in Switzerland (r=0.72, MAE=69\,cm).We then force the conceptual semi-distributed hydrological model COSERO with the 1 km$^2$ gridded meteorological INCA product, which are both operationally used for hydropower and flood forecasting, and model thirteen high-alpine catchments in Austria between 2016 and 2024 at 500\,m spatial and hourly temporal resolution.The assimilation of Sentinel-1 snow depths substantially improved overall model performance relative to modeling with uncorrected INCA data, indicated by a median increase of NSE by 8.3\% (0.77 to 0.84) and KGE by 41.9\% (0.61 to 0.86), and a reduction of the median runoff deficit from -25.5\% to -3.3\%. The data assimilation in the operational modeling setup proved more effective during snow-poor years, a finding that may become more relevant under an increasingly warming climate in the European Alps.The Sentinel-1 snow depth product showed good agreement with ground measurements and snow cover maps (MODIS). Its assimilation remedied the winter precipitation deficit in INCA, with on average 10\% runoff bias reduction per 1000\,m elevation gain in the study orography, while improving spatiotemporal snowpack simulation and enhancing snowmelt runoff prediction. This more realistic representation of the mountainous snowpack may benefit simulation of other hydrological variables including evapotranspiration, soil moisture, and groundwater recharge. The approach also shows promise for modeling remote, ungauged basins globally. These results demonstrate the value of integrating satellite-derived snow information for operational alpine hydrological modeling and water resource assessment.

Assessment and attribution of predictive hydrologic uncertainty in operational short-to-medium range ensemble streamflow forecasting
abstract: We assess the predictive hydrologic uncertainty in short-to-medium range (<Day 14) ensemble streamflow forecasting via 20-yr hindcast experiments for 398 headwater locations in the service areas of the 13 River Forecast Centers in the US. The assessment is based on the continuous ranked probability skill score (CRPSS) of ensemble streamflow prediction under clairvoyant future input forcings in reference to climatological ensemble streamflow forecast. The magnitude of hydrologic uncertainty is assessed in the CRPSS space relative to the total uncertainty represented by climatological ensemble streamflow forecast. Hydrologic uncertainty is attributed to selected uncertainty sources by isolating the lead time-dependent initial condition (IC) uncertainty via state updating. The limits of predictive skill under the current state of operational hydrologic modeling are assessed via the CRPSS of perfectly reliable ensemble streamflow predictions with and without state updating. The results show that there is large room for improvement in forecast skill from reducing hydrologic uncertainty. Significant unresolved hydrologic uncertainty exists for almost all locations for prediction of high flows. For prediction of all ranges of flow, unresolved hydrologic uncertainty is larger in the CRPSS space than the uncertainty resolved by hydrologic modeling and clairvoyant future forcings for most locations. The IC uncertainty at saturation is very significant and accounts for almost half of the unresolved hydrologic uncertainty on average. Isolation of the IC uncertainty indicates that many locations will likely benefit significantly from additional calibration of hydrologic models and fully utilizing the hydrologic memory via high-frequency state updating.

A novel framework for Identifying and predicting stratified land deformation: a case study of the Beijing Plain
abstract: Regional land subsidence research has advanced rapidly in recent decades, and integrating InSAR with machine learning has become an important research direction. However, InSAR-derived surface deformation reflects only total deformation and cannot resolve deformation within soil layers at different depths. To address this limitation, we propose a framework that integrates SAR data, stratified deformation ratios from extensometers, and hydrogeological information. By combining Persistent Scatterer Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (PS-InSAR), K-Means clustering, and a Spike-Transformer model, the framework identifies characteristic subsidence zones, estimates stratified deformation, and predicts stratified deformation with high accuracy. Taking the Beijing Plain as a case study, land subsidence is mainly controlled by the second (25.8%) and third (69.79%) compressible layer groups, with maximum subsidence rates of 61 and 83 mm/yr, respectively. Vertically, owing to the spatial heterogeneity of factors such as groundwater-level changes and the lithologic composition of the compressible strata, the dominant subsidence layer varies across the plain: the third compressible layer group dominates in the northeastern plain (Zone 1) and southeastern plain (Zones 4–5), whereas the second compressible layer group dominates in the northwestern plain (Zone 2) and central plain (Zone 3). In addition, the zonal and stratified predictions of the Spike-Transformer model capture variations in deformation rates across different compressible layer groups, with a maximum RMSE of 3.12 mm and MAE of 2.47 mm. This framework provides a transferable approach for zone-specific and stratified management of land subsidence, with important implications for refined subsidence prevention and control.

Enhancing water management in data-scarce watersheds using satellite and reanalysis precipitation: a combined SWAT+ and SMOGN machine learning approach

Enhanced identification of watershed hydrological extremes using an improved drought index incorporating hydrological non-stationarity
Hydrological controls on antibiotics and mixture risks in upland and lowland rivers: a dual-tracer study combining antibiotics and DOM optical properties
abstract: Understanding how antibiotics behave in upland and lowland rivers draining mixed urban-agricultural catchments is essential for hydrology-driven water quality management. We investigated 48 antibiotics and dissolved organic matter (DOM) optical properties at 49 sites along 12 rivers spanning upland headwaters influenced by urban land use and lowland reaches draining predominantly agricultural plains during dry (low-flow) and wet (high-flow) seasons. By combining antibiotic profiles with DOM fluorescence and absorbance indices, including PARAFAC components, we applied a dual-tracer framework that uses antibiotics together with DOM optical properties to interpret spatial and seasonal patterns under contrasting hydrological and land-use settings. Upland rivers subject to urban point sources showed pronounced dry-season antibiotic concentration peaks, consistent with wastewater-dominated inputs under limited dilution. In contrast, lowland rivers draining intensively cultivated areas exhibited the highest cumulative mixture-level ecological risks, driven by cocktails of antibiotics transported from both urban and agricultural sources. Protein-like DOM signals were associated with human-use antibiotics in urban-influenced upland reaches, whereas humic-like components aligned with veterinary antibiotic dominance in agricultural lowlands, indicating stronger runoff contributions during wet conditions. Overall, our results show that flow regime and land use jointly control the redistribution of antibiotic concentrations and mixture risks across multiple rivers, and demonstrate the value of a dual-tracer approach that combines antibiotics with DOM optical properties to diagnose point- and diffuse-source contributions in mixed-use river catchments.

Impact of floods on surface water quality: a systematic review and comprehensive assessment
abstract: Floods, as extreme flow events, are among the costliest and devastating natural hazards. Among the various domains impacted by flooding, environmental degradation, particularly the deterioration of water quality (WQ), is one of the most impacted yet often overlooked. Therefore, it is essential to understand the nature and source of water pollution associated with flooding. This study aims to evaluate and assess multiple studies conducted globally to determine the impact of floods on WQ. A literature review and assessment of 66 studies published between 2007 and 2026 was conducted using the total comprehensiveness score (TCS). To support the scoring process, studies that scored more than 70% of the maximum achievable TCS (15.4) are considered the most detailed and comprehensive in addressing the objectives of this review. 16 studies achieved a TCS above 15.4, indicating that a limited number of studies incorporate a broader set of factors in this domain. A higher number of studies were conducted post the year 2021, highlighting both scientific progress and a growing focus on WQ impacts from disasters such as floods, beyond the traditionally emphasized socio-economic loss. Among the shortlisted studies, fluvial floods are the most frequently examined, followed by pluvial floods and coastal floods. During fluvial floods, turbidity increased by up to two orders of magnitude, while nutrient concentrations (TN, TP) typically rose by ∼ 10–30%. In contrast, pluvial floods were characterised by dilution-driven decreases in EC and TDS, with DOX, BOD and COD showing variable responses across flood types. This review evaluates flood impacts on WQ, catchment characteristics, and sources of WQ modification. The findings of the research reveal that not all WQ parameters are responsible for WQ degradation during every flood event. Rather, it is a combination of certain parameters that leads to deteriorated WQ. WQ degradation depends on interacting factors such as flood duration, extent, depth, and flow dynamics. In overall, this study provides an overview of the multiple cascading impacts of floods on WQ, along with a detailed perspective on the set of criteria that should be considered in future research.

title: Inter-reservoir benefit compensation for water-sediment regulation in the Yellow River Basin: From status quo to multi-functional synergy
On nonlinear thermal dispersion and interfacial heat exchange in the filled fracture-matrix systems near the wellbore
A general two-dimensional analytical solution for solute transport in anisotropic porous media with time-varying velocity field, different contaminant sources, and initial contamination
abstract: This study presents a novel two-dimensional analytical solution for solute transport in homogeneous porous media accounting for the effects of anisotropy in presence of adsorption and decay. The solution is derived using Green’s function for an infinite domain and extends existing analytical formulations by relaxing several simplifying assumptions commonly adopted in literature. In particular, the proposed analytical solution accounts for the effects of mechanical dispersion along the non-principal direction of groundwater flow as well as for the dependency of the dispersion tensor on the actual groundwater velocity field, without simplifications or convenient orientations of the model domain. The solution is also general as allows to account for: i) bi-directional groundwater velocity field and its variation over time; ii) source terms of different geometries (e.g., point, line, and surface sources) and temporal variability; iii) general initial concentration distributions of the contaminant concentration. The proposed analytical solution is also tested over benchmark problems conceived with a well-known numerical model for flow and transport in porous media (COMSOL Multiphysics®), and the agreement between the two is excellent.
