Investigating catchment predictors of the fraction of young water variability in streamflow in mesoscale Precambrian Shield catchments in Northeastern Ontario, Canada
abstract: Understanding how catchments respond to precipitation under rapidly changing climate and land-uses, is key to long-term management of water resources, including in the understudied northeastern Ontario Canadian shield landscape. However, there is limited knowledge of streamflow generation processes in Precambrian Shield catchments beyond headwater catchments. We estimated the streamflow fraction of young water (Fyw) and damping ratios (DR) in the Sturgeon River-Lake Nipissing-French River (SNF) Basin in northeastern Ontario, Canada using five years of modelled precipitation isotope (δ18O) and 3 to 5 years of streamflow isotope (δ18O) records from sixteen catchments that ranged in size from 27 km² to 6,919 km². The Fyw varied between 16 % and 66 %, with no significant difference between unweighted (Fyw) and flow-weighted (Fyw*) estimates (r = 0.99, p < 0.001). Using Pearson correlation and hierarchical partitioning regression (HP), 70.1 % of total variance in Fyw was predicted by five landscape indices. Median topographic wetness index (TWI), fen + marsh area, and mixedwood forest areas were positively correlated with Fyw, while Fyw decreased with increasing area of lake and high runoff potential soil. The median TWI (slope and catchment area dependent) and percent area of fen + marsh were identified as statistically significant Fyw predictors across the basin, while lake area, mixedwood forest area, and high runoff potential soil were less important variables because they co-varied with the other statistically significantly independent variables (TWI and fen+marsh area). This study highlights how wetlands can play different hydrological roles (water storage versus conveyance) at new hydrological information at a scale (mesoscale) and landscape (Precambrian shield) that are underrepresented and yet critical for regional water management.

title: Two new analytical models for constant rate pumping test in double-porosity multilayered confined systems: New Robin flow equation for aquitards
abstract: Accurate numerical solutions to aquitard flow equations derived based on an infinitesimal cubic require fine spatial discretization in aquitards. This study applies the divergence theorem of Gauss to derive a new Robin flow equation based on a finite-thickness element enabling no discretization in aquitards. Two analytical models are built for constant rate pumping test in a double-porosity three-layer confined system of two aquifers and one aquitard in between. One model applies the new Robin flow equation while the other applies a traditional aquitard flow equation. The semi-analytical solutions of the models are derived. The finite element solutions are also derived. Results suggest the new Robin flow equation is applicable within 5 % relative error in predicting drawdowns when quantitative conditions are met. The new Robin flow equation reduces to a new double-porosity lagging Robin boundary condition, and a typical Robin boundary condition in groundwater textbooks. Temporal aquifer drawdown can be triple-humped distribution with three flats due to the storage effects of the matrices in aquifers and aquitard. The finite element solution with the traditional aquitard flow equation can be accurate but requires about 10 6 nodes to discretize the aquifers and aquitard. The accurate finite element solution incorporating the new Robin flow equation requires only 2 , 002 nodes representing coarse square discretization in the aquifers and no discretization in the aquitard and takes 1 / 1503 of the computing time of obtaining the other accurate finite element solution with the traditional aquitard flow equation. The present solution applies to a field constant rate pumping test.

title: Decoupling geogenic and anthropogenic drivers of groundwater natural background levels using machine learning and high-resolution maps
Enhanced data-based analysis introducing a previously unidentified empirical hydrological benchmark: baseflow dominance threshold
Hindcasting compound coastal-inland flood events caused by post-tropical storms
abstract: • Hindcasting framework reconstructs compound flooding during Hurricanes Fiona and Dorian in PEI. • Integrates observed rainfall and High-Water Marks into HEC-RAS 2D simulations. • Fiona caused greater flooding in eastern PEI, whereas Dorian dominated the northwest. • HRDEM breaching identified over twice as many hydraulic structures, improving hydraulic connectivity. This study presents a hindcasting framework for reconstructing compound coastal-inland flooding in Prince Edward Island (PEI) during post-tropical storms Fiona (2022) and Dorian (2019). Using observed rainfall and high-water marks (HWMs), with a high-resolution terrain model enhanced with hydro-infrastructure, we simulated flood extents at municipal and island-wide scales using HEC-RAS 2D. The hindcasting results show spatially varying impacts across the island, with Fiona producing greater inundation in eastern PEI and Dorian in the northwest. Fiona’s flood extent exceeded Dorian’s by up to 7.32% in parts of Kings County, while Dorian produced more than twice the inundation of Fiona in portions of Prince County (9.94%). This study advances previous PEI flood modeling efforts by explicitly integrating observed coastal HWMs with inland hydrological forcing within a unified 2D hydrodynamic framework, enabling more accurate reconstruction of compound flooding processes. The HRDEM breaching approach further improved hydraulic connectivity by identifying 2,895 hydraulic structures, more than twice the number contained in the official inventory, thereby enhancing island-scale flood routing. This hindcasting framework demonstrates the value of integrated coastal and inland data for accurately reproducing real flood events and supports future climate adaptation planning in storm-prone regions.

A decision-theoretic framework for probabilistic flood warnings
abstract: Early warning systems for weather-related hazards are critical tools for increasing societal resilience, but their effectiveness depends on reliability and ability to support decision-making in the face of uncertainty. While many operational contexts rely on expert judgment and predefined warning thresholds, decision-making processes rarely incorporate a formal assessment of the operational and economic impacts associated with the chosen actions. This study proposes a decision-theoretic approach for issuing flood warnings in Italy’s Sieve basin (Tuscany), integrating probabilistic precipitation forecasts from the national Civil Protection system with a statistical post-processing method to explicitly evaluate predictive uncertainty. The proposed framework introduces a loss function that adapts to multiple warning levels and accommodates different risk propensities (from risk-averse to risk-prone), effectively meeting the operational needs of diverse stakeholders. The system’s performance is evaluated by comparing a Bayesian decision scheme with one that explicitly accounts for precipitation forecast uncertainty, assessing cumulative economic costs against different baseline scenarios. Results demonstrate that adopting a Bayesian cost-based approach yields economic benefits and substantial improvements in the Relative Economic Value (REV). Furthermore, incorporating precipitation uncertainty drives the system toward more cost-effective warning strategies, reducing false alarms and expected losses.

Mapping temperate groundwater-dependent terrestrial ecosystems in Denmark
abstract: Groundwater-dependent Ecosystems (GDEs) are critical biodiversity hotspots and drought refugia that are driven by complex groundwater and ecological interactions. The detection of GDEs in temperate regions remains challenging due to weak phenological contrasts with surrounding vegetation. We developed a Positive-Unlabeled (PU) machine learning framework to detect temperate GDEs in Denmark using minimal input variables: two Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) variables derived from Sentinel-2 imagery, and Height Above Nearest Drainage. The approach exploits two NDVI signals: the drought-resilience of GDEs during dry summers (dry-season analogue), and their delayed spring green-up caused by waterlogged soils. Our model achieved 79% detection of field-mapped GDEs within Danish NATURA 2000 areas while identifying 7 times more potential GDE area (122.500 ha) and finds further 222.000 ha of GDEs in river valleys outside the monitored NATURA 2000 areas. Plausibility analysis using a Water table depth (WTD) dataset, and tree species dataset showed good agreement between labeled and predicted GDEs. Sensitivity analysis across different model parameterizations revealed predicted GDE coverage ranging from 22% to 65% of the study area, with true positive rates of 45% to 93%. The framework addresses key limitations in GDE mapping by requiring only positive training labels and few input variables. The model performs comparably to dryland GDE detection methods while operating without explicit dry season dynamics. These results establish a baseline for temperate GDE detection across regions, supporting land- and water-resources management, and compliance with environmental directives requiring GDE identification.

Identification of spatiotemporal sensitivity of karst spring discharge to precipitation and evaporation: an LSTM–Transformer Decoder framework
abstract: Karst hydrological processes are driven by seasonal precipitation and evaporation and modulated by anthropogenic activities within highly heterogeneous aquifers. These processes produce spatiotemporally differentiated and magnitude-dependent responses that remain difficult to simulate and interpret. This study develops an LSTM-Transformer Decoders (LSTM-TDs) framework that links discharge-difference prediction with attention-based hydroclimatic sensitivity identification. To characterize discharge-change dynamics, the LSTM encodes historical first-order discharge differences into a discharge-change state, which then serves as the query for two spatiotemporal Transformer Decoder pathways separately attending to precipitation and evaporation inputs. The resulting attention structures are used to identify meteorological relevance across space, lag, and forcing magnitude. Applied to the Niangziguan Springs in North China, LSTM-TDs outperformed the evaluated benchmark models, with NSE = 0.85, RMSE = 0.34 m³/s, MAE = 0.26 m³/s, and MAPE = 3.88%. Relative to the non-differenced version, the discharge-difference design increased testing NSE from 0.79 to 0.85 and reduced MAPE by 19.8%. Attention-based sensitivity identification showed hydrologically plausible spatial and temporal patterns. Precipitation relevance was mainly concentrated in the main recharge–runoff area with relatively high groundwater levels, evaporation relevance was stronger in soil-moisture-rich areas, and dominant lags were consistent with cross-correlation-derived response times. The model-derived sensitivity turning points were approximately 42.0 mm for precipitation and 130.2 mm for evaporation, and their spatial variations were consistent with differences in infiltration partitioning, terrain-controlled redistribution, and aquifer storage conditions. These results indicate that the LSTM-TDs framework can support spring discharge prediction while providing interpretable diagnostics of hydroclimatic sensitivity in karst systems.

title: Numerical modeling of redox-sensitive transformations in a dynamic capillary fringe
Coupled shallow-water hydrodynamics and reactive transport of emerging contaminants in unsteady flows
abstract: Emerging contaminants (ECs) pose persistent risks to aquatic ecosystems, yet their transport and fate in dynamic surface-water systems remain difficult to quantify because of trace concentrations and costly measurements. Existing shallow-water transport models often treat ECs as passive tracers or adopt simplified first-order decay formulations, limiting their ability to represent the integrated effects of hydrodynamic transport and physicochemical/biochemical reactions. To address this gap, this study develops one-dimensional (1D) and two-dimensional (2D) shallow-water reactive transport models for simulating the transport and fate of ECs in transient free-surface flows. The proposed framework integrates key EC-specific processes, including biodegradation, hydrolysis, photolysis, volatilization, bioconcentration/depuration, and sorption/desorption, within an advection–dispersion-reaction formulation coupled to shallow-water hydrodynamics. The models are first verified against reference solutions and then applied to a real flood event in the Ebro River using a hypothetical antibiotic release scenario. Results show that release timing strongly controls EC exposure patterns: for identical source loads, peak-flow releases produced lower concentration maxima because of stronger dilution and faster plume spreading, whereas recession-flow releases led to more persistent detectable concentrations. The 2D simulation also reveals flood-driven lateral transport from the main channel into inundated agricultural areas, highlighting the role of floodplain connectivity in shaping EC exposure under extreme events. To support high-resolution 2D applications, the model has been implemented on graphics processing units (GPUs), which reproduces the CPU results with significant computational saving. Overall, the study provides a computationally robust, efficient, and physically based framework for integrated simulation of EC transport and fate in dynamic shallow-water systems.

title: Global changes in precipitable water vapour during 1980–2100 and its spatial, temporal, radiative and causal insights for enhanced climate warming

Groundwater flow regimes and intrinsic vulnerability in a fractured bedrock aquifer: insights from hydrochemistry, isotopes, geophysics, and groundwater age
abstract: Intrinsic vulnerability in fractured bedrock aquifers is commonly evaluated using index-based approaches, yet these methods often underestimate the role of flow system architecture, recharge mechanisms, and groundwater renewal in controlling contaminant susceptibility. In structurally complex aquifers, vulnerability patterns are strongly controlled by heterogeneous flow paths and residence time distributions, which are not adequately represented by static approaches. This study integrates hydrochemistry, environmental isotopes (δ 18 O, δ 2 H, 87 Sr/ 86 Sr), tritium-based groundwater age modeling, multivariate statistical analysis, and geophysical investigations to constrain groundwater flow systems in a fractured bedrock aquifer in the Boeun region, Korea. Integration of these independent datasets reveals three distinct groundwater flow regimes: (i) a laterally dominated shallow system with strong surface connectivity, (ii) a vertically stratified mountain front recharge system with fracture-controlled deep circulation, and (iii) a rapidly renewed shallow system characterized by short residence times and diffuse recharge. The identified flow regimes provide a processed-based framework for interpreting intrinsic vulnerability. Despite groundwater quality index values indicating excellent water quality at present, DRASTIC results show moderate to high vulnerability associated with rapid recharge and structurally connected flow paths. This contrast demonstrates that intrinsic vulnerability is primarily controlled by recharge processes, groundwater flow systems, and renewal dynamics, rather than by static hydrogeological parameters alone. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating groundwater renewal dynamics, residence time structure, and flow system heterogeneity into vulnerability assessments of fractured aquifers

title: Improving reference evapotranspiration estimation by attention-enhanced autoencoders and hybrid neural networks under noisy chaotic conditions
abstract: The present study established a climate-adaptive Multi-Layer Perceptron-Self Attention (MLP-SA) framework for robust estimation of reference evapotranspiration (ET o ) under noise-distorted conditions under different climatic conditions. The proposed model redefined noise-resilient ET o estimation through a climate-physics-informed two-stage architecture design: i) a denoising autoencoder (DAE) that first purifies noisy input data (meteorological variables, e.g. air temperature) by convolutional encoding–decoding, and ii) an MLP enhanced with a climate-adaptive self-attention mechanism, which dynamically recalibrated feature importance based on climate-specific physics. The proposed methodology was evaluated by using data from humid (north) and arid (south) regions. Despite statistical-based evaluation, the process-based hydrological analysis, as well as time persistence and hydrologically-significant error assessments, revealed the superiority of the proposed model under both climatic conditions. In the humid region, the model demonstrated a promising goodness-of-fit (R 2 = 0.951; RMSE = 0.064 mm/day and MAE = 0.047 mm/day at 20% noise) by highlighting its dominance in suppressing high-frequency artifacts, outperforming hybrid models by more than 17% of R 2 . In the arid region, it provided optimal Lyapunov stability (λ = 0.531 at 40% noise, capturing 90.5% of observed chaotic dynamics), despite nonlinear degradation (ΔR 2 = 0.108 from 0% to 40% noise). Climate-based assessment revealed that the humidity reduced feature interaction nonlinearity with lower SHAP distortion in the humid (|ΔSHAP|=0.151) compared to the arid (|ΔSHAP|=0.450) region. Furthermore, the attention mechanisms dynamically prioritized radiation-dominated hierarchies in the humid region (weight: 0.639), while multi-factorial weight assignment was detected in the arid region (R s : 0.291, W s : 0.290, RH: 0.263). The pure-attention architectures failed catastrophically (λ deficits exceeding 25%) due to inadequate chaos management. Further chaos-based assessment via the correlation dimension, phase reconstruction, and recurrence quantification analyses confirmed the promising ability of the proposed model in estimating ET o under different climatic conditions and noise levels.

title: Precipitation water conversion rate variations and driving mechanisms in the Yangtze-Huang-Huai-Hai river basin over the past 60 years
abstract: Precipitation water conversion rate (PWCR) is a key indicator of the efficiency with which atmospheric vertically integrated water vapor content (IWV) is converted into precipitation. This study investigates the long-term variations and driving mechanisms of PWCR in the Yangtze-Huanghe-Huaihe-Haihe River (YHHH) basin, China, from 1956 to 2024. The results show that PWCR decreased significantly at a rate of −1.19%·dec −1 , while IWV increased by 2.83 mm·dec −1 and precipitation decreased by −18.95 mm·dec −1 . These opposite trends indicate that increasing atmospheric moisture did not translate into enhanced precipitation conversion. Seasonal analysis further reveals distinct mechanisms in summer and winter. In summer, PWCR is mainly controlled by precipitation changes jointly regulated by relative humidity (RH) and temperature. Higher RH favors precipitation formation, whereas warming may reduce conversion efficiency by increasing atmospheric moisture-holding capacity. In winter, PWCR is primarily governed by RH-mediated precipitation processes. Overall, the decline in PWCR reflects a weakening efficiency of atmospheric water vapor conversion under a warming and drying background. These findings improve understanding of water vapor–precipitation transformation in large monsoon-influenced basins and provide useful evidence for hydrological modeling and climate adaptation.

Eutrophication reshapes lake-size scaling and amplifies the dominance of large lakes in regional CO2 and CH4 emissions across eastern China
abstract: Accurate estimation of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) and methane (CH 4 ) emissions from lakes is essential for refining the global carbon budget and understanding climatic feedback from inland waters. Previous lake carbon-flux estimates have often relied on field datasets dominated by small lakes, which exhibit high areal emission rates but may underestimate the contribution of large lakes. Satellite remote sensing offers an opportunity for spatially continuous monitoring of large and heterogeneous lake systems, yet robust methods for concurrently estimating CO 2 and CH 4 fluxes remain limited. Here, we developed polynomial regression models using Sentinel-3 satellite data to quantify dissolved CO 2 and CH 4 concentrations and their diffusive fluxes across 113 meso- to eutrophic lakes larger than 10 km 2 in eastern China (R 2 : 0.50–0.78). By synthesizing multi-year midday observations under cloud-free conditions, we found that eutrophication reshaped conventional lake-size scaling of carbon emissions. Within the studied size range, smaller, highly productive lakes frequently acted as CO 2 sinks, whereas larger lakes remained important CO 2 sources. Nonetheless, the studied lakes acted regionally as net carbon sources because CH 4 emissions offset the CO 2 uptake in CO 2 -equivalent units. Large lakes (>100 km 2 ), representing only 23% of lake number but 85% of total surface area, contributed 92% of regional CO 2 -equivalent diffusive efflux. These results suggest that eutrophication can fundamentally alter conventional lake-size scaling and should be explicitly considered in regional carbon upscaling. This study demonstrates the potential of satellite-based approaches for improving spatially explicit assessments of global carbon budgets, while emphasizing the need for broader validation and improved temporal representativeness.

title: Physics-informed machine learning of hyporheic exchange driven by channel blockage and riverbed morphodynamics

Characterizing water quality responses to connectivity frequency and flow magnitude in a regulated river–lake system
abstract: The construction of large-scale hydraulic projects has disrupted hydrological connectivity between rivers and lakes, directly affecting water quality and posing profound risks to water security. However, the quantitative understanding of how different modes of connectivity affect water quality in the sluice-controlled river network area remains limited. In this paper, we proposed a novel scenario-based framework to assess the water quality responses to connectivity from the dual perspectives of temporal frequency and flow magnitude, which is regulated by hydraulic facilities’ operation. Regional water quality was simulated under a series of connectivity frequency scenarios using connectivity–water quality response formulas. Meanwhile, the water quality of major rivers under varying discharge conditions was evaluated by the hydrodynamic–water quality model. Results indicate that continuous operation of recession and regulating sluices, together with extending the nonflood season operation of pumping stations to 7–41 days, significantly reduces TP, TN, NH3-N, and CODMn concentrations by 1% to 4%. Besides, increasing inflow discharge results in moderate improvements in water quality, with a discharge of 50 m3/s reducing the mean TN concentration by approximately 1.4 mg/L compared with baseline conditions. Maintaining stable low-flow discharge at outflow sluices prevents prolonged stagnation and supports overall nutrient export. These findings demonstrate that water quality changes in regulated river–lake networks are jointly governed by connectivity timing and flow intensity, providing an analytical framework for adaptive water management in urbanized plain river networks.

AIFL: A global daily streamflow forecasting model using deterministic an LSTM pre-trained on ERA5-Land and fine-tuned on IFS
abstract: Reliable global streamflow forecasting is essential for flood preparedness and water resource management, yet data-driven models often suffer from a performance gap when transitioning from historical reanalysis to operational forecast products. This paper introduces AIFL (Artificial Intelligence for Floods), a deterministic LSTM-based model designed for global daily streamflow forecasting. Trained on 18,588 basins curated from the Caravan dataset, AIFL utilises a two-stage transfer-learning strategy to bridge the reanalysis-to-forecast domain shift. The model is first pre-trained on 40 years of ERA5-Land reanalysis (1980–2019) to capture robust hydrological processes, then fine-tuned on operational Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) forecasts (2016–2019) to adapt to the specific error structures and biases of operational numerical weather prediction. Ablation experiments confirm that this two-stage approach outperforms both a naive IFS-only baseline and a mixed-forcing single-stage alternative. To our knowledge, this is the first global model trained end-to-end within the Caravan ecosystem. On an independent temporal test set (2021–2024), AIFL achieves high predictive skill with a median modified Kling–Gupta Efficiency ( ) of 0.66 and a median Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) of 0.53. Benchmarking results show that AIFL achieves comparable accuracy to current state-of-the-art global systems. The model provides a streamlined and operationally robust baseline for the global hydrological community.

Introducing IQR–DEMO for precipitation network design optimization
abstract: This study introduces an integrated Information Quality Ratio (IQR) and Dual Entropy Multiobjective Optimization (DEMO) framework for optimizing precipitation network design. In the proposed IQR–DEMO framework, IQR analysis is directly embedded within the DEMO algorithm. Although entropy-based methods such as DEMO effectively maximize information content and minimize redundancy among selected stations, they often overlook spatial imbalances across the basin and generate a large set of non-dominated solutions that can hinder practical decision-making. IQR, which quantifies station redundancy within a network, has been used as a post-design evaluation method, thereby limiting its influence on the optimization itself. To address this gap, the proposed framework incorporates IQR as a spatial penalty during the evolutionary search. For each candidate solution, an IQR analysis is performed, and the resulting values are interpolated over a high-resolution grid. The fraction of the basin falling outside a predefined IQR range is then used to penalize spatially imbalanced configurations through the objectives. This integration guides the algorithm toward network layouts that are both information-rich and spatially representative of the entire basin. The framework is demonstrated using three contrasting case studies, and the results show that the IQR–DEMO generally improves spatial coverage, reduces clustering of stations, and enhances basin-wide information quality. Sensitivity analyses further highlight how variations in the upper IQR threshold and penalty coefficient can influence network spatial coverage. Overall, the proposed approach offers a practical, adaptive, and spatially sensitive tool for designing efficient and spatially representative precipitation monitoring networks

title: Responses of soil physicochemical properties to land preparation measures revealed by fractal parameters of soil particle size distribution: effectiveness and limitations
Hydrogeochemical dynamics of boron associated with groundwater discharge in river and lake basins
Intensifying negative asymmetry in gross primary productivity response to precipitation anomalies across the Northern Hemisphere: evidence and drivers
Wet-season observations of dissolved carbon and CO2–CH4 emissions in inland waters of the Lower Ogooué floodplain (Gabon)
abstract: Floodplain wetlands in tropical river basins play a disproportionate role in carbon cycling, yet their contribution to greenhouse-gas emissions in Central Africa remains poorly constrained. We quantified dissolved carbon, CO 2 and CH 4 concentrations, together with floating-chamber fluxes, across small streams, flooded forests, lakes, and the main channel of the Lower Ogooué River floodplain (Gabon) during two representative wet-season campaigns. Dissolved organic carbon (5–50 mg L −1 ), pCO 2 (1500–16,000 µatm), and dissolved CH 4 showed their highest observed values in small tributaries and flooded forests, whereas the main stem generally exhibited lower values. The highest observed chamber-measured CO 2 fluxes occurred in tributaries, although differences among water body types were not statistically significant. Despite 5–10-fold spatial variability in concentrations, CO 2 fluxes varied by only ∼2-fold among water body types and showed little diel or between-campaign variability. Dissolved oxygen was strongly associated with CO 2 distributions, whereas its relationship with CH 4 was weaker and season-dependent. First-order area-based upscaling suggests that flooded forests and floodplain lakes were the principal contributors to wet-season CO 2 evasion, whereas the main river contributed a smaller share. Limited chamber-based CH 4 flux observations ( n = 5, one campaign) suggest that flooded forests may be methane-emission hotspots, but do not support quantitative floodplain-scale partitioning. Scenario calculations applying wet-season CO 2 emission factors to assumed regional water coverage suggest that aquatic evasion could exceed downstream dissolved-carbon export by several-fold; however, these values represent order-of-magnitude illustrations rather than measured annual budgets. These results highlight the need to explicitly account for floodplain hydrology, wetland extent, and aquatic-landscape heterogeneity when constraining carbon budgets and projecting responses of humid tropical river basins to climate-driven changes in flooding dynamics.

title: Geostatistics-informed latent diffusion for conditional hydrogeological facies simulation under sparse hard-data constraints
Analysis of cross-sectional solute concentration profiles from pulsed point sources in 3D steady flow
Nitrate persistence and inland salinisation in an intensively irrigated Mediterranean river basin district: Diagnostic evidence from WFD monitoring data (Thessaly, central Greece)
abstract: Intensive irrigation in semi-arid Mediterranean basins generates two co-occurring but mechanistically distinct groundwater stressors, nitrate contamination from fertiliser leaching and inland salinisation from ionic enrichment processes, that standard regulatory assessments fail to capture as a linked system. This study develops a probabilistic diagnostic framework and applies it to five years of Water Framework Directive (WFD) compliance monitoring data (2019–2023, 98 stations, 964 samples) from the Thessaly River Basin District, central Greece, one of Europe’s most groundwater-dependent agricultural systems. Multi-year median nitrate exceeded the 50 mg/L WFD threshold at 15.3% of stations and the 25 mg/L Nitrates Directive alert level at 28.6%; annual basin-wide medians remained within a narrow range (12.4–17.9 mg/L), consistent with quasi-steady-state release from legacy vadose zone stores. A bootstrap exceedance analysis (10,000 iterations) identified six stations where the 95% confidence interval for P(NO 3 − > 50 mg/L) exceeded 0.50, three of which were located within officially compliant water bodies. Salinisation was spatially restricted, chloride-dominated (96.5% of high-EC records), and nearly completely decoupled from the nitrate footprint (7.1% co-exceedance). Na/Cl molar ratios and Gibbs diagram positioning indicate that evapoconcentrative and evaporitic processes are dominant salinisation mechanisms; however, ambiguous ionic signatures at a small number of stations preclude the definitive exclusion of relict or deep saline sources without isotopic confirmation. A Shannon entropy-weighted Compound Vulnerability Index and a classification concordance analysis (Cohen’s κ = 0.273) demonstrate that WFD spatial aggregation at the water body level systematically underestimates the active contamination footprint. The framework is reproducible from standard WISE data and can be directly transferred to any river basin district reporting WFD.

title: Climate network-based synchronized structural identification of extreme drought and pluvial events in cross-basin regions
Changing phosphorus dynamics across subtropical river networks in an urban watershed: insights from a 25-year record under a changing climate
How emergent-constrained precipitation projections reshape watershed hydrology?
Disentangling precipitation forcing and parameter uncertainty in a multi-objective surface–subsurface hydrologic modeling framework
A systematic approach to assess fused drone-satellite data for vertical water quality profile estimation in a deep reservoir
Integrated hydrological and economic assessment of hydropower and irrigation development in Sudan under climate change
abstract: Demands for water, energy, and food are rapidly increasing in many low- and middle-income countries, driving the development of large-scale hydropower and irrigation projects. As climate change poses major risks and uncertainties for large-scale infrastructure investments, it is essential to stress-test infrastructure development plans to address these challenges and strengthen resilience. The Nile is one of the world’s longest rivers, draining approximately 10% of Africa’s land surface; Sudan accounts for around 40% of the basin area, where several new large hydropower and irrigation infrastructure projects are planned. We develop an integrated analytical framework for the Nile River system, utilizing 16 climate projections from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP) 6, along with hydrological, river system, and Computable General Equilibrium models to evaluate the biophysical and economic impacts of hydropower and irrigation development in Sudan under climate change. The results indicate a projected increase in the naturalized streamflow of the Nile by 2050 due to climate change. A phased hydropower and irrigation development strategy in Sudan – targeting a total of 1,500 MW of hydropower capacity and approximately one million hectares of irrigated wheat – is projected to increase annual hydropower generation by up to 8.1 TWh and expand total wheat area by 283% by 2050. These developments increase the undiscounted national Gross Domestic Product (GDP) during 2030–2050 by US$ 0.1 to 0.4 billion per year, with larger increases occurring under high economic growth pathways. This research highlights the interconnected nature of climate change, water resource development, and economic performance, underscoring the importance of integrated assessment in informing investment decisions.

title: Source identification of multi-process clogging in a deep groundwater recharge well: a combined mineralogical-geochemical approach
HydEquivNet: bridging classical unit hydrograph theory and data-driven hydrology via scale-equivariant learning
How to overcome hydrologic data scarcity in assessing potential groundwater risk to subterranean infrastructure: a finite-difference modelling approach
abstract: Groundwater infiltration (GWI) in sewer networks is an increasing challenge under climate change and human pressures, threatening the sustainability of sewer infrastructure. However, data scarcity and complex hydrogeology complicate its risk assessment. This study develops a finite-difference groundwater flow model (MODFLOW) to identify GWI susceptibility hotspots in non-pressurised sewer networks in Dawlish, southwest United Kingdom. To address limited hydrological data and hard-rock hydrogeology, several transferable approaches were integrated into the modelling framework. Fracture flow was represented using a porous-medium approximation, while borehole logs were interpreted to define the bedrock surface and estimate hydraulic properties. Groundwater recharge was derived from land-cover data, missing river stages were estimated from discharge–stage relationships, and initial node heads were assigned from river-network connectivity and upstream–downstream positions. These inputs, together with hydraulic properties and recharge, were refined through calibration. The model was calibrated for October 2007 to September 2020 and validated over the following four years using monthly time steps, achieving a mean error of − 0.05 m, a mean absolute error of 0.94 m, and a root mean square error of 1.62 m. Then, sewer sections were classified as having high (groundwater level (GWL) above the sewer), intermediate (GWL within 2 m below the sewer), or low (GWL more than 2 m below the sewer) GWI susceptibility. More than 85% of storm overflow spills occurred in sewers classified as highly susceptible. The resulting hotspot maps provide a practical decision-support tool for prioritising sewer inspection, maintenance, and rehabilitation, supporting more sustainable sewer network management.

title: KURVE: A web-based tool for estimating soil water retention and hydraulic conductivity curves using a k-nearest neighbor approach
abstract: Direct measurement of the soil water retention curve (WRC) and hydraulic conductivity curve (HCC) is expensive and time-consuming. Pedotransfer functions (PTFs) are statistical models that estimate soil hydraulic properties using basic soil data that are typically available or easier to measure. This paper introduces KURVE, a novel web-based tool that uses a recently published HYPROP-WP4C-based German reference dataset and a k -nearest neighbor approach to estimate complete WRCs and HCCs. KURVE selects nearest soils from the reference dataset based on basic soil properties, including soil texture, bulk density (BD), and organic carbon content (OCC), and estimates target-soil hydraulic curves by averaging fitted van Genuchten (VG) and Peters–Durner–Iden (VG-PDI) hydraulic functions from the selected neighbors. The performance of KURVE was evaluated using two independent datasets, a large international dataset and a smaller regional dataset from California, USA, and was compared with the widely used Rosetta and Rosetta3 PTF models. KURVE showed promising performance for estimating both curves. For WRC prediction, KURVE achieved RMSE values as low as 0.061 cm 3 cm⁻ 3 for the international dataset and 0.039 cm 3 cm⁻ 3 for the California dataset, which was comparable to or slightly better than Rosetta-based models. For HCC prediction, KURVE substantially outperformed Rosetta-based models, with log(K) RMSE values of 0.594–0.610 for the international dataset and 0.560–0.643 for the California dataset when soil texture and BD were used as inputs. The results also showed that adding BD to soil texture improved model performance, whereas adding OCC as an additional predictor did not provide consistent improvement. KURVE is freely available at kurve-ptf.streamlit.app and provides the scientific community with an accessible tool for applications that require soil hydraulic information.

title: A machine-learning-enhanced fuzzy evaluation framework for hydrochemical evolution and ecohydrological attribution in a megacity river basin
Forensic hydrological assessment of flood response under land use/land cover (LULC) change using ANN and HEC–HMS
abstract: This study develops an integrative methodological framework that combines forensic hydrology, artificial neural networks (ANNs), and physically-based hydrological modeling to assess the cascading impacts of projected land use/land cover (LULC) changes on future flood dynamics in the upstream watershed of Golestan Dam, Iran. A large-magnitude flood event analogous to the destructive 2019 flood was simulated under evolving LULC scenarios for three future horizons: 2030, 2040, and 2050. The curve number (CN) and lag time (Tlag) were reconstructed using linear and nonlinear interpolation and projected with ANN-based regression modeling. Mann-Kendall trend analysis was applied to assess the temporal consistency of ANN-predicted CN and Tlag series and support the selection of the most reliable synthetic datasets. The simulations revealed highly non-linear growth in peak discharges, with the Qarah Shur sub-basin projected to experience a 163.78% increase in flood intensity by 2050, resulting from a substantial increase in the contribution of barren land to flood intensification (from 22.89% to 78.88%) and a threefold increase in the contribution of sparse vegetation (from 9.04% to 31.13%). These two factors, individually and in combination, were identified as the most critical contributors to flood amplification in this sub-basin. The Galikesh sub-basin followed with a 68.99% increase by 2050, being the only sub-basin where the contribution of road expansion (from 8.88% to 27.41%) emerged as the dominant factor driving flood intensification. The Tamar Gorgan and Tangerah sub-basins demonstrated more moderate increases in discharge, 13.89% and 10.44%, respectively, driven by modest land degradation and road building. This work’s findings underscore growing risks to infrastructure, including embankment instability, bridge scour, and urban inundation, and to groundwater recharge, aquatic ecosystems, and water quality through the mobilization of pollutants and sediments under increasing flood risk. The spatial comparison of sub-basin-level responses captures the heterogeneity of flood vulnerability and the urgency of instituting adaptive land use policies grounded in hydrological sensitivity, riparian corridor protection, and nature-based flood mitigation.

title: Seasonal river-level fluctuations regulate riparian nitrate removal through coupled hydrologic exchange and redox dynamics
Increasingly diverse allochthonous input promote recalcitrance and homogenization of dissolved organic matter along the land-sea continuum
Estimating daily evapotranspiration from remotely sensed instantaneous observations with surface flux equilibrium (SFE) theory and maximum entropy production (MEP) principle
Validation of GRACE, ERA5-Land and MODIS remote sensing products for groundwater monitoring in semiarid regions: A multi-basin study in Chile’s Coquimbo region
High-resolution spatiotemporal monitoring of chlorophyll-a in small inland reservoirs using multi-source remote sensing data fusion
Shared versus reservoir-specific policy architectures in multi-agent reinforcement learning for physically heterogeneous cascade reservoir operation
Intensifying dry-to-wet extremes across Europe: long-term evolution and contrasting impacts on vegetation dynamics
abstract: Dry‑to‑wet extremes (DTWEs) pose mounting risks to ecosystems and human societies, yet their large‑scale ecological consequences remain unclear. Here, we present the first pan‑European assessment of DTWEs and their impacts on terrestrial ecosystems by coupling long‑term changes in DTWEs (1950–2022) with vegetation dynamics (1980–2020). We quantify DTWEs-vegetation linkages using a dual framework that combines correlation analysis with causal diagnostics (convergent cross mapping, CCM) to distinguish statistical association from inferred directional dependence. Our analysis reveals a pronounced intensification of DTWEs across Europe, characterized by increasing spatial extent, frequency, and intensity. Vegetation responses are season-dependent. Low-to-moderate intensity DTWEs occurring before the core growing season are generally associated with enhanced vegetation productivity, whereas those occurring during the growing season tend to be linked to widespread suppression. CCM-based analyses indicate that causal signals are more detectable early in the season, while signals during peak growth are more likely to be influenced by confounding factors. Specifically, soil moisture (SM) acts as an intermediate variable: controlling for SM strengthens the DTWE-vegetation association in the pre‑season window but weakens it during the growing season. Spatial analyses reveal heterogeneous vegetation sensitivity, with humid regions showing the largest spatial extent of significant responses and transitional climates exhibiting greater relative vulnerability to DTWEs. These findings reveal the ongoing intensification of DTWEs and demonstrate that their vegetation impacts vary with seasonal timing, antecedent soil-moisture, and regional climate, thereby informing targeted adaptation strategies amid increasing hydroclimatic volatility.

Modelling a decade of daily open water evaporation for existing and planned water storages: A spatially explicit analysis for the Pilbara region of north-western Australia
abstract: We present a method that integrates physically based evaporation modelling approaches with high-resolution meteorological data interpolated from land-based observations to estimate daily open water evaporation at local and regional scales across the data-sparse Pilbara region of north-western Australia. The evaporation modelling approach considers water body heat storage and enables water bodies of different sizes, depth and salinity to be modelled. Daily meteorological data were interpolated at 0.01° resolution for the 440,000 km 2 Pilbara region based on the best performing model from up to 14 thin plate spline models per meteorological variable, which used varying combinations of latitude and longitude, elevation and a coastal distance index as spatial predictors. Using the interpolated meteorological data, the evaporation model was run across the study region (at a daily time step with 0.01° spatial resolution) for all combinations of water body size and salinity. Comparison of model results with measurements for three different sized water bodies yielded R 2 > 0.64 and an RMSE of < 1.6 mm d −1 giving confidence in results. Reference water body evaporation was high across the focus area and ranged between 2272 and 2965 mm y −1 . We showed that the spatio-temporal open water evaporation model can be used to estimate evaporation for both existing and proposed water bodies. To simplify model application to different waterbody characteristics we developed an evaporation scaling factor which was used to scale model results from a reference water body (surface area of 1 km 2 , salinity of 10 mS cm −1 and depth of 10 m) to any water body with surface area between 0.01 and 5 km 2 and salinity between 0 and 300 mS cm −1 . The method developed provides the first daily-scale open water evaporation estimates across the Pilbara region and can be applied to other locations where open water evaporation estimates are required for water resource management by using spatially interpolated meteorological grids and/or reanalysis products.

title: Competitive adsorption and co-transport of live and hypochlorite-inactivated Azospirillum brasilense in saturated sand
Diverging hydrometeorological drivers of flashier floods in a warming climate
InSAR-driven characterization of “ungauged” aquifer systems: Insights from the Gediz River Basin, Türkiye
abstract: Accurate characterization of key hydro-geomechanical properties, specifically hydraulic conductivity and specific storage , is essential for predicting the responses of aquifer systems to natural and anthropogenic stressors and ensuring sustainable groundwater management. However, such characterization remains particularly challenging in “ungauged” basins, i.e. where piezometric records, pumping test data, and information about production wells are sparse or unavailable. We propose an iterative framework based on coupling a three-dimensional(3D) groundwater flow (GW) model with a 3D geomechanical (GM) model, with a nested inversion scheme. The workflow begins with calibrating the GW model against piezometric records to acquire an initial estimation of heterogeneous distribution given a homogeneous . The resulting hydraulic head changes are then fused with Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) measurements to estimate point-wise values that are subsequently interpolated across the basin scale. This field is validated using the GM model and fed back into the GW model for a next iteration of calibration. This iterative cycle continues until the estimated parameters stabilize and further updates provide limited improvements in model performance. We apply this approach to the Gediz River Basin (GRB) in western Türkiye, a region experiencing severe land subsidence from groundwater over-exploitation for irrigation. Our results reveal significant heterogeneity in aquifer properties, and the inferred and distributions allow for the reproduction of both hydraulic head evolution and land subsidence patterns, with a consistent modeling set-up.

title: A spectral-constrained HVCE framework for adaptive optical-SAR fusion to enhance soil moisture retrieval
An orthogonal residual physics-informed neural network with Karhunen-Loève expansion for inversion of heterogeneous soil hydraulic parameters
Intensifying floods may not imply cascading flood risks in dryland rivers
Differential controls of warming and phosphorus enrichment on CO2, CH4, and N2O emissions in shallow lake mesocosms
Intensive anthropogenic activities control the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of river eutrophication at the watershed scale
Nonlinear flow behaviors through rough fractures in shale: Effects of fracture roughness and stress-induced closed-region evolution
Flowing cold and shallow: snowmelt controls on spring temperature and resilience to climate change
abstract: Headwater springs in Northern California’s Cascade Range sustain river baseflow and provide thermal refugia for salmonids, but their recharge source areas are largely unknown. To constrain where and when recharge occurs, and how much spring water warms en route to the discharge points, we analyzed stable water isotopes and dissolved noble gases from six major spring complexes across California’s Cascade region between July 2023 and August 2025. We analyzed a total of 31 samples for stable water isotopes, of which 18 were also analyzed for noble gases. We derived a regional δ 18 O lapse rate from 52 small springs and creeks spanning elevations from 177 to 2588 m, producing a slope of −2.0‰/km (R 2 = 0.89). Bootstrap analysis yielded a median lapse rate slope of −1.97‰/km with a 95% uncertainty interval of −2.17 to −1.70‰/km, which was propagated into recharge elevation estimates. Effective mean recharge elevations were consistently high, with values ranging from 1800 to 2900 m across the spring complexes. Noble gas thermometry yielded cold recharge temperatures (1.5–7.0 °C), commonly colder than local mean annual air temperature, consistent with high-elevation recharge during the snowmelt period. Comparing recharge temperatures with discharge temperatures indicates modest net subsurface warming of 2.9 to 8.6 °C and predominantly shallow theoretical flow depths, typically ∼75–250 m and up to ∼300 m. Because many recharge elevations overlap the band where snowpack declines are expected in Northern California due to climate change, these spring-fed systems are likely to warm and lose thermal buffering capacity. The integrated isotope, noble gases, and heat budget framework developed here provides a transferable approach for evaluating climate sensitivity in mountain spring systems.

title: Interpretable modeling of spatiotemporal variations of groundwater total hardness across China
Integrating deep-learning detection and hydrological monitoring for driftwood flux estimation in a steep tropical watershed during a typhoon-driven flood
Hydrogeochemical assessment and vulnerability analysis of mountain springs in a karstic water system in northeastern Italy
abstract: Mountain springs are essential freshwater resources for both communities and ecosystems, but they are increasingly threatened by climate variability and human pressure. This study investigates the vulnerability and recharge dynamics of two springs (LAR and CAN) in the Cansiglio Massif karst system (NE Italy). The novelty of this work lies in applying an integrated hydrogeological, hydrogeochemical, isotopic, and vulnerability-based framework to two springs in the foothills of a main karst system, showing how multiple complementary techniques can support the definition of recharge areas and protection zones even for small sources that remain essential for local water-supply management. Monitoring (September 2018 to September 2021) shows that recharge likely originates from the Mt. Pizzoc area and follows structurally and topographically controlled pathways toward the springs. Results reveal a dual recharge regime: rapid infiltration through fractured and karstified carbonates and coarse slope deposits, and slower, laterally redistributed flow where marly-silty-clayey layers hinder vertical percolation. A simplified water budget constrained the minimum and net recharge areas, while isotope-elevation relationships estimated mean recharge elevations of about 732–879 m a.s.l. for LAR and 617–767 m a.s.l. for CAN. Hydrological patterns and vulnerability indicators show that CAN responds much faster and is far more vulnerable (VESPA V = 14–38.7; MDHT 1–4 days) than LAR (VESPA V = 0.36–0.77; MDHT 9–22 days). By combining multiple approaches, this integrated framework offers practical support for identifying protection priorities, especially in shallow and highly responsive mountain spring catchments.

title: Predominant vegetation control on baseflow index variations across China’s climatic basins
A pioneer in hydrogeology is gone, but Tóthian groundwater flow systems live on
Reservoir releases and land cover interact to drive event-scale nitrate export in a large agricultural basin
abstract: Understanding the drivers of nitrate export in rivers is critical for developing effective nutrient management strategies. However, few studies have explored event-scale drivers of export in large river basins with human modifications like reservoirs. Here, we analyzed nitrate concentration-discharge (C-Q) relationships from 215 events at the outlet of the Kansas River Basin, USA (155,690 km 2 ) from 2014 to 2022 to (1) characterize event-scale nitrate export behaviors in a large agricultural basin, and (2) determine how different event characteristics are linked to these behaviors. We found that C-Q behaviors varied greatly, with 60% of events producing nitrate enrichment (n = 130) and 40% of events producing nitrate dilution (n = 85). These behaviors were correlated with complex spatial interlinkages between climate and land cover: across most of the basin, nitrate enrichment was correlated with drier antecedent conditions, but in wetter areas with higher proportions of urban and forested land cover, enrichment was more strongly correlated with precipitation magnitude/intensity. This difference in hydroclimatic controls on nitrate export might be related to differential distributions of nitrate sources within these land covers. Upstream of major reservoirs, however, neither variable was strongly correlated with C-Q behavior, suggesting that nitrate attenuation within reservoirs decouples event-scale concentration signals in upstream waters from those downstream. Reservoir outflows had variable impacts on C-Q behavior, reflecting reservoir-specific variations in nitrate attenuation efficiency. Together, these results identify specific complex interactions between hydroclimate, land cover, reservoir positioning, and individual reservoir properties that control event-scale nitrate export from large basins.

title: Trends in water quality and geochemistry research
From temperature to VPD: shifting drivers of flash droughts amplify ecosystem risks in high-latitude cold climates
Cascade-reservoir impoundment reshapes event-scale flood–sediment responses upstream of the Three Gorges Reservoir: evidence from rainfall patterns and driver attribution
abstract: Event-scale flood and suspended sediment dynamics in heavily regulated large river basins are shaped by both rainfall forcing and human activities. However, the ways in which cascade reservoir impoundment alters rainfall–flood–sediment relationships remain poorly understood. Focusing on the upper Three Gorges Reservoir (TGR) inflow region, we selected 91 flood events (2003–2020) and then used K-means clustering to classify rainfall patterns, followed by statistical comparisons and random-forest attribution to diagnose driver shifts after the impoundment of cascade reservoirs in the lower Jinsha River. Six rainfall patterns were identified: Uniform Moderate (UMR, 29.7%), Downstream Early-Peak Variable Light (DEPVL 22.0%), Upstream Widespread Gentle (UWG, 13.2%), Downstream Late-Peak Intense (DLPI, 13.2%), Basin-Wide Torrential (BWT, 11.0%), and Outlet-Proximal Abrupt Heavy (OPAH, 11.0%). Following the impoundment of cascade reservoirs in the upstream, floods entering the TGR weakened modestly: total flood volume, peak discharge, and duration decreased by 6.21~10.02%. Sediment responses, however, were far more pronounced, with suspended sediment load and mean/peak concentrations declining by 41.25~52.86%. Despite the overall decline, flood events contributed 1.09 percentage points more to annual sediment load, reflecting greater sediment contribution during events under reduced supply. Random forest attribution revealed that rainfall magnitude remained the dominant control on floods, with its contribution increasing from 29.47% to 43.03%; reservoir regulation emerged as the second most important driver (26.37%). For suspended sediment, controls shifted from a regime dominated by rainfall magnitude and baseflow to one led by rainfall spatial distribution and magnitude, with the contribution of spatial distribution rising from 11.07% to 42.23% and upstream cascade reservoirs impoundment accounting for 20.53%. These findings reveal a systematic decoupling of flood and sediment responses due to cascade reservoir impoundment, accompanied by a reordering of dominant drivers of event-scale sediment delivery. The results have important implications for sediment monitoring and adaptive reservoir operation in the upper Yangtze River system.

title: From longitudinal dispersal to vertical sequestration: Hydraulic regulation drives divergent antibiotic fates via suspended particulate matter dynamics across natural and engineered waterways
Quantifying hillslope-to-river phosphorus contributions to water quality through a cascading framework of hydrological connectivity
Hierarchical multi-objective management of cascade reservoirs: coordinating long-term strategy and daily operation under hydrological variability
Estimating drain spacing in non-steady state drainage with constant recharge
abstract: The paper presents a numerical solution for determining the spacing of subsurface drainage systems under unsteady drainage conditions, when a constant recharge rate ( R ) is incorporated into the linearized Boussinesq equation under specified boundary and initial conditions. To date, the exponential-series solution of the Boussinesq equation has been used to compute the water table elevation at the midpoint ( m ) between parallel drains, as well as the discharge per unit area into the drains ( q ), but not for determining the drain spacing ( L ) , since L appears both algebraically and within the exponential term. To address this issue, only the first term of the exponential series was used. The results indicate that the proposed numerical solution, together with necessary conditions guaranteeing solvability and convergence, provides reliable estimates of L over a wide range of hydraulic and design parameters. The largest errors are obtained when the hydraulic conductivity ( K ) and drainable porosity ( S ) are varied, with RMSE values of 0.33 m and 0.36 m, respectively, followed by variations in the observation time ( t ) (RMSE = 0.20 m). In contrast, variations in R and drain depth ( D ) result in considerably smaller errors, with RMSE values of 0.06 m and 0.09 m, respectively. Overall, the proposed scheme provides reliable and stable (with respect to measurement noise) estimates of drain spacing and can be effectively applied to the design of subsurface drainage systems.

title: Hydrologic connectivity from cryospheric waters to groundwater in the Southeastern Tibetan Plateau, China: recharge pathways and seasonal regulation from multiple tracers
Global patterns and declines of precipitation persistence over the past six decades
A hyperparameter tuning strategy for an LSTM model to simulate reservoir outflows: large-scale evaluation across 441 dams in the CONUS
SURGIN: SURrogate-guided Generative INversion for subsurface multiphase flow with quantified uncertainty
abstract: We present a direct inverse modeling method named SURGIN, a SURrogate-guided Generative INversion framework tailed for subsurface multiphase flow data assimilation. Unlike existing inversion methods that require adaptation for each new observational configuration, SURGIN features a zero-shot conditional generation capability, enabling real-time assimilation of unseen monitoring data without task-specific retraining. Specifically, SURGIN synergistically integrates a U-Net enhanced Fourier Neural Operator (U-FNO) surrogate with a score-based generative model (SGM), framing the conditional generation as a surrogate prediction-guidance process in a Bayesian perspective. Instead of directly learning the conditional generation of geological parameters, an unconditional SGM is first pretrained in a self-supervised manner to capture the geological prior, after which posterior sampling is performed by leveraging a differentiable U-FNO surrogate to enable efficient forward evaluations conditioned on unseen observations. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate SURGIN's capability to decently infer heterogeneous geological fields and predict spatiotemporal flow dynamics with quantified uncertainty across diverse measurement settings. By unifying generative learning with surrogate-guided Bayesian inference, SURGIN establishes a new paradigm for inverse modeling and uncertainty quantification in parametric functional spaces.

title: Overlooked pathogenic dissemination and water security risks driven by hydrophobic lipid-like DOM under routine rainfall
Depth-dependent lag, persistence, and hydro-thermal coupling of soil moisture in a basin of Northern China
Projected depletion of high mountain Asia glaciers by 2100: linking mass loss to asynchronous peak runoff
Hierarchical water partitioning across different scales in sloped field: evidenced by soil pore water isotopic signatures
The seasonality of geogenic-anthropogenic interplay drives iron and manganese mobilization in groundwater
Balancing segmentation accuracy and hydrological plausibility in multi-source remote sensing flood inundation mapping with adaptive terrain-constrained learning
Deep learning-based precipitation nowcasting integrating radar echoes and rain gauge data
abstract: For flood protection and disaster mitigation, reliable and accurate short-term heavy rainfall forecasts are essential. However, precipitation nowcasting is a very difficult task due to the great temporal and spatial variability of precipitation at small spatial scales. To improve precipitation nowcasting accuracy, a radar echo extrapolation model (SAAR-UNet) and quantitative precipitation estimation model (RST-RainNet) were developed. By using an ASPP module, residual convolution, and a spatial attention mechanism, the SAAR-UNet greatly improved the extrapolation ability for the variation of strong echoes. In order to accomplish high-precision precipitation nowcasting, RST-RainNet innovatively employed a dual-branch strategy to perform residual correction on the quantitative precipitation nowcasting results of the extrapolated echoes. Extensive comparative experiments demonstrated that SAAR-UNet outperformed other attention-based and convolutional variants in echo extrapolation. RST-RainNet outperformed the optimized Z-R relationship, machine learning models (MLP, RF, XGBoost), and the single-branch UNet-ConvLSTM model in precipitation nowcasting tests. RST-RainNet best captured the regional characteristics and temporal dynamics of precipitation while maintaining the highest correlation coefficients and lowest errors for both one-hour and two-hour lead times. The results illustrated that deep learning techniques which combine rain gauge observation data with radar echoes can greatly improve precipitation nowcasting accuracy.

title: Selective transferability mapping for cross-basin prediction of river electrical conductivity
Unveiling the propagation and driving mechanisms of socioeconomic drought in the Aral Sea Basin: A vine copula and system dynamics ensemble simulation framework

Is every flood rough on built environment? Flood fragility and vulnerability modeling for residential buildings
abstract: Flood is one of the most frequent natural hazards, which often causes fatalities, injuries, physical damage to the built environment, and economic consequences. Although widely recognized as a frequent natural hazard/disaster, damage quantification models are sparsely reported in the literature, and most of those models consider well-known structural systems only. To quantify physical damage to buildings, plan flood-resilient housing construction, conduct risk/loss assessments, deploy insurance systems, and formulate evacuation and relocation programs, flood fragility/vulnerability models are instrumental at both local and regional scales. However, challenges persist in obtaining reliable data to construct high-fidelity models. To address this, the present paper develops high-fidelity fragility models for reinforced concrete (RC), wattle and daub, masonry, and hybrid construction systems using one of the largest actual damage survey datasets. Uncertainties are also quantified for each fragility/vulnerability model. We propose a new damage state definition framework that captures contents, nonstructural components (NSCs), structural components, and global damage in residential buildings. Equivalent damage ratios are also proposed for each damage state. The results highlight that the wattle and daub system is the most vulnerable construction system under flooding. In addition, functionality loss cannot be ruled out even in robust construction systems such as RC. Comparison between the proposed and existing models from other basins highlights that scalability and generalizability considerations are instrumental in adopting flood fragility/vulnerability models.

Pore-scale sedimentary architecture controls the emergence and constitutive scaling of asymptotic hydrodynamic dispersion
abstract: This study demonstrates that the magnitude and spatial organization of pore-scale heterogeneity jointly govern the emergence of asymptotic hydrodynamic dispersion in porous media. Two-dimensional digitally constructed pore networks representing graded, laminated, and random sedimentary architectures were generated with systematically varied heterogeneity index σ g . Flow and solute transport simulations were performed over longitudinal domains exceeding 20 cm across multiple Péclet numbers to quantify the evolution from pre-asymptotic to asymptotic transport behavior. Results show that spatial architectural organization—rather than the magnitude of heterogeneity alone—exerts a first-order control on emergent continuum-transport behavior. Bulk velocity variance remained comparatively insensitive to σ g , yet the asymptotic hydrodynamic dispersion coefficient and accompanying longitudinal dispersivity varied by orders of magnitude following the hierarchy laminated > graded > random, reflecting how spatially coherent velocity segregation imposed by sedimentary architecture governs emergent continuum-transport behavior. In the graded and laminated architectures, both transport metrics increased exponentially with σ g , while the laminated architecture additionally exhibited power-law relationships with the permeability contrast between coarse and fine sediment layers, defining architecture-specific constitutive relationships absent in random architectures. The transition length to asymptotic Fickian transport depended on both sedimentary architecture and σ g , exhibiting only a weak dependence on the Péclet number in the laminated and graded domains. In contrast, the relative increase from early-time to asymptotic dispersion showed no systematic Péclet number dependence, indicating primary structural control. Once asymptotic conditions were reached, longitudinal dispersivity became independent of the Péclet number, consistent with classical hydrodynamic dispersion theory. Asymptotic dispersivity values reproduced both the magnitude and vertical scatter of compiled field dispersivity–length datasets, supporting the interpretation that much of the observed field-scale variability at a given length likely reflects the impact of geological architectural heterogeneity rather than measurement uncertainty.

title: A pore-scale hydraulic conductivity model for frozen saturated soils incorporating wall-first and center-first freezing mechanisms
abstract: Hydraulic conductivity of saturated frozen soils exhibits strong nonlinearity with temperature due to progressive changes in pore-scale liquid connectivity. To capture this behavior, a physically based hydraulic conductivity model for frozen soils is developed within a freezing-modified capillary-bundle framework that represents the potential coexistence of wall-first and center-first freezing mechanisms. An effective pore radius is derived to reflect both the volumetric distribution of unfrozen water and the geometry of hydraulically active pore classes. The model is parameterized directly from the soil freezing characteristic curve (SFCC), providing a physics-consistent link between temperature, unfrozen water content, and pore-scale flow properties. A machine-learning model based on a weighted ensemble of Transformer architecture and XGBoost is developed to estimate SFCCs from basic soil properties to facilitate its use when measured SFCC information is unavailable. The measured or estimated SFCCs serve as inputs to the proposed pore-scale saturated hydraulic conductivity model. The proposed model was validated against independent experimental datasets covering a wide range of soil textures and testing methods. Predictions show strong agreement with measured hydraulic conductivity over several orders of magnitude and successfully reproduce the observed nonlinear dependence on temperature and unfrozen water content. The results indicate that accurate prediction of hydraulic conductivity of saturated frozen soils requires information of both unfrozen water content and pore-scale freezing geometry. Overall, the proposed framework provides a robust and scalable approach for predicting the hydraulic conductivity of saturated frozen soils in cold regions.

title: Multi-task learning of reservoir inflow and outflow for streamflow simulation
Evaporation, energy balance, and paleohydrology of the lakes along the Dead Sea rift
abstract: Lake evaporation is a dominant yet poorly constrained component of water and energy budgets. This uncertainty critically undermines necessary paleoclimate reconstructions, particularly for terminal lakes, whose levels are considered the best direct indicators of the precise balance between catchment precipitation and evaporative losses. We address this by applying a physically grounded framework for lake evaporation based on a hybrid approach of direct measurements and theoretical analysis of lake energy-balance and its thermal-equilibrium solution, combined with calibrated bulk formulae. High-resolution data from long-term eddy-covariance measurements at three adjacent Dead Sea Rift lakes—spanning wide gradients in salinity (freshwater to hypersaline), climate (Mediterranean to hyper-arid), and thermal structure—were used to calibrate bulk formulae relating environmental forcing to heat fluxes. We show that the thermal equilibrium approach depends on the lake’s thermal response time; shallow lakes reach equilibrium at intra-annual timescales, whereas deeper stratified lakes require annual forcing. This observations, combined with accurate bulk formulae that relates to the environmental conditions, provides tools for modeling global lake evaporation using only standard environmental data and for reconstructing paleo-evaporation. Applying this framework to the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) highstand of Lake Lisan (the Levant), we bound evaporation rates and determine that a minimum annual water inflow approximately four times greater than modern levels was required to stabilize the lake. These results indicate significantly higher precipitation in the Dead Sea watershed during the LGM.

A new breakthrough pressure model for coal considering effective stress and water saturation
abstract: Gas breakthrough pressure is a key parameter governing gas migration in reservoirs and plays a critical role in assessing the safety of geological storage of gases such as CO 2 and H 2 . However, existing breakthrough pressure prediction methods largely rely on empirical correlations fitted to experimental data, which lack a solid physical basis and are unable to simultaneously account for the coupled effects of water saturation and effective stress. In this study, a series of gas breakthrough pressure experiments were conducted on coal samples from Bowen Basin under varying effective stress and water saturation conditions. The experimental results demonstrate that cleat networks, effective stress, and water saturation jointly control breakthrough behavior in coal reservoirs. Based on these observations, a new physics–informed gas breakthrough pressure model for coal was developed by incorporating effective stress, water saturation, cleat compressibility, porosity, and initial permeability within a unified theoretical framework. The proposed model enables direct prediction of breakthrough pressure curves using sample-specific physical parameters and improves prediction accuracy compared with existing models, particularly for low-permeability samples. Compared with the J-function and the exponential model, it reduces the overall mean absolute error across the five samples from 36.8 kPa and 18.7 kPa to 12.1 kPa, corresponding to reductions of 67.1% and 35.3%, respectively. This study provides a robust approach for predicting gas breakthrough pressure in coal reservoirs and offers insights into underground gas storage assessment.
