Performance analysis of the OS LISFLOOD hydrological model using nearly three decades of satellite laser ranging data
abstract: We evaluate the performance of the OS LISFLOOD hydrological model by comparing its terrestrial water storage (TWS) estimates with long-term geodetic benchmark products derived from Satellite Laser Ranging (SLR), GRACE, and DORIS, over the period 1995–2022. Our analysis focuses on the 100 largest river basins, assessing the model’s ability to capture both seasonal and interannual variability. We find that OS LISFLOOD outperforms a model widely applied in geodetic studies, the Land Surface Discharge Model (LSDM) in representing large-scale TWS variations, particularly in tropical and subtropical basins and in seasonal and low-frequency dynamics of TWS. Comparisons with SLR-based gravity field models extend the evaluation into the pre-GRACE era (1995–2004), highlighting OS LISFLOOD’s robustness in depicting long-term hydrological changes. We also find that combined SLR + GRACE and SLR + DORIS datasets provide useful long-term geodetic benchmarks for assessing hydrological model consistency, particularly in large tropical basins. This work contributes to advancing long-term reconstructions of the global water cycle and supports geodetic applications, including environmental loading corrections and studies of Earth rotation. The results emphasize the importance of high-resolution hydrological models in improving the accuracy of TWS simulations and their application to geophysical research

title: Flood-generating mechanism attribution across U.S. catchments: the role of soil-layer depth and framework sensitivity
Antarctic lakes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of major ions chemistry across the continent
abstract: Antarctic lakes represent highly sensitive recorders of polar environmental shifts. However, evaluating continent-scale geochemical baselines has been historically impeded by fragmented, localized data ( Heywood, 1972 ). This study presents a comprehensive synthesis of major ion chemistry from 4,457 water samples across 83 peer-reviewed publications to establish a unified hydrochemical framework. Major ion concentrations were harmonized and analyzed using compositional ratios and multivariate approaches to isolate dominant solute sources and geochemical control mechanisms. Across the continent, a dominant sodium-chloride signature emerges in coastal zones, with sodium-chloride molar ratios closely tracking seawater values (0.86), demonstrating a pervasive marine aerosol imprint. Conversely, inland isolated basins, particularly within the Continental Inland Ice-Free Valleys, exhibit profound geochemical modifications driven by the interplay of cryogenic concentration, intense sublimation, and localized rock-water interactions. Calcium-rich brines indicate advanced freeze-concentration cycles or localized carbonate leaching. By integrating these disparate datasets into a harmonized framework, this study clarifies the regional organization of Antarctic limnological systems and provides a crucial quantitative baseline for tracking future climate-driven variations in hydrologic fluxes, ice-free area expansions, and localized anthropogenic footprints.

title: Molecular-level source contribution of dissolved organic matter in a typical plateau lake using end-member mixing analysis based on spectroscopic, stable isotope and molecular fingerprint
Historical evaluation and future projections of soil temperature at representative sites in the Huaibei Plain, China
A hybrid machine learning and physics-based approach to model high-resolution inundation
abstract: Large-scale high-resolution hydrologic modeling is necessary to understand future water availability and flood risk. This study uses a combined physics-based and machine learning modeling approach to produce accurate high-resolution inundation maps at a much lower computational cost than high-resolution physics-based modeling. The test domain is an 1800km​2 watershed in Colorado during the 2019 water year which is modeled in the integrated surface-subsurface model ParFlow-CLM at a 1km resolution and then downscaled to a 100m resolution binary inundation product using a random forest model. In addition to the 1km resolution modeled inundation depth, other relevant parameters such as topographic slope, upstream area, and Manning’s roughness are inputs for the machine learning model, which was trained on modeled inundation from a 100m resolution ParFlow-CLM model. The hybrid physics-based and machine learning approach is 97.6% accurate in predicting high-resolution inundation status when compared to the 100m resolution ParFlow-CLM model at 1/500th of the computational cost. This is more accurate than the 1km model on its own, which is 67.4% accurate at a 100m resolution. The spatial and temporal transferability of the random forest model were also tested and it was found that the model is 96.2% accurate in unseen timesteps and 86.3% accurate in unseen locations. This study demonstrates the applicability of a hybrid physics-based and machine learning approach to produce accurate high-resolution surface inundation maps at a dramatically lower computational cost than high-resolution hydrologic modeling.

title: Large-scale circulation anomalies at drought occurrence over northern China during El Niño developing stage
Hierarchical prediction of streamflow and organic carbon at event scale using a physics-guided AI hybrid framework
abstract: Agricultural watersheds are major contributors to storm-driven export of streamflow (Q) and organic carbon (particulate organic carbon, POC; dissolved organic carbon, DOC), which strongly influence downstream water quality and biogeochemical processes. However, accurately predicting hydro–carbon dynamics, particularly during high-impact storm events, remains challenging due to structural limitations in process-based models and the lack of physical consistency in data-driven approaches. Hence, this study presents a novel physics-guided spatial–temporal hybrid framework (PhyST-HC) that integrates the uncalibrated Soil and Water Assessment Tool-Carbon (SWAT-C) with Graph Neural Networks and Transformer-based attention mechanisms to improve event-scale hydro–carbon predictions. Within this framework, it preserves the watershed connectivity and implements a hierarchical prediction strategy (Q → POC → DOC), thereby enforcing physically consistent coupling between hydrological and carbon processes and mitigating non-physical carbon responses independent of flow dynamics. The proposed approach was applied to the agriculturally dominated Tuckahoe Creek Watershed in the USA. The results demonstrated that the PhyST-HC achieved superior performance over SWAT-C, with KGE increasing from ~0.20 to 0.82–0.85 and discharge bias reduced from ~−40% to −7%. In addition, the results show a strong correlation between Q and (POC, DOC) at the event scale. Furthermore, the framework improves the representation of event-scale dynamics, accurately capturing POC flushing and DOC transport, and reveals hydrologically consistent memory scales (~12 days Q, 8 days DOC, 2 days POC) aligned with watershed structure. These findings highlight the potential of hybrid modelling frameworks to advance event-driven water-quality predictions amid increasing hydroclimatic extremes, even in data-sparse regions.

title: Ecological water replenishment improves water quality and environmental capacity in a tributary of the Yellow River: insights from MIKE 21 coupled modeling
Rapid hydrologic flushing and biogeochemical recovery after Hurricane Helene in a heterogeneous coastal karst system
abstract: Extreme storms can substantially alter hydrologic and biogeochemical processes in coastal systems, yet the coupled responses of surface water and groundwater, particularly within karst terrains, remain poorly understood. This study integrated continuous United States Geological Survey (USGS) monitoring with multi-compartment water sampling conducted between October 2024 and May 2025 to evaluate coastal system responses to Hurricane Helene, which made landfall along Florida’s Big Bend coast in September 2024. The regional karstic Upper Floridan Aquifer (UFA), together with the connected Wakulla Spring–Wakulla River system, responded rapidly to the hurricane, with river, spring, and groundwater stages increasing to approximately 3, 1.5, and 1.1 times their respective baseflow levels within hours of landfall. USGS monitoring records indicate that the Wakulla River, Wakulla Spring, and regional UFA system returned to near-baseflow conditions within approximately 14 days, 23 days, and 3 months after landfall, respectively. These recovery trends were further supported by stable water isotope signatures and nutrient dynamics. River and spring conductivity time series and major ion patterns suggest minimal storm-surge-driven salinization throughout the study area. In contrast, shallow porous groundwater responses varied among hydrogeologic compartments. Sites located closest to the river exhibited recovery trajectories similar to those of surface waters, likely reflecting stronger hydrologic connectivity. More isolated shallow groundwater systems showed slower and more variable biogeochemical recovery, with ammonia and phosphate concentrations continuing to increase more than eight months after the hurricane, indicating prolonged biogeochemical processing within coastal sediments. Overall, the regional karstic system recovered more rapidly than many previously reported storm-affected coastal systems, likely due to the high transmissivity of the karst conduit network and the rapid inland progression of Hurricane Helene. The contrasting responses among hydrologic compartments demonstrate that conduit-dominated aquifers can rapidly flush storm-derived waters while still sustaining localized and persistent biogeochemical disturbances within shallow coastal sediments. These findings further suggest that future hydrologic and reactive transport models should incorporate multiple groundwater endmembers and vertical aquifer heterogeneity to better predict water quality responses to increasingly frequent extreme events.

title: Simulation of rainfall-runoff flow using three-dimensional smoothed particle hydrodynamics
Elevation-dependent hydrological vulnerability of lakes and reservoirs to evaporation loss in the Yarlung Zangbo River Basin, Tibetan Plateau
abstract: The Tibetan Plateau’s Yarlung Zangbo River Basin is undergoing rapid hydroclimatic transitions compounded by extensive reservoir development. Accurately quantifying evaporative water losses and water balance and interpreting their associated isotopic signatures is critical for improving hydrological models and regional water security assessment. In this study, we tested the application of an isotope-based Bayesian framework for quantifying evaporation and water balance dynamics. Utilizing steady-state models for the long-term water balance of natural lakes and transient models for the short-term water balance of artificial reservoirs, this framework calculated a unified mass-balance metric, the evaporative loss index (E/(E+Q)), where E represents evaporative water loss and Q denotes water outflow. Results reveal that despite operating on different temporal scales, the inflow-dependent evaporative loss indices exhibit diametrically opposed altitudinal dependencies between lakes and reservoirs, which can substantially mask the natural riverine δ 18 O altitude effect. Natural lakes, for which evaporative loss index is functionally equivalent to the evaporation-to-inflow ratio under steady-state conditions, are found to have average values of 0.27 ± 0.19 and show a strong positive correlation with elevation. In high-altitude basins (> 4500 m a.s.l.), limited natural inflows cause substantial proportional evaporative losses relative to the water balance (mean E/(E+Q) = 0.51), highlighting severe hydrological vulnerability to evaporative loss despite low absolute evaporation rates. This intense fractionation can substantially modify the pristine cryospheric baseflow, acting as a contributing mechanism to the reversal of the steep negative gradient in localized surface waters.. Conversely, artifically-constructed reservoirs exhibit a negative altitudinal evaporative gradient, with evaporation accounting for 0.47 ± 0.16 of total water losses in low-elevation shallow basins during the dry season. Rapid downstream transport of water from high-altitude reservoirs disrupts and homogenizes natural isotopic gradients in rivers. This systematic disruption of natural isotopic baselines by both climate-driven evaporation and human water retention explicitly warns against utilizing uncorrected surface water isotopes for hydrological tracing or paleoaltimetry reconstructions. These findings highlight extreme vulnerabilities in regional water security, demanding altitude-specific management adaptations.

Slope-weighted cost distance for modeling flood dynamics: a physics-informed random forest approach
abstract: Rapid flood inundation forecasting is a crucial tool for disaster mitigation; however, physically-based models are computationally intensive, and conventional data-driven models often exhibit poor generalizability and limited interpretability. To address these deficiencies, we propose a novel physics-informed random forest framework that incorporates a slope-weighted cost-distance feature to represent spatiotemporal flood dynamics and validate the framework using data from the Kinugawa River Basin, Japan. By weighting the distance with the terrain gradient, this feature approximates gravity-driven flow paths, enabling the model to significantly outperform the static baselines (F1-score improvement from 0.507 to 0.893). To improve performance for hydrographs withheld from training but drawn from the predefined 31-scenario set, we introduced a hydrograph feature-space sampling strategy. The strategy selects representative training cases by clustering peak discharge and total volume; using only four training cases, it achieved an F1-score of 0.904 for the withheld scenarios. Furthermore, a SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis provided quantitative evidence that the model learned statistical relationships consistent with flow-path selection and volume-related flood expansion. The proposed framework offers a transparent and computationally efficient alternative to black-box deep learning models for real-time forecasting, while its reliability for hydrographs beyond the sampled discharge-volume and waveform range remains untested

title: Assessment of long-term nitrate storage and transport in an agricultural basin
Climate-informed streamflow forecasting based on a Bayesian autoregressive exogenous stochastic volatility model and its use for hydrological drought forecasting
abstract: In the context of South Korea’s recurring drought challenges, this study explores season-ahead predictability of hydrological drought, focusing on Bayesian autoregressive modeling incorporating stochastic volatility. To better understand uncertainty, our approach integrates Bayesian inference and stochastic volatility, with comparisons of conventional autoregressive (AR), autoregressive with exogenous variables (ARX), and autoregressive exogenous with stochastic volatility (ARXSV) models. Our study explores the integration of climate-based information with statistical modeling, presenting a comprehensive framework for water resource management. We aim to predict June–July–August (JJA) streamflow and to assess the influence of large-scale climate predictors, such as the sea surface temperature and sea level pressure associated with the North Atlantic Oscillation. The methodology encompasses exploratory data analyses, the use of hydrological drought indices, and considerations related to dam operation. The research provides tailored season-ahead streamflow forecasts specifically for the critical monsoon season JJA, where hydrometeorological variability is paramount. By incorporating climate information within a Bayesian inference framework and stochastic volatility, we show that the proposed approach outperforms conventional autoregressive models, providing decision-makers with an efficient tool to address climate risk and support dam operation planning, ultimately contributing to improved water-resources management.

title: Regional atmospheric pattern shifts associated with weather whiplash events in the upper Yangtze River Basin
abstract: Global warming and intensified water cycles have led to an increase in weather whiplash events (WWEs), threatening ecosystems and human societies. However, the connection between WWEs and atmospheric circulation dynamics remains poorly understood, particularly through the lens of spatial clustering. This study applies the self-organizing map algorithm to cluster 500 hPa geopotential height (1979-2022) in the upper Yangtze River Basin (UYRB) and identify WWEs based on atmospheric circulation pattern shifts. We evaluate long-term trends in representative atmospheric patterns, extreme events, and WWEs, while exploring their linkages to large-scale circulation backgrounds. Results indicate a significant increase in the frequency of dry-warm patterns and a corresponding decrease in wet-cold patterns, confirming a warming and drying trend in the UYRB. Extreme warm events have risen across all seasons, with increased precipitation volatility in dry-warm patterns, suggesting a higher risk of drought-flood abrupt alternations. The persistence of dry-warm patterns has also increased, along with a growing number of WWEs originating from dry-warm patterns to wetter and colder patterns. These changes are closely linked to dynamic changes in synoptic circulation patterns and moisture transport anomalies.

title: A hybrid decision-support framework for managing salt intrusion via controlled freshwater pulses in regulated estuaries
abstract: Managing salt intrusion in estuaries is critical given increasing freshwater scarcity and human-induced salinization. This study presents a transferable hybrid framework to support salt intrusion management in regulated estuaries, combining a three-dimensional Delft3D-Flow model with parameterized analytical equations for predicting salt intrusion under varying discharge. Model implementation is based on estuarine domains with idealized geometries, reducing human-resource demands while enhancing accessibility and reproducibility. The steady intrusion equation follows Hansen and Rattray (1966), whereas the unsteady intrusion equation follows Monismith (2017). The framework is demonstrated in the Guadiana Estuary and applied to: (1) identify the key variables controlling the salinity response to short-duration freshwater pulses, and (2) optimize freshwater-release strategies based on limited freshwater volumes. Results highlight the critical role of background flow over pulse configuration (i.e., peak discharge and duration) when pulse volume is constant: the period during which salt intrusion remains below x = 47 km varies from 29 to 55 days as background flow increases from 6 to 8 m 3 s −1 , while increasing peak discharge from 300 to 1800 m 3 s −1 extends that period by one day. For a fixed freshwater volume of 45 hm 3 and a background flow of 4 m 3 s −1 , optimized release strategies yield maximum control durations of 15–125 days for intrusion threshold values between 30 and 50 km, respectively. Overall, the framework offers a practical decision-support tool that enhances stakeholder engagement in water resource and salt intrusion management, particularly by enabling rapid optimization of freshwater-release strategies under limited freshwater availability and user-defined salinity thresholds. Plain Language Summary. Estuaries around the world are experiencing rising salinity levels and growing pressure on limited freshwater resources. This study introduces a new decision-support tool to support the management of salinity in regulated estuaries. The framework is applied to investigate practical ways to reduce salinity in the Guadiana estuary, a highly affected area, by using short freshwater releases. To do this, a three-dimensional hydrodynamic model is calibrated with real observations. The approach involves simulating pulse experiments with constant volume but different peak (maximum) and background (base) river discharges to understand which factors most influence salinity reduction. In this situation, model results reveal that the peak discharge has a negligible influence on salinity intrusion reduction. From the simulations, two main equations are derived to predict salt intrusion under both steady and changing river flow conditions. These equations are then used to guide the design and evaluation of effective salinity mitigation strategies to meet ecological conservation and water-use demand.

title: Domain-knowledge-guided deep learning for probabilistic precipitation downscaling over southeastern Tibetan Plateau
Effect tracking and flux tracking to quantify preferential flow responses at the hillslope scale
abstract: Understanding runoff generation and water dynamics in hillslopes exhibiting preferential flow effects remains a persistent challenge in hydrology. In this study, we combined effect and flux tracking with a two-dimensional dual-continuum model to investigate hillslope runoff generation and water age composition in runoff components (stormflow and deep percolation), root water uptake, and hillslope soil water storage. The model, previously validated against observed discharge and isotope data, was used to simulate water flow and virtual tracer transport during a sequence of five rainfall–runoff events. Effect tracking showed that stormflow responded rapidly during large rainfall events through activation of preferential flow paths, whereas smaller events produced weaker and delayed responses. Hillslope storage exhibited pronounced soil moisture memory, with earlier events conditioning subsequent flow responses. Flux tracking indicated that stormflow was largely composed of pre-event water, with event water contributing both during the event itself and through remobilization in subsequent storms. Root water uptake accounted for a substantial fraction of event water loss, with sustained contributions over multiple events, whereas deep percolation showed the longest delays. Ensemble analysis indicated that approximately 60 % of the cumulative stormflow response occurred within five days, whereas only about 40 % of the event water recovered in stormflow was exported during the same period. This finding demonstrates a clear decoupling between rapid hydrological responses and much slower event water turnover, reflecting substantial subsurface storage and mixing. By combining effect and flux tracking at the hillslope scale, this study quantified process-specific hydrological memory and the remobilization of event water in stormflow, deep percolation, root water uptake, and soil water storage.

title: Interaction between dispersive soil and liquid water: From temperature-ponding driven water-salt dynamics to water content-mediated microstructural evolution
Legacy effects amplify baseflow nitrogen export: Watershed-scale evidence from the largest lake-inflowing river on the Tibetan Plateau
A Bellman equation-based unified framework for evaluating and optimizing reservoir hedging rules: Incorporating inflow temporal dependence and non-stationary environments
Optimising river sampling and load calculation methods for total phosphorus: influence of catchment size and population
abstract: Reliable estimates of river nutrient load are critical benchmarks for catchment and receiving waterbody management. Low – frequency monitoring is known to underestimate phosphorus (P) loads in small catchments, yet performance in large catchments, sometimes including large urban areas, remains poorly evaluated. This study used synchronous sub-daily river discharge and concentration datasets from three catchments of contrasting size and population to evaluate how these characteristics influence the performance of sampling and load calculation methods for total P load estimation. Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were used to assess the impact of catchment size and population on load estimate accuracy, with bias and precision derived from accuracy distributions. Sampling method performance was strongly dependent on catchment size and, less consistently, population. The smaller, flashier, and lower – population catchments required higher – frequency sampling to better capture short – duration runoff events and temporally variable diffuse inputs, which likely contributed to a greater proportion of total loads. The larger, higher – population catchment produced more accurate load estimates under low – frequency sampling, likely due to steadier point source contributions. While load calculation method performance varied with catchment population, flow – weighting was the most robust approach. However, even when combined with this approach, low – frequency sampling in the large catchments resulted in biased or imprecise load estimates: for example, a standard weekly sampling produced minimal bias (−7.0%–+2.1%) but poor precision (20.3%–72.8%). The findings reveal the need to adapt monitoring protocols to catchment characteristics and to increase monitoring frequency in large rivers to at least daily (ideally 7 – hourly) to better support effective catchment and waterbody management.

title: Coupling reservoir supply potential with load allocation: A framework to enhance water supply security in multi-reservoir systems
abstract: Increasing water demand is intensifying spatial mismatches between reservoir capacity and supply obligations in regional water-supply systems. Existing studies mainly optimize reservoir operation under fixed supply loads, whereas the distribution of those loads among heterogeneous reservoirs is less often treated as a decision variable. This study presents an integrated regional decision-support framework that links reservoir water-supply potential (RWSP) with reservoir water-supply load allocation (RWSLA) in multi-reservoir systems, providing a pre-operational load-configuration complement to conventional operation simulation. Reservoir-specific ecological water demand is reserved as a non-adjustable priority requirement before socioeconomic load redistribution. RWSP defines feasible allocation ranges for the residual urban and agricultural demands, and candidate schemes are generated by truncated normal sampling within those bounds. Long-term joint operation simulations and multi-criteria evaluation are then used to assess reliability, resilience, vulnerability, water stress, and allocation equity. The framework is applied to five medium and small reservoirs in northeastern Chongqing, China. Results show that RWSP exhibits a clear hierarchy shaped by active storage capacity, mean annual runoff, total available water volume, and dry-period runoff reliability. System performance improves when loads are aligned with reservoir potential: overloading low-potential reservoirs increases vulnerability, whereas assigning higher loads to high-potential reservoirs improves reliability but may reduce equity. Threshold-like responses are observed within the tested load-allocation ranges, and partial-correlation and sensitivity analyses indicate weak competition-complementarity among reservoirs. The framework supports regional screening of spatial load configurations as a pre-operational complement to temporal reservoir-operation rules, while the derived allocation ranges and thresholds remain case-specific.

title: Lagged global relationships between teleconnection indices and hydrological drought: a continental-scale analysis using ERA5-Land runoff data
Integrating scale-matched spatial scales into water scarcity risk screening in China
Spatial and temporal dynamics of E. coli in streamwater, sediments and rock biofilm
abstract: Most studies address the dynamics of Escherichia coli (E. coli) in streamwater during storms, while baseflow conditions in streambed environments have received less attention. Specifically, few explored how E. coli is distributed across biofilms and sediment size fractions. Thus, the objective of this study was to quantify the distribution of E. coli in streamwater, biofilm, and sediment fractions, and to determine how these niches influence spatiotemporal variations in E. coli concentration in a highland Mediterranean stream. E. coli dynamics across streamwater, rock biofilms, and size-fractionated sediments (<75, 75–300, and 300–2000 μm) were measured over 12 months across five sites along the Meshushim Stream, Israel. E. coli concentrations in streamwater ranged between 1 and 1.4 × 10 4 MPN 100 ml −1 . E. coli concentration increased significantly during the warm season (May-September) and was significantly correlated with temperature and, to a lesser extent, with total suspended solids. While streamwater E. coli concentrations fluctuated seasonally, the concentrations of E. coli associated with biofilms (250–1.4 × 10 5 MPN m −2 ) and sediment (40–5.4 × 10 3 MPN g −1 SDW) reservoirs did not have a temporal trend. E. coli was found attached to the finest sediment fractions, yielding concentrations that are 50 times higher than those in the coarsest material. These findings suggest that fine sediments serve as an important habitat for E. coli under both high-flow and baseflow conditions. During high flows, E. coli is often transported bound to particles that resuspend in the water, whereas during baseflow, fine-sediment reservoirs may influence stream-water dynamics even without substantial resuspension.

A synergetic framework for land-atmosphere coupling-based remote sensing inversion of evapotranspiration, surface resistance, and aerodynamic resistance
abstract: Evapotranspiration (ET) is a key link in land–atmosphere interactions, governing the coupled exchange of water and energy. However, conventional remote sensing-based ET estimation methods generally parameterize aerodynamic resistance ( r ae ) and surface resistance ( r s ) independently, which may limit the representation of their interplay and overlook the scale mismatch between them. To address this limitation, we propose a remote sensing-based ET coupling estimation framework (hereafter referred to as the ETC framework). Grounded in the intrinsic physics of surface energy balance, the ETC framework enables the simultaneous estimation of global ET, r ae , and r s , with the land–atmosphere coupling coefficient (Ω) clarifying their coupling relationships. The reliability of the inverted resistance parameters was evaluated at 195 globally distributed flux sites. The inverted r s agrees well with PM-derived values, with an R 2 of 0.56 and an RMSE of 73.86 s/m. Sensible heat flux estimated based on the inverted r ae shows strong agreement with observations, with an R 2 of 0.84 and an RMSE of 42.57 W/m 2 . The proposed ETC framework also demonstrates high accuracy in ET estimation: (1) at the half-hour scale, the mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), and R 2 for ET estimates are 26.52 W/m 2 , 42.86 W/m 2 , and 0.88, respectively. The ETC framework also consistently outperformed the conventional PM baseline in reproducing measured ET; (2) at the monthly scale, ETC achieves higher accuracy than ERA5-Land, GLEAM, and TerraClimate products; (3) at the spatial scale, the global ET estimates show strong consistency with the three ET products. Consequently, by overcoming the critical limitations associated with independently parameterized resistances and neglected scale mismatches in conventional ET retrieval, the ETC framework enables the first synergetic, accurate estimation of ET, r ae , and r s under physically constrained conditions across site-to-global scales. This achievement is expected to significantly advance the quantification of ET and the resistances.

Reactive transport processes in unsaturated porous media: inclusion of capillary geochemistry
abstract: Reactive transport in unsaturated porous media is governed by coupled hydro-geochemical processes, where capillary water exists under negative pressure. Conventional reactive transport models assume that geochemical reactions in such systems behave identically to those in bulk water, i.e., they neglect the thermodynamic effects of capillary conditions. Porewater in unsaturated media, however, is often in a stretched state, which alters its thermodynamic properties and influences the mineral-water-gas interactions. Developed in this work is a hydro-geochemical reactive transport model that explicitly incorporates capillary geochemistry by extending the thermodynamic description of water, aqueous species, gases, and minerals into the negative pressure domain. The formulation is based on classical thermodynamics and implemented in OpenFOAM within a coupled multiphase flow and transport framework. The model is verified against thermodynamic databases and validated using laboratory-scale experiments and is further applied to field-scale CO 2 injection. The results show that capillary influences geochemical behaviour primarily through pressure-dependent changes in molar volumes, which modify reaction Gibbs free energy and shift equilibrium constants. In contrast, the impact on activity coefficients is comparatively minor. Simulations demonstrate that stretched porewater enhances CO 2 dissolution, promotes mineral reactions, and alters the evolution of porosity and permeability in unsaturated regions. At the field scale, these effects lead to enhanced near-well mineral precipitation, with implications for injectivity. Neglecting capillary geochemistry can therefore result in systematic errors in predicting reactive transport processes in geological CO 2 storage systems. The work provides a physically consistent framework for linking capillary-dependent geochemistry with continuum theory in unsaturated porous media and highlights the importance of accounting for capillary geochemistry in geoenvironmental applications.

title: Erratum to “Flood monitoring: An innovative application of multisource image fusion and transfer learning” [J. Hydrol. 669 (2026) 135107]
Hydraulic tomography for characterizing subsurface heterogeneity in fractured rocks: implications for in-situ recovery mining
abstract: In-situ recovery (ISR) mining demands reliable forecasts of groundwater flow and solute transport, which are highly sensitive to subsurface heterogeneity. This study evaluated alternative modeling approaches for characterizing heterogeneity using data from Denison’s Wheeler River Property, Saskatchewan, Canada. Spatial distributions of hydraulic conductivity (K) and specific storage (Ss) were characterized using four modeling cases: a homogeneous case, a geology-based zonation case, and two hydraulic tomography (HT) cases. All models were calibrated against 17 cross-hole aquifer tests, with one HT model additionally constrained by long-term feasibility field test (FFT) responses. Estimated K and Ss fields from four cases were subsequently validated against independent tracer test data. Results revealed systematic improvements in predictive performance with increasing model complexity, with HT models reproduced observed hydraulic responses and breakthrough curves with higher fidelity. Incorporating FFT data further enhanced delineation of large-scale hydraulic connectivity and improved BTC prediction at the more distant extraction well. These findings underscore that treating K and Ss fields to be heterogeneous and accurately characterizing their spatial distributions are essential for realistic simulations of groundwater flow and solute transport in ISR operations. Overall, we conclude that HT is an effective approach to support ISR wellfield design, recovery optimization, and environmental protection.

title: Constrained stochastic data sampling for deep learning–based time-lapse hydraulic tomography under reactive-induced permeability evolution
abstract: Most neural-network-based inversion methods are trained under specific statistical conditions, and their performance often deteriorates when the statistical properties of the target parameter fields deviate from those represented in the training dataset. This issue is particularly critical when employing neural-network-based inversion in remediation sites, where reagent injection may induce nonstationary permeability evolution through pore clogging and precipitation. To address this challenge, this study proposes a constrained stochastic data sampling strategy (SDSS) integrated with a three-dimensional Hydraulic Tomography Neural Network (HT-NN) for post-injection hydraulic conductivity (K) estimation. By using prior structural information from the pre-injection field and systematically resampling conditioning locations and conductivity values within physically constrained bounds, SDSS generates nonstationary training realizations that span a broad range of plausible post-injection K-field configurations. This strategy enables the generated training ensemble to span diverse statistical properties rather than being restricted to fixed statistical conditions, thereby reducing the mismatch between the training and target domains. The proposed framework was evaluated using field-informed semi-synthetic realizations and a field case study. The field-informed semi-synthetic validation results show that the SDSS–HT-NN framework can capture nonstationary K-field patterns. The field results indicate that, compared with the Successive Linear Estimator (SLE), HT-NN reproduces a more continuous band-like low-K structure near the injection region, shows a stronger near-field permeability decrease, and yields more accurate predictions of an independent hydraulic head dataset. These results demonstrate that the proposed SDSS–HT-NN framework provides an efficient approach for time-lapse K-field estimation under nonstationary reactive perturbations.

title: The iFLUX sensor for real-time measurement of horizontal groundwater flux magnitude and direction
abstract: Groundwater management requires reliable insights into subsurface water flux, yet effective long-term remote flux monitoring remains technically challenging due to power requirements, the difficulty of detecting low flux magnitudes, and the high operational on-site effort required by some methods. Here, we present the iFLUX horizontal flux sensor, which measures groundwater flux magnitude and direction in real time by using two perpendicularly oriented microfluidic flow chips, representing the first in situ hydrogeological application of this technology. The sensor is designed for use in fully saturated, non-cohesive porous media and is installed within a dedicated prepack filter. The complete system is deployed in a borehole drilled specifically for this purpose to ensure controlled and reproducible installation depth and orientation of the sensor. We evaluated the sensor’s magnitude and directional accuracy and assessed the stability of the measurements in a controlled laboratory sand tank experiment. Furthermore, we calibrated the sensor for flow-field distortion across a range of hydraulic conductivities using numerical modelling. Within the imposed range of 1 – 35 cm/day Darcy flux, the measured flux magnitude followed the imposed flux with an RMSE of 1.15 cm/day and an R 2 of 0.99, while directional accuracy was 4.55° (RMSE). A sensitivity analysis indicated that sensor-based flux measurements are less sensitive to uncertainty in hydraulic conductivity than Darcy-based flux calculations, where flux errors scale linearly with hydraulic conductivity errors. Overall, the sensor’s low power demand, fast response and sensitivity for low flux magnitudes suggest potential for long-term autonomous monitoring of groundwater flux in low-gradient and dynamic environments.

A copula-based stochastic simulation method for the penman wind function (PWF) in in-stream evaporation
abstract: Accurately estimating in-stream evaporation is crucial for understanding surface water losses, but it remains challenging due to the sparse availability of flux data and the complex dynamics of flowing systems. This study introduces a modeling framework that combines the Penman Wind Function (PWF) with empirical-prior-based stochastic simulation to quantify uncertainty in in-stream evaporation estimates under data-limited conditions. Rather than demonstrating universal transferability of PWF coefficients, this study focuses on identifying how coefficient uncertainty and cross-site transfer bias emerge when reservoir-, stream-, and literature-derived parameters are applied across hydrologically distinct environments. Direct calibration of PWF coefficients using high-resolution flux data from the Andong Stream Experiment Center produced the most reliable estimates ( r = 0.862 , C o E = 0.731 , R M S E = 1.500 m m / d a y ), confirming that site-specific calibration remains the preferred option when local observations are available. To support applications where such observations are unavailable, we constructed a literature-derived empirical prior parameter library of PWF coefficients and used log-space Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) with copula-based Monte Carlo sampling to propagate parameter uncertainty. The literature-derived coefficient pairs were treated as a heterogeneous empirical prior library rather than as homogeneous i.i.d. samples. Copula sensitivity analysis showed that coefficient dependence was weak and model-selection uncertainty was substantial; therefore, the Gaussian copula was used only as a parsimonious working copula and was evaluated against the independence copula. Cross-site application showed that reservoir-derived and ensemble-based coefficients retained part of the temporal co-variation driven by meteorological forcing, but they also produced non-negligible magnitude errors and systematic bias under stream conditions. At Andong, the Yongdam-derived coefficients and copula ensemble showed relatively high correlations but substantially degraded bias and RMSE compared with site-specific calibration, indicating limited coefficient transferability and reservoir-stream aerodynamic regime mismatch. Overall, the proposed framework is best interpreted as an uncertainty-aware baseline estimation approach for data-limited environments, while direct calibration remains the benchmark for reliable in-stream evaporation estimation.

title: New insights into lacustrine groundwater discharge within the groundwater-wetland-lake system in arid regions
Synergy between lacustrine groundwater discharge and dissolved organic matter in regulating seasonal CH4 and CO2 emissions in an ice–covered lake–groundwater system
Climate change projections of probable maximum precipitation over large areas through depth-area-duration analysis: A case study in Brazil
abstract: Extreme rainfall events can be catastrophic if not anticipated. Global warming is expected to intensify such events, thus any kind of human settlement must be planned and adapted to the emerging climate conditions. In this study, we investigated projections of rare extreme rainfall in large areas (>50,000 km 2 ), consistent with the horizontal resolution of global climate models (GCMs). This spatial scale is particularly suitable for assessing extreme flood hazards in large river basins, providing insights into the evolving risks due to global warming. The analysis was conducted by comparing the envelopes of Depth-Area-Duration curves between the historical and future periods of 23 GCMs, considering the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios, across four extensive and relatively homogeneous regions in South America. Regional aggregation allowed the detection of statistically significant signals for rare extreme rainfall. Through a spatiotemporal assessment, we conclude that: (i) stronger temperature increases lead to greater intensification of extreme rainfall; (ii) there are no significant differences in the magnitude of intensification among the four regions; (iii) rainfall events of different area size exhibit similar degrees of intensification; and (iv) shorter events present greater intensification. In particular, the 1-day extreme rainfall exhibit an increase consistent with the Clausius–Clapeyron relation. These results are in line with literature and provide a clear and robust summary of what to expect for rare rainfall events in large basins.

Large-scale climate teleconnections and multiscale controls on river water temperature
abstract: River water temperature dynamics are influenced by climate variability and large-scale atmospheric teleconnections, particularly in regulated river systems where anthropogenic controls interact with natural hydroclimatic drivers. This study investigates the multiscale influence of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) on river water temperature variability in a cold-region Pacific watershed influenced by Pacific climate variability. Long-term daily water temperature series were reconstructed for 1950–2024 using the hybrid Air2Stream model, and the resulting series were analyzed over the common 1950–2021 period using wavelet techniques, including the continuous wavelet transform and bivariate, partial, and multiple wavelet coherence. Results indicate that while seasonal atmospheric forcing dominates the annual thermal cycle, significant non-stationary variability emerges at interannual (2–7 years) and decadal scales. The PDO exhibits persistent and coherent coupling with river water temperature over multi-year to decadal timescales, whereas ENSO influences are episodic and primarily confined to interannual timescales. Joint PDO-ENSO interactions are most pronounced at decadal (8–16 year) periods. Comparison between regulated and natural stations suggests that flow regulation may differentially filter low-frequency variability, reducing raw interannual-to-decadal power while partially preserving coherent phase relationships with basin-scale climate modes in regulated reaches. Summer-focused analyses reveal that positive PDO phases are consistently associated with elevated river water temperatures, with mean July-September (JAS) anomalies of approximately 0.2–0.8 °C and increased exceedance frequencies above ecologically relevant thresholds (e.g., 20 °C). In contrast, ENSO-related summer temperature anomalies are weaker and spatially inconsistent. Overall, the results demonstrate that decadal-scale Pacific climate variability, particularly the PDO, plays a persistently influential role in shaping river water temperature variability in cold-region systems, highlighting the importance of accounting for non-stationary climate controls in hydrological thermal assessments.

Soil-crop hydrology modelling approaches for conjunctively estimating recharge, crop demand and pumping in irrigated agriculture: a review
abstract: Soil-crop hydrology models are frequently used to estimate regional-scale groundwater recharge, crop water use, runoff and freshwater extraction rates to support irrigation demands. Because interactions between soils, crops and irrigation practices influence recharge, crop water requirements and pumping, it is important to apply models that can simulate these processes simultaneously. This review examines 16 soil-crop hydrology models and 13 case study applications in which recharge, irrigation demand and extraction rates (i.e., from surface water and/or groundwater) were estimated to support regional water accounting and water-resource investigations. Model functions for runoff, soil water movement, root water uptake, crop growth and irrigation were compared to identify differences between models and their limitations. This review showed that 13 of the 16 models incorporate crop growth simulation linked to soil water dynamics, while 7 also account for salinity stress. Twelve models allow irrigation to be triggered based on soil water content, with 4 also allowing irrigation to respond to crop stress factors. The reliability of soil-crop hydrology models for estimating pumping rates remains uncertain because pumping was validated against metered data in only 2 of the 13 case studies reviewed. In those studies, metered extraction data provided important constraints on model parameterisation. Although runoff was simulated, it was reconciled with field observations in only 1 of the 13 case studies. Soil-crop hydrology models remain important tools for estimating recharge and irrigation demand, however, the representation of conjunctive use of groundwater and surface water, and the resulting pumping estimates, are commonly imposed externally and remain weakly validated against field observations.

Recent intensification of the negative physiological effect of CO2 on terrestrial evaporation
abstract: Abstract The net physiological effect of rising atmospheric carbon dioxide (aCO2) on terrestrial evaporation (ET) is highly uncertain. While increased CO2 fertilization elevates ET through more biomass production, the reduction in stomatal conductance (gs) that it downregulates ET. Here, using satellite-based estimates of ET and dynamic vegetation models, we investigate the physiological influence of aCO2 on ET, and isolate the respective contribution of biomass increase and gs reduction. Our results indicate that the CO2 fertilization had a net negative effect of –4.4±0.3×10–2 mm ppm–1 on ET over 1982–2018. The negative physiological effect tends to intensify with increasing aCO2, particularly in warm and humid forests. The high sensitivity of ET to gs may attenuate the expected water cycle acceleration over land, although the future evolution of these two competing physiological processes remains uncertain.

title: Integration of vertical and lateral erosion in modelling landslide mass flows, debris flows and flash floods

Coastal aquifer vulnerability to salinization under sea-level rise and groundwater abstraction pressure in a Mediterranean karst system
abstract: Sea-level rise and groundwater abstraction are reshaping coastal systems in karst environments, particularly in low-gradient coastal plains where groundwater-dependent ecosystems are strongly coupled to aquifer dynamics. However, most coastal assessments remain based on topographic inundation and shoreline retreat, neglecting groundwater processes that control the inland propagation of marine influence. This study develops an integrated hydrogeomorphological framework to quantify coastal influence under combined scenarios of sea-level rise and groundwater decline in Mallorca (Spain), and to assess implications for the spatial definition of the maritime–terrestrial public domain (MTPD). The approach integrates (i) DEM-based marine inundation, (ii) hydrogeological signals of piezometric decline and salinization derived from monitoring data, and (iii) a multi-criteria hydro-coastal vulnerability index incorporating ecological sensitivity, hydrogeological susceptibility, anthropogenic pressure, and system resilience. Direct marine inundation alone affects between 9.24 and 43.76 km² (0.25–1.20% of the island) across sea-level rise scenarios, but underestimates the inland extent of coastal influence. Including groundwater processes expands the functional coastal domain and increases ecosystem exposure, with up to 97% of wetland area and a significant proportion of springs and coastal caves located within the integrated coastal-influence zone under high-end scenarios. Vulnerability is concentrated in low-lying coastal plains, particularly in s’Albufera, Campos–Es Trenc, and Albufereta, where strong aquifer–sea connectivity and anthropogenic pressure converge. These findings show that coastal evolution in Mediterranean karst settings emerges from the interaction between surface and groundwater processes, and suggest that static representations of the MTPD may underestimate the effective extent of coastal influence under future environmental change.

Climate change impacts on alpine springs in Austria: shifts in discharge seasonality and water availability
abstract: Spring water supplies about half of Austria’s drinking water demand and is the sole source in some regions. Climate change is rapidly altering hydrological conditions in the Alps, making projections of future spring discharge essential for sustainable water management. This study assesses climate change impacts on 70 alpine springs across the Austrian Alps, covering a wide range of climatic and hydrogeological settings. Plausible catchments were identified using a rainfall–runoff model with a snow module, which was forced with climate projections from three emission scenarios (RCP 2.6, 4.5, and 8.5) and 40 model realizations to evaluate impacts until 2100. Changes were assessed by comparing a historical reference period (1980–2009) with a near-future period (2030–2059) and a far-future period (2070–2099). Analyses were conducted for individual springs and hydrologically classified spring groups. Results indicate decreasing spring discharge in western Austria under all scenarios and periods. Under RCP 4.5 and 8.5, discharge reductions also emerge in southern Austria. Annual discharge changes generally remain within single-digit percentages, in both positive and negative directions, but differ among spring groups. Snow-dominated and recession-dominated springs show the highest sensitivity to emission scenarios, whereas fast-responding springs maintain positive annual changes. Seasonal shifts are pronounced, with increased spring time discharge for snow-dominated springs and reduced summer and autumn discharge for both snow-dominated and fast-responding springs. Low flows shift from late winter and early spring toward summer and autumn, intensifying under higher-emission scenarios. These results provide a basis for climate adaptation and sustainable water management in Austria.

title: Hydrodynamic reconstruction of tidal river networks based on sensitivity analysis of responses to sluice–pump scheduling: a case study of episodic pollution control
Learning water diversion behaviour in regulated river networks using graph neural networks and neural decision trees
abstract: Human water diversions alter river dynamics and are difficult to represent when operational rules are uncertain or discontinuous. This study investigates how graph-based deep learning models represent diversion behaviour in river networks under varying degrees of prior operational knowledge. Using SWAT+ simulations as an internally consistent synthetic benchmark, we design controlled diversion scenarios of increasing rule complexity. We compare graph attention networks that embed river network topology and diversion connectivity directly into their model structure, with no prior operational information, with partial structural constraints, with fully prescribed rules applied in post-processing, and with a hybrid architecture that explicitly separates hydrological prediction from operational decision-making via a Neural Decision Tree. All approaches reproduce total flow before diversion robustly, while diverted flow skill declines with operational complexity. Additional operational knowledge does not consistently improve predictive accuracy, as diversion errors are dominated by propagation from total-flow uncertainty. The hybrid model achieves comparable skill while providing explicit and analysable decision representations, highlighting trade-offs between flexibility, robustness, and interpretability. The modular and structurally explicit formulation illustrates how graph-based AI components can support transparent and interpretable representations of operational decision-making in regulated river systems, though validation across diverse catchments and real-world operational conditions remains necessary.

Multivariate and hydrochemical assessment of rivers and groundwater in the Mediterranean Besòs basin (Spain)
abstract: In the context of climate change, integrated strategies to preserve water quantity and quality in Mediterranean basins are increasingly needed. Here, we investigate hydrochemical patterns of rivers and aquifers in the Besòs basin (NE Spain) and assess how hydrological variability influences these patterns at basin scale. Long-term monitoring data (2007–2024) from river stations and wells were analysed using site-level median concentrations of major ions and nutrients, wet-dry contrasts, flow and groundwater level time series, and multivariate statistical analyses. Groundwater shows higher Ca 2+ , HCO 3 - and NO 3 - concentrations, particularly in forested and agricultural areas, consistent with recharge and carbonate mineralization. Lower concentrations in wells close to rivers are consistent with groundwater-river interactions, including groundwater discharge and local mixing along losing reaches. River waters display higher pH and lower geogenic solute concentrations, consistent with groundwater influence and dilution by runoff. Spatial salinity patterns in both compartments are associated with Na + , Cl - and K + inputs from urban and industrial land use and with dilution capacity. In impacted sites, Na + and Cl - may dominate over Ca 2+ and HCO 3 - and are often accompanied by higher TOC and PO 4 3- . Rivers’ salinity-related ions increase during low-flow periods, sometimes exceeding groundwater concentrations, whereas concentrations decrease during high-flow periods indicating rainfall-driven dilution. Groundwater-related ions show limited sensitivity to hydrological variability, consistent with a buffered origin. Overall, groundwater-river connectivity and land use are associated with spatial hydrochemical patterns, while hydrological variability modulates dilution and anthropogenic influence.

title: Understanding hydrological drought recovery patterns in a changing environment: Insights from a non-stationary multivariate analysis
Hillslope lag times for flood runoff are extremely short in high-relief meso-scale catchments
abstract: Understanding flood propagation in mountainous areas during heavy rainfall is crucial for disaster prevention. A previous study on flood propagation reported that the hillslope lag time is extremely short and almost negligible in meso -scale (1–10 km 2 ) and medium-relief catchments. However, hydrological observations during heavy rainfall events in high-relief meso -scale catchments remain scarce. Therefore, this process has rarely been discussed. This study aimed to clarify flood propagation in high-relief meso -scale catchments with long and steep hillslopes. Seven mountain catchments (0.16–9.01 km 2 ) underlain by accretionary sedimentary rock in Japan were investigated. Rainfall and water-level data over approximately 1.5 years were analyzed. The modal flow path lengths in the channel and hillslope at each site were calculated, and their relationships to the peak lag time (the time difference between rainfall and runoff peaks) were analyzed. Events showing a significant positive correlation between modal channel length and peak lag time accounted for only up to 15% of all events; in these events, hillslope lag time was estimated to be relatively uniform and extremely short (mean: −0.84 min; maximum: 160 min). This rapid hillslope response was confirmed even when the contributing area expanded. Conversely, some events exhibited a significant negative correlation. Although the lag time in larger catchments was similar to that observed in positively correlated events, a remarkably long peak lag time occurred in smaller catchments. This suggests that the initial rainfall loss and groundwater contribution may have been relatively greater in smaller catchments.

Corrigendum to “A causality-informed and copula-based framework for predictive assessment of downstream water-quality risks under extreme scenarios” [J. Hydrol., 669, Part B (2026) 135123]
Physics-guided symbolic regression of nonlocal transport memory from sparse observations in aquatic systems
abstract: Predicting non-Fickian transport in aquatic systems from sparse observations is challenging because historical effects and spatial heterogeneity often control present behavior. We introduce a physics-guided, sequential hybrid framework that couples nonlocal transport theory with deep-learning-assisted symbolic regression to infer transport memory directly from one-dimensional observations, such as breakthrough curves (BTCs) or spatial concentration snapshots. The physics module maps observations to a nonparametric memory representation derived from the statistics of microscopic particle dynamics, including temporal memory associated with mass-transfer-controlled transport and spatial (kinematic) memory represented by the streamtube velocity probability density function (PDF) for conductivity-driven spreading, thereby unifying temporal and spatial nonlocality within a single construct. Neural reconstruction, coupled with a stable numerical Laplace transform, produces denoised, high-resolution spectral representations, from which symbolic regression identifies compact, closed-form expressions for transport memory that are embedded back into the nonlocal model. Validation spans synthetic and experimental systems: semi-analytical fractional diffusion and a Cr(VI) column experiment (power-law kernels); a Red Cedar River tracer test (reach-specific, exponentially tempered kernels); random-walk particle tracking (Gamma-family velocity laws); groundwater tracer transport at the MADE field site (independently referred inverse-Gamma velocity PDFs for MADE-1 and MADE-2 with out-of-sample predictive skill); and sediment transport in the North Loup River (a symmetric heavy-tailed velocity PDF capturing both backward and forward scaling). Across all cases, the inferred models reproduce observed transport behavior and accurately predict withheld profiles while remaining interpretable and parsimonious, without requiring prior characterization of aquatic system properties beyond geometry and boundary conditions. Compared to a purely data-driven sparse-regression approach on the same MADE-2 dataset, which yields only a near-integer-order advection equation (\alpha = 0.99​) with no dispersion, our physics-guided framework captures the anomalous spreading and predicts withheld concentration snapshots, demonstrating enhanced robustness under sparse, noisy conditions. By bridging data-driven inference with nonlocal transport physics and expanding the concept of transport memory to encompass both temporal and spatial nonlocality, the proposed framework provides a practical and interpretable pathway for modeling anomalous transport under observational constraints common in laboratory and field hydrologic systems. This capability enables practical inference of dominant transport mechanisms and plume evolution in field systems where only sparse monitoring data are available.

title: Organic phosphorus fractions drive microbial diversity and assembly in the largest freshwater lake in northeast Asia
Organic carbon dynamics in a subtropical watershed: hydrological processes and land use controls
Depth-dependent freeze–thaw propagation and antecedent controls on post-thaw soil water storage in a seasonally frozen basin
Grounding large language models in hydrologic modelling
abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) possess extensive hydrological knowledge, they often struggle to appropriately simulate complex physical processes in hydrological systems. To address this limitation, we present an LLM-based agentic intelligent modelling approach for hydrological time-series forecasting (HydroAIM). HydroAIM decouples the multi-agent architecture through the model context protocol (MCP) to integrate an expert task workflow, a standardised algorithmic workflow (SAW) library, and an iterative feedback closed-loop execution toolbox. Comprehensive experiments demonstrated that across 100 modelling tasks of varying types utilising four LLMs, HydroAIM achieved an execution success rate of 91%. Ablation studies have revealed that removing the expert task workflow causes complete system failure owing to planning chaos, plummeting the success rate to 0%. This result indicates that long-horizon task planning is the core bottleneck restricting LLMs from executing hydrological modelling tasks. Furthermore, when applied to 671 catchments in the Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-sample Studies (CAMELS) dataset without human intervention, HydroAIM achieves median Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) values of 0.63 and 0.64 for local and global modelling, respectively, meeting the application benchmarks established by traditional physical models. This study not only demonstrates the capability of LLMs as a hydrologic modelling tool but also provides a scalable pathway for grounding general LLMs in quantitative tasks within specialised scientific domains.

title: Controls on carbon and nutrient transport in a tidal creek across a coastal forest-marsh transition under sea-level rise
abstract: Sea level rise (SLR) and saltwater intrusion (SWI) drive ecological and biogeochemical changes in coastal forests that alter solute fluxes between marshes and estuaries. Tidal creeks mediate transport of carbon (C), iron (Fe), and nitrogen (N) during flood and ebb tides, yet quantifying elemental fluxes is challenging due to bidirectional tidal flow and frequent bank overtopping. We quantified surface-water transport of C, Fe, and N during spring tides and storm events (2022–2023) in a tidal creek draining a transitioning coastal forest along the Delaware Bay. Discharge was estimated using a novel rating-curve model that incorporates bank overtopping dynamics. Groundwater wells and redox probes along a marsh-to-forest transect monitored water table elevation, salinity, and redox potential. We observed net imports of dissolved organic carbon (DOC), dissolved organic nitrogen (DON), dissolved Fe, and ammonium (NH4-N). DOC hourly loads were positively correlated with dissolved Fe loads, suggesting microbial dissolution of C-bearing Fe oxides during flood tides, and reprecipitation and C retention on ebb tides. Plant uptake and nitrification drove NH4-N and DON imports, as plant uptake during high tide could remove N from the water column. There was no import or export of nitrate (NO3-N), but NO3-N hourly loads were positively correlated with marsh redox potential, consistent with denitrification under reduced conditions. As the coastal zone responds to accelerating SLR, dissolution of Fe protected C will inhibit C sequestration and marsh loss to SLR could increase N delivery to coastal waters as plants uptake less N, with downstream implications for eutrophication.

A digital twin framework for real-time probabilistic forecasting of permeable pavement performance
Self-similarity criticality of the world’s large river systems
abstract: River networks, as hierarchical conduits of material transport and energy conversion, exhibit self-similar structural patterns that are fundamental to hydrological processes. Yet, the mechanisms constraining their self-similarity boundaries remain elusive. Here, by analyzing 66 global large river basins (≥ 100,000 km 2 ) using HydroATLAS data, we define a self-similar validity ratio (SVR) to quantify the normalized stream-order domain over which scale-invariant organization persists. River networks converge at low-to-medium stream orders (1–5) but diverge at higher orders (6–10), with the global SVR distribution has a dominant range of 0.57–0.67 that statistically aligns with the golden-ratio conjugate (φ = 0.618). It motivates classification of three self-similar criticality regimes, i.e., sub-golden, golden-aligned, and supra-golden rivers. By further constructing a self-similar criticality framework supported by three domain-guided composite hydrogeomorphic indices, validated against an energetic response index derived from the criticality thresholds at the self-similar collapse boundary, we reveal that the three regime types of rivers respectively correspond to energy-limited, energy-balanced, and energy-surplus states, and the alignment between SVR and φ marks a stable equilibrium state of hierarchical energy redistribution within river networks, where hydrological carrier capacity, geomorphic potential energy, and network geometry coordinate well to maintain long-term self-similar organization. These findings transform self-similarity from structural descriptions into physically based energetic analysis, which advance predictive tools for basin resilience under climate change, enabling optimized flood-hazard screening, erosion risk diagnosis, sediment management, and strategic hydropower planning

title: Spatiotemporal dynamics of reference evapotranspiration in China (1981–2020): Insights into its teleconnection with sea surface temperature patterns

P-FLOOD: a probabilistic framework for flood hazard mapping in levee-protected floodplains
abstract: The paper presents a probabilistic framework for mapping hazard induced by river floods in levee-protected floodplains. Large-scale hazard maps of water depth (or any other hazard variable) are derived from their cumulative probability distributions, estimated throughout the domain from a set of flood simulations that combine different inflow hydrographs and multiple levee-failure scenarios. For each simulation, levee breach probabilities are estimated using fragility functions conditioned on the local hydraulic loading. By accounting for the joint probability of hydrological and breaching events, the method enables a probabilistic characterization of hazard metrics and produces hazard maps associated with any exceedance probability, not constrained by the discrete return periods of the hydrological inputs. Flood simulations require integrated two-dimensional hydrodynamic models to include flood routing, breach formation, and ensuing floodplain inundation. To limit the computational load, a scalable parent–child strategy is proposed to reduce the number of simulations while retaining acceptable accuracy in the estimated probability field. Moreover, the available simulations can be reused to recompute hazard maps at negligible cost to consider varied probability of hydrological and/or breaching events (due to climate change, levee reinforcements, etc.). The framework is applied to a pilot case study in the Adige River (Northern Italy), considering fragility functions for overflow-induced failures and a flood-prone area of ∼ 100 km 2 . The results suggest that, if supplied with realistic estimations of levee fragility, P-FLOOD can provide improved hazard predictions than traditional approaches, especially for frequent flood events, thereby supporting more informed flood risk management and planning.

title: Impacts of submarine groundwater discharge on inland and seaside basins of estuaries
Real-time control of rainwater harvesting in an urban catchment: a model predictive control approach under forecasting uncertainty
abstract: Rainwater harvesting (RWH) is gaining popularity in urban water systems as a tool to address the challenges posed by urbanization and climate change. Urban areas face water scarcity and increased runoff due to growing population and the conversion of natural areas into impermeable surfaces. RWH systems can serve as stormwater control measures while storing and supplying rainwater for non-potable uses. However, RWH systems become less effective as storm events exceed their storage capacity. To overcome this limitation, the field of real-time controlled RWH systems has emerged in the latest research. These systems release water from tanks before and during significant rain events, reducing uncontrolled overflows. This study examines the effects of favourable control policies on an urban catchment retrofitted with RWH systems. A simulation-optimisation procedure is developed to generate flexible control policies that adapt to changing rainfall forecasts using concepts from the Model Predictive Control approach. The methodology aims to reduce peak flows, minimise rainwater release, and optimise a single objective function without complex procedures. The methodology is evaluated through simulations of 73 rain events in a case study catchment. The MPC achieved a median peak flow reduction of 29% while maintaining low rainwater availability losses (median rainwater availability reduction: 1.5–2.0%). Forecast uncertainty had only a minor impact on performance, and the MPC consistently outperformed rule-based control strategies, providing superior flood mitigation while preserving stored rainwater. The results show promising outcomes in mitigating flows while maximising water availability, suggesting potential to enhance urban resilience.

title: Integrating hydrogeomorphic changes into flood hazard assessment: approach for an eco-touristic mountainous river
abstract: Traditional flood risk assessments often overlook the hydrogeomorphic changes that occur during extreme events, despite their significant impact on subsequent flood behavior. This study investigates the influence of riverbed evolution on flood hazards in the Boi River catchment, located in a mountainous region in southern Brazil characterized by canyons, intense orographic precipitation, and ecotourism activities, through the application of the CAESAR-Lisflood Landscape Evolution Model. The Boi River has experienced recurrent flash floods that reshape its morphology. The model was calibrated using historical flood data, and its morphological response was locally evaluated at one downstream cross-section using pre- and post-event field surveys. Simulations were conducted for design storms with return periods of 2, 5, 25, and 100 years to analyze morphological changes, and the resulting Digital Elevation Models were then used as fixed terrain inputs in controlled RP002 simulations to isolate the hydraulic legacy of each individual antecedent event. Findings reveal that more extreme events cause significant bed aggradation and hydraulic spreading, altering flow depth, velocity, and hazard at selected exposed locations. Notably, the flood extent for a 2-year event increased by 16% when preceded by a 100-year event. A supplementary mobile-bed diagnostic for the RP100–RP002 case produced similar domain-wide inundation and HI-threshold exceedance results. These findings underscore the importance of accounting for sediment transport and morphological dynamics in flood hazard assessments. The CAESAR-Lisflood model provided a useful framework for exploring how flood-induced morphological changes may modify subsequent hazard patterns, although its morphological performance could only be evaluated locally.

title: Enhancing river flow prediction accuracy in data scarce catchments using a time varying ensemble deep learning approach
