Integrated remote sensing retrieval of surface and root-zone soil moisture through physical mechanisms-guided machine learning
Ensembling or not? On the value of boosting and bagging for physics-aware machine learning in hydrology
abstract: • Ensembling adds limited value to physics-aware Machine Learning (PaML) models. • Single well-configured PaML matches ensemble performance • Classical boosting compensates low-capacity PaML learners. • Bagging provides limited additional predictive benefit. • GrowNet-inspired boosting shows non-monotonic behavior. Ensemble machine learning methods such as bagging and boosting are widely used to improve predictive performance in hydrological modeling. However, their value when applied to physics-aware machine learning (PaML) models remains largely unexplored. This study investigates whether ensemble strategies provide tangible predictive gains over a standalone PaML model for streamflow simulation. Four controlled experiments were conducted on five representative catchments from the Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-sample Studies dataset for the contiguous United States (CAMELS-US) to evaluate the influence of training epochs, base learner capacity, ensemble size, and training data length. Bagging, classical boosting, and a growth-based boosting formulation inspired by GrowNet were compared against both weak and well-configured single PaML models. Predictive performance was assessed using the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), the Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) and the normalized root mean square error (NRMSE). Results show that ensemble strategies do not yield substantial improvements over a properly configured standalone PaML model, despite requiring greater computational resources. While classical boosting can compensate for intentionally reduced model capacity by aggregating low-capacity PaML learners, the resulting gains remain marginal relative to a moderately expressive single model. Bagging provides limited additional benefits, and the growth-based boosting formulation exhibits non-monotonic and basin-dependent behavior. Overall, the findings suggest that, within the investigated framework, refining the architecture and capacity of a single PaML model is generally more effective than adopting ensemble strategies. These results contribute to clarifying the practical role of ensemble learning in physics-aware hydrological modeling.

title: Straw return enhances groundwater nitrate attenuation by fueling subsurface carbon–nitrogen coupling: Evidence from field monitoring and metagenomics
Well-balanced lattice Boltzmann modelling of the depth-averaged age equation and its correlations with environmental indicators in a typical urban flood retention area
A generalized three-dimensional manifold for the Budyko hypothesis: analytical derivation and structural stability in open hydrological systems
abstract: The classical Budyko framework provides a foundational description of long-term hydroclimatic partitioning but assumes hydrological closure, making it structurally inadequate for basins influenced by glacier melt, groundwater depletion, reservoir regulation, or inter-basin water transfers. This study presents the ShakyaQX (SQX) manifold — a generalized three-dimensional extension of the Budyko hypothesis that represents hydroclimatic partitioning as a surface in the state space (x, γ, φ), where x = PET/P is the climatic aridity index, γ is a landscape response parameter, and φ = 1 + ΔS/P is an orthogonal openness coordinate derived from the generalized water balance. By introducing φ as a true independent geometric axis rather than embedding it in the climatic coordinate, SQX eliminates the hyperbolic singularity that afflicts all input-rescaling (IR) approaches ([[EQUATION]] → ∞ as P + ΔS → 0) and avoids the piecewise bimodal formulations required by Gao et al. (2020) and He et al. (2025). The SQX formulation is proven to satisfy strict monotonicity and global concavity, to maintain bounded sensitivity [[EQUATION]]), and to reduce exactly to the Mezentsev-Choudhury-Yang curve when φ = 1.For the special case γ = 1, SQX reduces to the harmonic sum of x and φ, directly linking Budyko theory to the dual-resistance (Penman-Monteith) framework at the basin scale. Application to the Brahmaputra Basin at Golpara (2002-2021) yields [[EQUATION]] at annual scale.At monthly scale, 63 of 242 observations satisfy the SQX admissibility conditions (φ > 0, ET ≥ 0, [[EQUATION]]), yielding [[EQUATION]] with NSE = 0.650 and KGE = 0.651. The three admissibility violation years (2010, 2013, 2017) are diagnosed as probable GRACE overestimation events, demonstrating that the SQX admissibility bound functions as a sensitive detector of satellite storage uncertainty in cryosphere-influenced basins. SQX outperforms IR on four of five performance metrics and provides a structurally robust, physically interpretable foundation for hydroclimatic analysis under non-stationary and anthropogenically influenced conditions.

title: Integrating SWOT data and machine learning for high-resolution river surface velocity retrieval in data-scarce headwater regions
A historical data curation (HDC) framework integrated with GIS-based multi-criteria decision analysis to inform flood risk prioritization in data-scarce regions
abstract: Data-scarce regions lack reliable long-term gauging records and standardized flood databases which constrains classical flood risk assessments and fail to adequately reflect local contexts. Global initiatives emphasize investments in non-traditional data curation to improve the representation of vulnerability and to transform how disaster risk is addressed, complementing systematic flood risk assessment strategies. In this study, we present the outcomes of past flood information curation from newspapers and archives to build a national flood database and evaluate the basin-scale flood risk. We particularly propose a reproducible Historical Data Curation– Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (HDC–MCDA) framework that transforms qualitative historical archives into standardized quantitative Curated Historical Flood Descriptors (CFD) and integrates them with conventional GIS-based MCDA flood risk analysis. We curated a database of 700 flood events (1955–2020) in Lebanon with documented description and impacts. Two CFD, Historical Flood Occurrence ( Ne ) and Historical Flood Severity ( Sev ), were developed through text processing and integrated in the MCDA analysis. The study was applied for 16 basins, where hazard and vulnerability are represented by conventional morphological, hydrological and land-use descriptors extracted from available data. Across the studied scenarios, HDC-MCDA led to notable shift in flood risk level, suggesting that HDC captures the realized impact and recalibrates flood risk prioritization by perceived impact information that is often not reflected by scarce hazard and vulnerability data. The study provides a reproducible framework for “soft” documentary data curation and integration into risk assessments, informing prioritization of mitigation and early warning efforts in data-scarce countries.

title: Hydroclimatic seasonality, bacterioplankton, and dissolved organic matter in a semi-enclosed plateau lake

Investigating streamflow dynamics in heterogeneous catchments through sensitivity function analysis
abstract: Comprehending hydrological responses in heterogeneous catchments poses a considerable challenge, primarily due to the spatial variability and complexity of rainfall-runoff processes. This study investigates the streamflow recession behavior within the Vipava River catchment in southwestern Slovenia. The catchment is characterized by contrasting hydrogeological regions, including karst plateaus and impermeable flysch valleys. The analysis focuses on comparing the karst spring-fed upper Vipava river and the torrential Branica stream draining flysch areas. An analysis of long-term daily discharge data was conducted to extract information on streamflow recession. The catchment sensitivity functions were derived to discern discrepancies in hydrological response under varying antecedent conditions. The karst spring sensitivity function exhibits sustained discharge, with activation of underground karst conduits during periods of high flow. Conversely, the flysch-dominated Branica stream demonstrates rapid increases and fast recession, leading to extremely low flows and possible drying out during extended rainless periods. The results highlight the information content of discharge recession data for identifying spatial heterogeneity and distinct flow mechanisms in catchments with different storage characteristics. When expressed through catchment sensitivity functions, this recession-derived information can be incorporated into diagnostic hydrological simulations to compare the hydrological responses of heterogeneous catchments and improve understanding of their functioning under contrasting antecedent conditions.

title: Assessment of agricultural drought resilience in China based on coupled drought propagation and recovery processes
Climate change both increases and decreases winter snowmelt across North America
abstract: Snowmelt, a vital source of freshwater for a large portion of North America’s population, is increasingly vulnerable to the impact of climate change. Air temperature and precipitation are significant climatic controllers regulating snowmelt dynamics. In this study, we quantified the response of winter snowmelt magnitude to changing temperature and precipitation across North America (Canada and the United States) using gridded, observation-driven data and future projections. Our analysis of far-future conditions (2091-2100) reveals a significant increase (>60%) in winter (November-March) snowmelt in northern latitudes, while southern latitudes are projected to experience a decline (<38%). Projected snowmelt changes are strongly associated with changes in winter temperature, while projected declines are consistent with regions experiencing reduced snowfall under warming climates. Our findings suggest that the probability of an increase in winter snowmelt is high under the warmer and wetter climatic conditions prevailing in northern regions. In contrast, winter snowmelt across southern latitudes is likely to decrease. Plain language summary Snowmelt plays a critical role in sustaining water resources for large populations across North America. As temperature and precipitation are major climatic factors regulating snowmelt dynamics, changes in these variables can affect the magnitude of snowmelt. Given projected climate change, it is essential to assess the vulnerability of snowmelt magnitude to changing temperatures and precipitation to understand future water availability. Our analysis of future winter snowmelt under compound changes in air temperature and precipitation across North America indicates that winter snowmelt could increase by 60% in many regions of Canada. In contrast, in southern areas, the winter snowmelt volume could decrease by as much as 38%. These results suggest that warmer winters are the primary driver of increased snowmelt, while reduced snowfall primarily governs the projected snowmelt declines.

Shifting controls on DIC export in the Doce River Basin during baseflow conditions: from rock weathering to anthropogenic forcing
abstract: Tropical rivers play a disproportionately important role in global carbon fluxes, yet they remain underrepresented in biogeochemical datasets. This study investigated the fluvial fluxes of Dissolved Inorganic Carbon (DIC) and dominant hydrochemical processes in 499 small tropical rivers and streams across the Doce River Basin (DRB), Brazil, a region affected by the 2015 Fundão Dam collapse, the world’s largest mining tailings dam failure and Brazil’s most severe environmental disaster. Water samples were collected during dry-season baseflow conditions in 2010. Surface-water chemistry reflects the combined influence of silicate weathering and anthropogenic inputs, with a mean DIC fluvial flux of 5.44 kg C km −2 day −1 . Rock weathering is the dominant basin-scale control on DIC concentrations, as indicated by a factor explaining 40.6% of the total hydrochemical variance (Ca2 + , Mg2 + , Na + , HCO 3 − ), consistent with the basin’s predominantly silicate lithology and localized contributions from carbonate-bearing units upstream. Anthropogenic inputs act as a secondary but systematic control, particularly in the midstream sector, where pasture land use is associated with higher DIC concentrations (r = +0.448, p < 0.001), while mining and urban effluents locally enrich alkalinity and major ions. Micro-basins dominated by natural land cover show lower mean DIC concentrations (5.24 mg C L −1 ) than anthropogenically influenced sub-basins (11.13 mg C L −1 ), a 2.1-fold difference. As these results derive from a single dry-season campaign, they should not be extrapolated to an annual DIC budget. Overall, this study provides a hydrogeochemical characterization of tributary systems in the DRB, supporting future monitoring and environmental assessment efforts.

title: Monthly dynamics of global surface water from 2015 to 2023
Corrigendum to “PINN framework for urban flood depth prediction: integrating data-driven insights with physical constraints” [J. Hydrol. 665 (2026) 134693]
Coupled thermal-hydraulic model of the continental subsurface: theory, regimes, and reduced solver
abstract: The thermal regime of the continental subsurface is shaped by the interplay of atmospheric forcing, groundwater flow, and solid Earth heat. While many existing models couple groundwater flow and heat transport, and in some cases incorporate freeze-thaw or thermo-hydro-mechanical processes, representing the full spectrum of two-way feedbacks often remains challenging. This paper has two components and keeps them distinct throughout. The first is theoretical: a continuum formulation that explicitly couples two-way thermal-hydraulic feedback with a smooth freeze-thaw treatment. From first principles, we derive the governing equations for mass and energy and perform a scaling analysis that yields nine dimensionless numbers, including a newly identified thermal-hydraulic coupling metric (ΓN α ). These numbers quantify the competition between pressure diffusion, saturation storage, thermal expansion, conduction, advection, and latent heat, and they define quantitative regime diagrams for the three interfaces (land surface, subsurface, crust-mantle). We reduce the full three-dimensional system to a closed one-dimensional vertical column suitable for basin-scale applications. The second component is a reduced thermal-hydraulic numerical implementation, narrower than the theory. This open-source finite-volume solver (implicit time stepping, upwind advection, apparent-heat-capacity freeze-thaw) carries the thermal-expansion feedback, Darcy advection and freeze-thaw, but omits the phase-change mass source, the poroelastic porosity evolution, the skeleton momentum balance, and the gas phase. The solver reports its own mass-and energy-budget residuals, and those diagnostics show that the omitted source is a first-order wherever the freezing point is crossed. The solver is cross-verified against an independent finite-difference Crank-Nicolson code and passes six analytical benchmarks (Carslaw-Jaeger, Stefan, Theis, Terzaghi, undrained thermo-poroelastic ratio, Bonacina), most of which are operator verifications. Four canonical 1-D case studies (permafrost, geothermal reservoir, arid basin, thermo-poro coupled) demonstrate consistency between the designed inputs and the proposed theoretical classification, and a 2-D extension explores lateral basin recharge-discharge and permafrost edge effects. The open-source solver, within its applicability domain, equipped with a test suite and conservation diagnostics, provides a computational tool for attributing subsurface thermal anomalies to their physical drivers and for projecting future thermal evolution under changing environmental conditions.

title: Strategies for correcting nonstationary resistivity–water content relations in time-lapse electrical resistivity tomography
abstract: Time-lapse Electrical Resistivity Tomography (ERT) provides an attractive framework for quantifying spatially distributed water-content dynamics, yet quantitative interpretation remains limited by uncertainty in the petrophysical relationship between resistivity ( ρ ) and volumetric water content ( θ ). This uncertainty is distinct from that associated with lithological heterogeneity, measurement resolution, or inversion artefacts, and can arise from temporal variability in the ρ – θ relationship itself. We examine two approaches for representing this nonstationary behaviour: a particle-filter data-assimilation framework that requires continuous or periodic co-located water-content observations from an independent sensor system to dynamically calibrate time-varying petrophysical parameters, and a machine-learning model that predicts θ from resistivity-based predictors together with auxiliary environmental information, including surface water content and contact resistance, after training. Synthetic experiments indicate that the imposed time-varying petrophysical scaling coefficient, a ( t ) , and saturation exponent, b ( t ) , can be recovered with low trajectory error across the tested ranges of parameter amplitudes, frequencies, and resistivity-noise levels. Applications at two sandy vadose-zone sites in Western Australia show that data-assimilation-based dynamic calibration of the petrophysical relationship substantially improves consistency between ERT-derived water-content reconstructions and the co-located water-content observations assimilated by the particle filter. The particle-filter reconstructions should therefore be interpreted as assimilation-constrained dynamic reconstructions that evaluate the benefit of updating the ρ – θ relationship through time relative to a stationary petrophysical calibration. The data assimilation framework provides a direct depiction of how the relationship evolves through time, capturing gradual seasonal shifts as well as extended periods of relative stability. Machine learning offers a practical alternative when sufficient and representative data are available. The observed variability in the effective petrophysical relationship covaried with near-surface environmental and electrode-contact conditions, as indicated in part by contact-resistance diagnostics. We interpret these associations as empirical and installation-specific, rather than as evidence that contact resistance is an intrinsic soil property or an independent causal control. Accounting for temporal variability in the petrophysical relationship improves the interpretability and reliability of quantitative time-lapse ERT analyses.

title: Overcoming phosphate scarcity in summer: DOP bioavailability mediates nutrient cycling in the Yellow Sea
On non-axisymmetric flow near circumferentially partially clogged artesian wells with mixed boundary conditions
abstract: Conventional models of well hydraulics assume a fully penetrating well screen, imposing axisymmetric flow at the well face. In practice, partial clogging can restrict the hydraulic connection to only a portion of the circumference, creating a non-axisymmetric flow field that existing radially symmetric models cannot describe. In this study, we develop a non-uniform flux (NUF) semi-analytical model for transient groundwater flow to and from a circumferentially partially clogged well in a confined aquifer. A mixed boundary condition, consisting of an impermeable condition on the non-screened section and a uniform-drawdown condition on the screened section, allows well-face flux to vary angularly. We solve the resulting initial-boundary value problem with mixed boundary conditions by discretising the screened section into piecewise-uniform flux segments, sequentially applying the Laplace transform and finite Fourier cosine transform, and performing time-domain inversion using the Stehfest algorithm. The NUF solution reduces to the uniform-flux (UF) solution when the number of flux segments is set to one. Parametric analysis reveals that partial circumferential screen blockage mainly produces a localized near-well effect under constant-rate test (CRT) conditions, whereas its influence can persist throughout almost the entire flow domain under constant-head test (CHT) conditions. Across all conditions, NUF predictions fall between the UF and fully penetrating-well solutions and are consistently closer to the latter, indicating that the UF assumption overestimates the mitigating effect of the non-screened region. These findings establish the NUF model as a more accurate framework for interpreting pumping or injection tests in wells affected by circumferential clogging and improve understanding of flow behaviour in circumferentially partially clogged wells.

Assessment of multi-driver human interventions on streamflow and its components based on information and complexity metrics
abstract: Human activities increasingly modify river systems, yet quantifying their independent and combined effects on streamflow remains challenging due to nonlinear, multi-driver interactions and time-lagged hydrological responses. This study proposes a framework that combines information-theoretic and complexity metrics to evaluate how diverse human interventions affect total streamflow and its components. Total streamflow was decomposed into fast-streamflow, intermediate interflow, slow-streamflow, and dry-weather flow through an improved multi-component streamflow separation method. Complex relationships between anthropogenic drivers and streamflow components were assessed through a Multi-Source Human Intervention Index (MSHI) derived from information-theoretic dependence, with human activities represented by remote-sensing indicators. Case-study results show that fast-streamflow and dry-weather flow are most sensitive to human activities, with mean MSHI values exceeding 0.6 in study cases. Night-time light and impervious surface percentage were the most influential drivers. Basin complexity was further employed to examine the consistency and interpretability of the assessment results. Building on these findings, this study provides a scalable approach for assessing the complex, nonlinear impacts of human interventions on river systems.

title: Grain size and thickness of event layers in relation to the flood magnitude: examples from floodplains in the middle and lower Yangtze River, China

Dual urban runoff response to urbanization and contradictory precipitation trends driven by climate change
abstract: Urban flooding poses a growing threat to cities worldwide, driven by the compounding effects of climate change and urbanization. This study examines the effect of urbanization and contradictory precipitation trends, defined as increasing storm intensity and decreasing total precipitation, on urban runoff. Analysing CMIP6 projections, we show that contradictory precipitation is projected to impact 26% of urban areas globally. To examine how these trends manifest at finer scales, we analyse changes in heavy precipitation events at both regional and catchment scales using convection-permitting WRF simulations. Their hydrological implications are then assessed using a calibrated SWMM urban runoff model driven by an ensemble of over 5,300 spatially shifted simulations. We find that future storms become more spatially confined while their short-duration maximal intensities increase at both regional and catchment scales. Consequently, from a catchment-scale hydrological perspective, weak runoff peaks become weaker, while strong peaks become stronger, a pattern that is amplified by urbanization. Furthermore, peak runoff is increasingly governed by short-duration rainfall intensities under future conditions, an effect amplified by urbanization. Additionally, we suggest a mechanism whereby more compact future storms suppress runoff when they miss the catchment, yet amplify peaks when they overlap with it. Concurrently, drier antecedent conditions suppress runoff from weak events while intense bursts rapidly exceed infiltration and storage capacities. This contrasting urban hydrological response to climate change poses a critical challenge for urban flood management.

Multi-scale mapping of GDEs from remote sensing and field surveys in the Urumqi River–Chaiwopu Basin
abstract: Groundwater-Dependent Ecosystems (GDEs) are widely distributed in arid and semi-arid regions and provide critical ecological services. However, their precise identification and mapping remain challenging due to insufficient integration of geospatial technologies with field measurement techniques. This study selected the terminal year of a prolonged drought and the most recent year for analysis, covering the period 2001–2023. We employed key indicators including Fractional Vegetation Cover (FVC), the difference between evapotranspiration and precipitation (ET-P), the Terrain Wetness Index (TWI), and the Vegetation Groundwater Accessibility Index (VGUI). The K-means clustering algorithm was applied for classification, and spatial overlay analysis was conducted in the Urumqi River–Chaiwopu Basin in Xinjiang, China, to assess the spatial distribution and temporal variations of GDEs. The results were validated by integrating wetland distribution data with field investigations. The findings indicate that areas classified as “likely” or “very likely” GDEs are predominantly concentrated around Dongdao Haizi, Chaiwopu Lake, the salt lakes, and adjacent regions, covering 45.4% of the potential area (4,197.89 km2). Wetland-based validation yielded a producer’s accuracy of 84.1%. Over time, the area classified as “unlikely” or “very unlikely” for GDEs showed an increasing trend. After incorporating VGUI, the likelihood class decreased across 41.0% of the typical areas, with cultivated and built-up land accounting for 64.9% of this decrease. By incorporating field-based VGUI data, the study reduced interference from anthropogenic factors such as irrigation in the identification of GDEs within typical areas, enabling refined mapping.

title: Regional landslide early warning through machine-learning-based rainfall threshold and hydromorphological slope units
abstract: Regional landslide early warning (LEW) remains a fundamental challenge because of the spatial heterogeneity of hydrological–geomorphological units and the nonlinear responses inherent in rainfall-triggering processes. This study develops an integrated LEW framework that combines landslide susceptibility prediction (LSP) with rainfall-threshold modeling based on machine learning (ML) to advance the quantitative characterization of regional-scale rainfall-landslide hydrology. For spatial characterization, we propose a novel LSP model that integrates hydrological analysis (HA) and multi-scale segmentation (MSS) to better represent hydromorphological controls on the spatial distribution of slope failures. The HA–MSS model demonstrates strong spatial discriminability: “very high susceptibility” zones capture 69.33 % of observed landslides while occupying only 6.76 % of the total area. For temporal prediction, an ML-based rainfall-threshold model trained jointly on triggering and non-triggering events achieves a probability of detection of 0.82, an accuracy of 0.85, a probability of false detection of 0.13, and a Hanssen–Kuipers index of 0.69, substantially outperforming the empirical E–D baseline. Feature-importance analysis identifies event cumulative rainfall (ECR), maximum intensity (Imax), intensity (I), and duration (D) as dominant predictors, whereas antecedent rainfall variables (AR3, AR5, AR7) contribute 35.2 % of the total feature importance, highlighting the importance of antecedent wetness conditions in rainfall-induced landslide triggering. The integrated framework supports dynamic warning updates at hourly resolution through a spatiotemporal warning matrix. Retrospective assessment of the integrated LEW showed that approximately 87 % of historical landslides were associated with red or orange alert levels, while the August 2021 hindcast reproduced the temporal escalation and spatial evolution of warning levels during an intense rainfall event.

title: Inverse modeling for post-wildfire hydrologic process understanding over snow-dominated watersheds
abstract: Wildfire-induced changes to vegetation and soil properties can alter snowpack dynamics and hydrologic processes in ways that complicate predictions of post-wildfire water availability. To better understand these effects, we coupled the Parameter ESTimation in C++ (PEST++) software with the Weather Research & Forecasting Hydrologic model (WRF-Hydro) across three burned, snow-dominated watersheds in the western United States. We incorporated three burn-severity-based land cover categories into WRF-Hydro and used an iterative Ensemble Smoother (iES) within PEST++ to estimate model parameters controlling snow accumulation and melt, infiltration, and streamflow generation. This framework supported three complementary objectives: (1) assessing parameter sensitivities under pre- and post-wildfire conditions, (2) comparing pre- and post-wildfire parameter ensembles to identify wildfire-driven shifts in hydrologic processes, and (3) using counterfactual simulations to isolate the hydrologic response to wildfire from interannual climate variability. Our findings indicate that model parameter sensitivity varied by domain and shifted following wildfire. Maximum snow albedo and snow albedo decay were most influential in the higher-elevation East Troublesome domain, while the rain-snow partitioning temperature threshold dominated in the lower-elevation Chippy Creek and Las Conchas domains. Following wildfire, streamflow sensitivity shifted away from snowpack parameters toward soil hydraulic parameters, consistent with wildfire-driven reductions in evapotranspiration and increases in soil moisture. Incorporating wildfire effects led to complex changes in simulated snowpack accumulation and streamflow timing, generally leading to earlier snowmelt freshet initiation and cessation and reduced late season flows. Simulations were more sensitive to interannual climate variations than wildfire land cover changes. These results highlight both the potential and challenges of ensemble-based inverse modeling for understanding post-wildfire hydrologic change in snow-dominated watersheds.

Improving flood forecasts: the combined impact of data assimilation and machine learning post-processing
abstract: Accurate streamflow forecasts are essential for flood risk management and impact mitigation. Coupling hydrological models with machine learning techniques has gained increasing attention as a means to improve forecast skill, with post-processing emerging as a promising approach to correcting systematic model residuals. However, the interaction between machine-learning post-processing, data assimilation and calibration strategies remains insufficiently explored. In this study, we assess the contribution of machine-learning-based post-processing to hourly streamflow forecasts for 687 catchments in metropolitan France, generated using a GR-family hydrological model (GR5H-RI) under three forecasting approaches differing in calibration strategy and use of data assimilation. Random Forest and Multilayer Perceptron models are used to post-process forecasts at lead times of 3, 6, 12 and 24 h. Forecast performance is evaluated using both continuous skill metrics relative to persistence and threshold-based metrics for flood event detection. Results show that (1) post-processing consistently improves forecast skill at short lead times, especially for slower-response catchments, with the median persistence score increasing from 0.33 to 0.54 at a 3-h lead time in the highest-skill forecasting setup and performance improving in 89.7% of catchments; (2) the largest gains occur for forecasts without data assimilation, suggesting that post-processing can partially compensate for the lack of state updating but cannot fully replace it; and (3) neural network-based post-processing slightly outperforms tree-based models in continuous metrics, while differences are more limited for event detection. Overall, results highlight the complementary roles of data assimilation and machine-learning post-processing and demonstrate the potential of such frameworks for operational flood forecasting.

Warm-wet shift reshapes hydroclimatic synchronization networks across the Arid Area of Northwest China
abstract: Global warming has profoundly reshaped hydroclimatic regimes in the Arid Area of Northwest China (AANC), yet how the regional warm–wet shift reorganizes hydroclimatic synchronization and drought propagation dynamics remains poorly understood. Based on multi-timescale SPEI records (1962–2021) from 114 stations, we built constrained hydroclimatic synchronization networks via normalized mutual information. Temporal autocorrelation was accounted for through prewhitening, while spatial dependence was assessed and statistically controlled using topography-constrained null models, allowing us to examine stage-varying network topology and propagation dynamics. The warm–wet transition was initiated by an abrupt precipitation increase in 1987, followed by a stepwise temperature rise in 1997. During the transition period (1988–1996), short-timescale synchronization networks became highly fragmented, with sharply reduced connectivity, enhanced community partitioning and strongly inhibited propagation, indicating a temporary breakdown of regional hydroclimatic coherence. In contrast, long-timescale networks remained relatively integrated, with weaker community boundaries and more efficient large-scale propagation driven by persistent low-frequency hydroclimatic variability. Across all stages, longer SPEI accumulation timescales consistently strengthened network connectivity while weakening community partitioning and propagation barriers, revealing robust timescale-dependent reorganization of hydroclimatic synchronization. Comparisons between raw and residual networks further confirm the robustness of observed patterns and highlight notable long-timescale biases induced by temporal persistence. These findings demonstrate that the AANC warm–wet shift represents a nonlinear reorganization of hydroclimatic synchronization through coordinated reorganization of network topology, community structure and propagation dynamics, rather than a simple regional wetting process, providing new insights into drought synchronization mechanisms and hydroclimatic risk propagation in arid regions.

title: Recirculated and fresh submarine groundwater discharge fluxes of dissolved carbon in a temperate seagrass lagoon
abstract: Submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) is a fundamental hydrological process linking coastal aquifers, sediments, and ocean water. However, bulk SGD estimates often cannot resolve the relative contribution of fresh groundwater discharge and recirculated seawater in dissolved carbon export. Here, we combined a radium isotope mass balance model, Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis, dissolved carbon measurements, and optical characterization of dissolved organic matter to quantify pathway-specific SGD-derived carbon transport in a temperate seagrass-dominated coastal lagoon. Radium-based models showed that recirculated saline groundwater discharge (RSGD) was substantially greater than fresh submarine groundwater discharge (FSGD), with fluxes of 11 (0.7-54) and 1.6 (0.4-20) cm d-1, respectively. RSGD also dominated dissolved carbon export, producing area-normalized dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) fluxes of 247 (28-1654) and 34 (3-205) mmol m-2 d-1, respectively. Optical analyses further showed that SGD transported both humic-like and protein-like fluorescent DOM components, with humic-like components dominating the exported FDOM pool. These results indicate that recirculated seawater flow through permeable lagoon sediments acted as a hydrological conveyor releasing dissolved carbon to surface waters. Our findings demonstrate that pathway-specific separation of FSGD and RSGD is necessary for attributing dissolved carbon fluxes in coastal aquifers and for evaluating groundwater-mediated lateral exchange in blue carbon budgets.

title: Influence of water network structure on regional water allocation under supply variability
Drivers and controls of salinization in prairie ponds
abstract: High sulphate (SO 4 2− ) concentrations in ponds can support distinctive aquatic communities but can also promote salinization and disrupt aquatic ecosystem functioning, with implications for livestock watering. These contrasting effects are widespread across pondscapes of the Northern Great Plains, yet the interacting biophysical, limnological, and hydrological controls on SO 4 2− dynamics remain underexplored. We investigated SO 4 2− dynamics across upland soils, water columns, and sediments of prairie ponds comprising naturally occurring wetlands and artificially constructed dugouts (small, excavated water-storage ponds) spanning gradients in salinity, depth, upland vegetation cover, and hydrological setting. Wetlands exhibited higher SO 4 2− concentrations in water and sediment than dugouts, consistent with differences in pond morphology, hydrological connectivity, and longer-term solute accumulation. Hydrological setting was strongly associated with pond SO 4 2− concentrations, with discharge systems generally exhibiting higher concentrations than recharge systems. Across pondscapes, sediments had the highest SO 4 2− concentrations, followed by upland soils and the water column, highlighting sediments as an important long-term SO 4 2− reservoir. Structural equation modelling further identified hydrology, sediment and soil SO 4 2− , soil organic matter, total dissolved nitrogen, and water depth as important predictors of pond salinization. Upland vegetation cover was negatively associated with SO 4 2− desorption, suggesting a potential role in limiting solute mobilization, although its contribution appeared secondary to hydrological and geochemical controls. Collectively, these findings highlight the importance of hydrological setting, pond morphology, and long-term SO 4 2− storage in regulating salinization across prairie pondscapes and provide insights into processes that may influence the suitability of ponds as livestock-water resources.

title: Toward AI-driven digital twins for metropolitan floods: A conditional latent dynamics network surrogate of the shallow water equations
abstract: AI-driven flood digital twins demand fast hydrodynamic surrogates for ensemble forecasting and observation assimilation. Yet even GPU-accelerated two-dimensional shallow water equation (SWE) solvers still require minutes per -hour run on a -million-active-cell metropolitan basin (the Des Plaines River basin at resolution), making such workloads prohibitive at native resolution. We present the Conditional Latent Dynamics Network (CLDNet): a low-dimensional latent neural ODE driven by rainfall, paired with a coordinate-based decoder conditioned on static terrain (elevation, slope, Manning roughness) that reconstructs depth and discharge at arbitrary query points. Pointwise decoding decouples memory from grid size and handles irregular watersheds natively, enabling metropolitan-scale training on a single compute node and direct queries at exact gauge coordinates without raster snapping. We evaluate CLDNet on a synthetic -cell Texas benchmark and on a new Des Plaines case study of real-rainfall Stage IV storms whose reference simulator we validate against United States Geological Survey (USGS) gauges at the April 2013 flood-of-record (Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency on mean-recentered water-surface elevation). CLDNet reduces the relative root-mean-squared error of an unconditional baseline by , outperforms regular-grid VAE–ConvLSTM and FNO baselines on the Texas benchmark (both presuppose a Cartesian grid and do not apply to the irregular Des Plaines watershed), reaches a critical success index of at the inundation threshold, and produces a full -hour basin-wide forecast in seconds—a speedup. Finally, we demonstrate that CLDNet’s compact latent state supports online observation coupling: using the Latent Dynamics Ensemble Score Filter (LD-EnSF), we assimilate water-depth observations at gauge locations into the surrogate’s latent dynamics and recover a mean Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency of against USGS observations at six held-out gauges, from for the rainfall-perturbed open-loop forecast, realizing the observation-update step required of an AI-driven flood digital twin.

Geodetic constraints on regional scale mountain bedrock aquifer properties
abstract: Groundwater in mountainous, fractured-bedrock systems is increasingly recognized as a critical component of water storage and transmission, yet characterizing the hydraulic properties of these systems remains challenging due to sparse observations. Here, we use estimates of groundwater storage change in the Sierra Nevada and Cascades mountain ranges over the last two decades derived from Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) observations of vertical surface displacement to estimate mountain-range-scale effective groundwater hydraulic parameters. We estimate mountain-range-scale hydraulic conductivity and specific yield by fitting models of groundwater storage change to GNSS-derived storage estimates during groundwater discharge periods. We estimate hydraulic conductivity (7.03 × 10 −6 m/s and 5.1 × 10 −5 m/s) and specific yield (0.063 and 0.15) for the Sierra Nevada and Cascades, respectively, which align with published values based upon their unique bedrock lithologies. The relatively high hydraulic conductivities within each region indicate that fractured and/or weathered bedrock strongly influences the storage and release properties of these regional groundwater systems. The estimated characteristic drainage lengths of 727 m for the Sierra Nevada are consistent with average channel spacing of both perennial and intermittent streams, while the characteristic drainage length of 984 m for the Cascades is consistent with the average spacing of perennial streams only, indicating differing connections between surface water and groundwater within each region. This new method demonstrates the utility of geodetic observations in studying mountain groundwater systems and may provide improved constraints on large-scale simulations of mountain groundwater flow, furthering our understanding of these systems

abstract: Representing subsurface heterogeneity in hydrological models is particularly challenging, as geological and geophysical data are often sparse and infrequent. Hydrologists face two main challenges in subsurface characterization: determining the necessary depth and detail for accurate flow modeling, and developing cost and time-effective methods to capture subsurface heterogeneity. In this study, we conducted preparatory geological and geophysical surveys to investigate subsurface structures and develop conceptual models for the studied catchment. We began with a simple single-layer subsurface model based on initial field investigations and progressively refined it into a more complex three-layer model that incorporates geological, geophysical, and hydraulic properties measured in the field. These conceptual subsurface models were used to inform a 3D hydrological model applied to a 15.28 ha subalpine catchment at Lautaret Pass. Results show that both the three-layer homogeneous and three-layer heterogeneous models perform best, yielding comparable results for runoff (KGEnp = 89, 91), soil moisture (MAPE = 0.23, 0.22), and evapotranspiration (MAPE = 6.65, 6.60). The three-layer model introduces an active regolith layer at an optimal depth, which is responsible for storing and releasing infiltrated water. We argue that conceptual homogeneous models can meet hydrological objectives, provided they are grounded in reliable geological and geophysical field data. However, we also show that the heterogeneous model performs slightly better in capturing snowmelt amplitude, baseflow, evapotranspiration, and surface heterogeneities. These results highlight how cost and time-effective geophysical methods that capture vertical heterogeneity can be leveraged to upscale critical zone processes.

AnytimeHydroTwin: A deployment-valid inference-orchestration layer for AI-driven hydrological digital twins
abstract: When does a water-quality nowcast need a process-resolving model, and when is the previous observation enough? Across eleven regimes on three tidal-estuarine systems, the answer is set by the signal, not the model. Estuarine pH and dissolved oxygen are persistence-dominated everywhere (lag-1 autocorrelation – ): a high-fidelity (HF) neural nowcaster beats the previous observation in none of the nine such regimes. Only Sacramento Delta 15-min turbidity genuinely decorrelates ( ), reflecting episodic sediment resuspension, and it alone rewards HF ( ). Variability is not the discriminant—the two highest-variance regimes are persistence-dominated—giving an operational screen: above , an expensive nowcaster will not repay its compute. We exploit this with AnytimeHydroTwin , an inference-orchestration layer rather than a full digital twin, whose deployment-valid pre-HF causal gate reads only observations available before the HF forward pass, so a skipped HF call is a real compute saving, not a post-hoc blend ratio. The gate is itself paid every step: an HF-invocation rate is not a compute saving, and we account for it in full. Our headline is a leakage-clean nested-split evaluation on Sacramento turbidity—NSE parity with HF-only, at HF, an estimated to end-to-end wall-clock saving from measured component latencies—closed for the two LSTM headline regimes, open for the TCN stress case and ancillary CAMELS variant. On the nine persistence-dominated regimes it safely defers to lag-1 of the time. This regime classification is robust across the three backbone families we evaluate (TCN, LSTM and Transformer): the structure reflects the signal more than the learner.

Deep learning with upstream-aware terrain representations and rainfall adapter for generalizable pluvial flood prediction
abstract: Deep learning-based surrogate models can substantially accelerate pluvial flood simulations. However, most existing approaches struggle to generalize across heterogeneous terrains or modified topographies, limiting their applicability for real-world flood risk assessment unless retrained for each specific terrain.In this work, we investigate how deep learning flood surrogates can be designed to achieve robust spatial generalization across previously unseen terrain configurations without retraining. We train models on diverse terrain and introduce upstream-aware input maps that propagate terrain properties into downstream regions, allowing the model to capture long-range spatial dependencies and supporting the learning of more generalizable spatial features. In addition, we add architectural design choices to improve the model’s capacity to generalize beyond the training domain. We further propose a two-stage training strategy with an adapter-like rainfall encoder that enables efficient adaptation to previously unseen rainfall intensities while preserving spatial generalizability.The resulting model predicts maximum water depths and is evaluated on unseen catchments in Austria and Denmark, as well as on artificially modified terrains such as dikes. Our results demonstrate that combining a large training dataset with upstream-aware terrain representations and a generalization-oriented architectural design enables accurate flood predictions across unseen terrains and rainfall scenarios, reaching a RMSE below $0.05$ and CSI$_{0.3}$ of up to $0.91$ in test cases, outperforming previous models in both prediction accuracy and Critical Success Index.

Hydrologically constrained genetic programming for interpretable rainfall–runoff model discovery: A process–informed machine learning approach
abstract: Advances in machine learning have improved rainfall–runoff prediction, but integrating these capabilities with interpretable, process-based model structures remains an open challenge. This study seeks a middle ground between conceptual hydrological modelling and modern data-driven prediction by automating model structure discovery while retaining interpretability and hydrological consistency. We introduce HydroXGP (Hydrological Model eXplorer using Genetic Programming) to reduce reliance on legacy model choices and subjective a priori structural assumptions by learning model structure directly from data during optimization. The framework evolves models from a modular, process-based component library adapted from the open-source MARRMoT toolbox, making the search process-informed through reusable flux and routing components and hydrologically constrained by enforcing mass balance during simulation. GP jointly optimizes model structure and parameters, while each discovered model remains explicit and interpretable. Evaluation on the CAMELS-US dataset showed that a proof-of-concept test in a snow-dominated basin achieved strong performance over the out-of-sample test period (NSE=0.849), and, when transferred to a hydrologically similar basin, the learned structure retained useful predictive skill (NSE=0.724). Across 18 basins (one representative basin per U.S. hydrologic region), median NSE reached 0.702, generally outperforming the mean performance of an ensemble of conceptual benchmark models while remaining competitive with some regional LSTM baselines. The findings support a modelling perspective in which structural hypotheses can be revisited and adapted as new data, diagnostics, or environmental signals become available, enabling basin-specific configurations that evolve in response to changing information rather than relying on a single fixed template.

Hybrid physics–AI modeling in hydrogeology: a review of concepts, applications, and challenges
abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping hydrogeological modeling. The question is whether hybrid physics–AI approaches can reconcile the explanatory power of process-based models with the flexibility and speed of machine learning. We try to answer this question with a concept-driven review which traces the progression from purely data-driven approaches to emerging modeling paradigms incorporating physical knowledge. We show that hydrogeological modeling is moving beyond a simple opposition between mechanistic simulators and black-box algorithms toward a continuum of physics–AI integration, including theory-guided machine learning, physics-informed neural networks, physics-aware architectures, neural operators, generative models, and differentiable programming. Applications across key hydrogeological domains are reviewed, followed by a discussion of current limitations and barriers to operational deployment, including data requirements, transferability across hydrogeological settings, verification and validation, uncertainty quantification, and issues of trust. We conclude that hybrid physics–AI modeling should not be understood as a replacement for hydrogeological theory, but as an emerging methodological framework in which physical laws, numerical simulation, and machine learning are combined to produce models that are faster, more interpretable, more robust, and more useful for decision-making in groundwater science and management.

Proposal for using daily thermal amplitude to estimate reference evapotranspiration without relative humidity
abstract: The application of the standard Penman-Monteith (PM) method to estimate reference evapotranspiration (ETo) is frequently limited by the scarcity of air relative humidity data. In this case, it is common to assume the dew point temperature (Tdew) is equal to the minimum temperature (Tmin), to calculate the actual water vapor pressure (ea), but this practice tends to underestimate ETo in drier environment conditions. Thus, this study aimed to propose a new approach to estimate Tdew as a function of Tmin and the daily thermal amplitude (TA), aiming to estimate the vapor pressure in scenarios with limited relative humidity data. For this, daily data from 584 automatic weather stations distributed across Brazil were used, comparing the performance of the proposed method with the standard FAO-56 PM. The results demonstrated that the proposed general equation (Tdew=Tmin-0.2∙TA) outperformed traditional approaches in most Brazilian climates (Af, Am, Aw, Cfa, Csa, Cwa, and Cwb), which represent about 87% of the country's area, significantly reducing the error (RMSE) and mitigating systematic underestimation or overestimation biases observed in other approaches. In Bsh, Cfb, and As climates (13% of the area), the general equation presented limited performance, and a regional calibration is indicated to improve its efficiency in estimating Tdew and, consequently, ea and ETo. Therefore, it is concluded that the use of the daily thermal amplitude eliminates the subjectivity in the choice of correction factors to estimate actual vapor pressure and offers a physically more consistent alternative to estimate ETo on a daily scale.

title: Hydrogeochemical relationship between large river and adjacent aquifer controls nitrogen accumulation and transformation in riparian zone
A hybrid smoothed particle hydrodynamics framework for modelling erosion in deformable riverbank
abstract: Riverbank erosion is an important geomorphological process that significantly influences river morphology, ecological systems, and infrastructure stability. Existing morphodynamic modelling approaches are generally unable to fully reveal the underlying hydro-mechanical mechanisms governing riverbank erosion because of the lack of suitable numerical models capable of simultaneously modelling free-surface flow, seepage, soil deformation, and large-deformation failure processes. This study proposes a hybrid smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) framework to address the challenging coupled riverbank erosion processes. The proposed fully coupled SPH framework is first validated through benchmark problems involving submerged soil column consolidation, submerged deformable landslide motion, and wave-scouring-induced landslide failure. Subsequently, a field-scale riverbank erosion simulation is conducted to demonstrate the capability of the proposed approach and to investigate the hydro-mechanical mechanisms governing riverbank erosion and retreat. The results show that repeated wave fluctuations induce long-term seepage erosion near the riverbank surface, resulting in progressive mass loss and degradation of soil strength. Continuous erosion causes undercutting and stress deterioration within the bank, eventually leading to instability of the overhanging riverbank and subsequent block collapse. The collapsed soil mass is further fluidized and eroded by cyclic wave action, producing repeated cycles of erosion, collapse, and retreat that progressively reshape the riverbank geometry. The proposed SPH framework provides a promising hydro-mechanical modelling tool for investigating complex riverbank erosion processes involving strong fluid-soil interaction and large deformation.

Probabilistic sensor placement in water distribution networks: a Dynamic Residual Masking framework using game-theoretic pseudo-Jacobians
Recirculation tracer tests in long uncased boreholes: a simple way to identify hydraulic conductivity
abstract: Standing column wells are ground heat exchangers that offer significant energy savings potential, yet their optimal design requires accurate site-specific hydrogeological data. While continuous groundwater recirculation tests are routinely performed for thermal assessments, their potential to characterize aquifer hydrogeological properties remains underexploited. In this study, we improve the exploitation of these tests by injecting a conservative tracer to estimate the effective hydrogeological parameters of a fractured aquifer. A field protocol was deployed in a 215 m deep well located in Varennes, Canada, where fluorescein was injected during continuous recirculation and monitored in real time. To interpret the tracer signal, a 2D-axisymmetric finite-element model simulating groundwater flow and solute transport was developed and coupled with an inverse optimization algorithm. The numerical model accurately reproduced the experimental breakthrough curve, capturing the early-time homogenization oscillations with high accuracy and a characteristic period of 31.3 min. This enabled the simultaneous estimation of the rock mass flow and transport properties, identifying hydraulic conductivity with high precision. The hydraulic conductivity estimated from the recirculation tracer test was consistent with independent pumping-test estimates obtained at the same site, demonstrating that the proposed method can recover realistic hydraulic properties from a simple operational test. These results show that this new tracer-test method can transform a routine recirculation procedure into a high-precision and reliable hydrogeological characterization tool.

title: Coupling water balance and vegetation carbon dynamics in a parsimonious global hydrologic model
abstract: Understanding ecohydrological responses to environmental change requires parsimonious models that can represent interactions between water balance and vegetation carbon uptake. Simple conceptual hydrologic models efficiently simulate runoff and evapotranspiration, but they usually lack dynamic vegetation representation. We extend the abcd monthly water-balance model to simulate coupled water–carbon dynamics by integrating the Horton Index framework with a two-parameter Gross Primary Productivity–Evapotranspiration (GPP–ET) functional relationship. The resulting eight-parameter framework is calibrated using observation-constrained runoff and GPP, while ET is withheld from the calibration objective and evaluated independently. Using GSWP3-W5E5 forcing, FLUXCOM-X BASE GPP and ET, and GRUN-ensemble runoff over 235 global basins, we calibrate the model for 2001–2014 and evaluate it independently for 2015–2019. During validation, the model reproduces GPP robustly, with a median Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE) of 0.758 and positive KGE in 97.9% of basins. ET performance is also broadly positive despite not being directly calibrated, with a median validation KGE of 0.673 and positive KGE in 87.7% of basins. Runoff skill is moderate and more heterogeneous, with a median validation KGE of 0.435 and positive KGE in 81.7% of basins. Seasonal-cycle and anomaly analyses show that the model strongly captures the climatological timing of GPP and ET while retaining meaningful anomaly skill after removing the mean annual cycle. The calibrated coupling parameters λ , β , and α exhibit geographically organized patterns consistent with their physically interpretable roles in evaporative partitioning and water–carbon coupling, while β and α remain effective model-scale rather than intrinsic physiological coefficients. These results show that a parsimonious monthly hydrologic model can be extended to diagnose first-order coupled water–carbon dynamics while retaining interpretable structure and computational efficiency.

title: Deep learning meets spectral analysis: reproducing long-term persistence in synthetic streamflow
abstract: Synthetic streamflow generation requires simultaneous reproduction of flow distributions and temporal dependence across multiple scales, including long-term persistence (LTP). This study evaluates a three-stage framework that combines latent-space generation with a temporal convolutional network (TCN), low-frequency spectral adjustment, and quantile-based rank reordering. The framework was applied to daily discharge records from 24 UK river basins and benchmarked against autoregressive moving average (ARMA), k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN), and long short-term memory (LSTM) generators. Marginal distributions were reproduced closely (median Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic = 0.00069; 99th-percentile ratios = 0.986–0.999). The median absolute difference in the rescaled-range persistence estimate was 0.028, with 79% of basins within a tolerance of 0.05. Detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) produced a median scaling-exponent difference of 0.076; Monte Carlo tests showed that part of the R/S-DFA discrepancy reflects estimator-specific finite-sample behavior. The same experiments indicate that a 0.05 tolerance is approximately a two-standard-deviation band at the 7,300-day synthetic-series length, and that shorter records tend to inflate persistence estimates. ARMA produced a statistically indistinguishable median R/S error (0.024). For the nine records with no missing days, the proposed framework and k-NN showed very similar paired low-flow spell-duration errors. The proposed framework is therefore not uniformly superior to simpler alternatives; its main value is the combination of close marginal matching with an explicit spectral mechanism for controlling long-term persistence. Remaining limitations include weaker short-lag autocorrelation reproduction and incomplete recovery of threshold-conditioned spell clustering.

title: Scaling properties and classification of urban drainage networks in an Asian megacity
abstract: Urban drainage networks (UDNs) are critical infrastructure for public health and the mitigation of flood risk. As UDNs age and expand in scale and complexity, their structural properties are adapted to cope with new needs. Self-similarity of the structure of such drainage networks has been proposed as a naturally self-organized and optimal state of such systems but it remains unclear whether self-similarity is a universal feature of UDNs globally and how to interpret any differences in scaling from the classical scaling as seen in rivers. To address this, we analyzed 221 UDNs (3,942 km) in Seoul. We assessed three classical scaling metrics describing the spatial organization of river networks i.e., Hortonian scaling ratios, the power-law relationship between main-channel length and drainage area, and the area-exceedance probability distribution. While the latter two metrics had similar power-law scaling, UDNs showed a wider range of the power-law exponent in the length-area relationship and a lower power-law exponent in the area-exceedance probability distribution as compared to rivers. Just 50.2% of UDNs (68.5% of total length) satisfied Hortonian scaling invariance. Employing these ratios as criteria, we grouped UDNs and found that their structural properties are associated with sewershed size and commercial area ratio. Moreover, UDNs with scaling more similar to that of rivers had a lower side-to-main pipe-size ratio. These findings provide a systematic diagnosis of scaling heterogeneity across a large set of UDNs within a single megacity and offer a preliminary screening approach for identifying UDNs that may warrant further hydraulic assessment.

title: An improved Green-Ampt infiltration model of depth-dependent initial soil water content and its experimental verification
Hysteretic response of water temperature and persistent thermal regime shift under extreme hydrological pulses
Pore-network structure and transport responses across textures and salinization levels in seasonally frozen saline soils: evidence from CT scanning and lattice Boltzmann simulations
Linking urban sanitation practices to water resource quality: A multi-tracer approach in a humid tropical context using nitrate isotopes and emerging organic contaminants
abstract: Urban water resources in large cities of sub-Saharan Africa are increasingly impacted by anthropogenic activities, mainly due to the limited access to adequate sanitation systems. In these highly anthropized contexts surface water and groundwater contamination sources are multiple. However, the interactions between these contamination sources and urban water bodies remain poorly investigated, despite the need for such understanding to support sustainable water-resource management. This study applied a multi-tracer approach combining hydrochemistry, nitrate stable isotopes (δ 15 N-NO 3 and δ 18 O-NO 3 ), and Emerging Organic Contaminants (EOCs) to identify contamination sources and pathways, and to characterize the biogeochemical processes affecting shallow aquifers and surface waters in a tropical urban environment. High Cl/Br molar ratios (>1000), indicated that NO 3 – and Cl - primarily originate from domestic wastewater inputs. Enriched δ 15 N-NO 3 (6.6 to 25‰) and δ 18 O-NO 3 (+3.3 to + 9.9‰), further confirmed the predominance of wastewater-derived contamination and revealed the occurrence of partial denitrification processes. Intermediate isotopic ranges (soil organic nitrogen and sewage) suggested the influence of mixed contamination sources. Widespread occurrence of EOCs, particularly persistent contaminants such as fluconazole (FCZ), highlighted the significant impact of wastewater on both groundwater and surface water quality. Strong correlations of FCZ with Cl - , δ 15 N-NO 3 , together with their similar spatial distribution, identified FCZ as the most effective wastewater co-tracer in the study area. Furthermore, the co-occurrence of FCZ with non-persistent compounds such as paracetamol indicated recent and continuous wastewater inputs affecting urban water resources. Sporadic detection of non-ubiquitous compounds such as carbamazepine reflects localized wastewater infiltration from septic or pit latrine sources. These results underscore the high vulnerability of shallow urban aquifers and demonstrate the relevance of nitrate isotopes and EOCs coupling to better understand contamination dynamics and support sustainable urban water management.

title: Seasonal reversals in surface environmental gradients and a novel phytoplankton bloom risk assessment framework in the trans-Arctic Ocean
abstract: The Arctic Ocean is undergoing unprecedented environmental changes driven by global warming, with profound consequences for biogeochemical cycles and ecosystem functioning. However, high-resolution spatiotemporal characterization of surface physicochemical heterogeneity and quantitative phytoplankton bloom risk assessment remain limited, hindering informed environmental management. Here, we conducted two zonal trans-basin transects (outbound and inbound) across the Arctic Ocean from August to October 2025, collecting continuous underway data at 1,271 stations spanning six major sea regions. Our results revealed striking seasonal reversals in environmental gradients: in late summer, temperature decreased poleward while salinity increased from shelf to basin; in early autumn, the highest temperature shifted to the Chukchi Sea shelf and salinity increased westward. Notably, dissolved inorganic nitrogen concentrations in the Pacific-Arctic region increased 33-fold from late summer to early autumn. We developed a novel phytoplankton bloom risk assessment framework based on integrated nutrient concentrations and stoichiometric matching to the Redfield ratio, identifying discrete high-risk zones in the Pacific-Arctic region and the East Siberian Sea. This study delivers the most comprehensive high-resolution dataset of Arctic surface environmental properties to date and offers a robust, management-oriented tool for predicting phytoplankton bloom dynamics under accelerating climate change.

Hydrometeorological and hydrogeological trends and drought dynamics in a cold-humid, coastal region
abstract: Quantifying groundwater response to droughts remains challenging, as aquifers typically respond to meteorological conditions with delays, and long-term groundwater records remain limited. This study investigated statistical relationships among meteorological, hydrogeological, and hydrological datasets in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia. Standardized Groundwater Index (SGI) values were calculated using daily groundwater level data (2009–2025) from 32 observation wells and compared with meteorological (Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index, SPEI) and hydrological (Standardized Base Flow Index, SBFI) drought indicators. To complement the statistical analyses of drought dynamics, geospatial drought layers were used to examine spatiotemporal patterns in drought severity and distribution. In most groundwater systems, SGI exhibited short (< 1 month) lag times and strong correlations (> 0.5 on average) with both SPEI and SBFI, suggesting the atmosphere-aquifer-stream hydrologic continuum patterns are strongly associated. Trend analysis revealed that the fall season is experiencing the most significant and persistent negative trends across the hydrological cycle (net precipitation, baseflow, and groundwater level). Significant negative fall trends were identified in 67% of net precipitation records, 60% of streamflow records, 40% of baseflow records, and 25% of groundwater level records. Kernel density analyses for summer and fall indicated significant shifts toward drier SPEI, SGI, and SBFI distributions (p < 0.05) after 2016. The geospatial drought layer analysis reveals that more intensive droughts are becoming more frequent and spatially extensive. Collectively, the results yield a better understanding of drought characteristics in a cold, coastal region, an essential step towards evaluating ongoing climate change impacts in similar environments worldwide.

title: Constrained differentiable hybrid hydrologic modeling across multiple process backbones: accuracy gains and risks to physical consistency
Characterization and quantification of compound drought-heatwaves events along with population exposure
Flood modeling incorporating spatially heterogeneous rainfall and nonlinear routing mechanisms
The hydrological effects of dispersed stormwater management at the catchment scale
abstract: Urban stormwater drainage alters stream flow regimes. Even small rainfall events produce greater quickflow volumes and peak flows from catchments drained using traditional stormwater management, degrading stream ecosystems. Stormwater Control Measures (SCMs) aim to mitigate such impacts. However, the cumulative effect on stream flow regimes of SCMs applied across a catchment, including widespread application of at-source SCMs, has been little studied. We assessed storm-event quickflow volume and peak-flow responses to dispersed SCMs retrofitted into existing urban catchments across five experimental catchments on two streams, including three upstream tributaries of one stream, over eight years, alongside observations from three reference and two control streams as part of a BACRI (Before-After-Control-Reference-Impact) experimental design. Results showed that the dispersed implementation of SCMs reduced quickflow volume and peak flow at the storm-event scale. The effect was greatest for frequent small storm events (2–8 mm). This is the first catchment-scale study to demonstrate such effects for the retrofit of SCMs, largely applied at-source, into urban catchments, and thus increases confidence that such investments will reduce flow-induced degradation of urban streams.

title: Distributed modeling reveals the evolution of supraglacial lakes: a multi-basin study on the Greenland ice sheet
A large-scale molecular dynamics investigation of anisotropic hydraulic conductivity in compacted clay system
abstract: This study developed a large-scale molecular dynamics framework to investigate anisotropic hydraulic conductivity by linking directional water transport to compaction state, platelet fabric, and surface chemistry. A total of 150 multi-particle nanoflow models were constructed across dry densities ( ρ d ) of 1.2–1.8 g·cm −3 , orientational order parameters ( S ) of 0.60 to 0.92, and cation exchange capacities (CEC) of 0.11–97.44 cmol·kg −1 . Simulated hydraulic conductivities ranged from 0.77 × 10 -14 to 1.96 × 10 -12 m·s −1 , with 97.0% of available experimental measurements falling within this envelope. Mean horizontal hydraulic conductivity ( k h ) consistently exceeded mean vertical hydraulic conductivity ( k v ) by factors of approximately 2.4–5.6. Increasing dry density narrowed water-accessible pores, reduced independent spanning pathways and critical spanning diameters, and increased tortuosity, thereby decreasing both k h and k v . Platelet orientation differentiated the two flow directions by maintaining more direct horizontal pathways. Increasing CEC shifted pore water toward Na associated states and reduced the flux carried by interfacial only and free water, further lowering both k h and k v . Random Forest models achieved mean testing R 2 values of 0.92 for k h and 0.88 for k v and identified dry density as the dominant descriptor in both directions. Platelet orientation had a greater relative influence on vertical than horizontal conductivity, whereas CEC made a smaller but consistent contribution. Fixed-density sensitivity analysis showed that increasing dry density shifted the relative sensitivity weight from platelet orientation toward CEC, particularly for k v . These findings clarify the distinct structural and physicochemical controls on directional water transport and hydraulic anisotropy in compacted clay barriers.

title: Trends in the frequency and duration of high flow events across climates
abstract: Flood events play a critical role in infrastructure design, floodplain management, water supply and natural ecology. While large floods are a risk to life and infrastructure, smaller flood events, here termed high flow events, are essential for maintaining biodiversity of wetlands and filling our water supplies. With climate change altering extreme rainfall magnitude, frequency, and timing there is a need to understand the impact of these changes on catchment flow response. Globally, studies have generally focused on changes in flood magnitude, and the drivers of these changes, and there remains a gap in understanding the historical changes in the frequency and duration of high flow events – those critical for sustaining ecosystem health and water supply. Here, using a set of 476 long record streamflow gauging stations across the continent of Australia, which span a wide range of climate zones, we investigate the trend in the frequency of high flow events and their duration. We find that, across most arid and temperate regions, the frequency of high flow events has decreased and their duration shortened, suggesting a reduction in water availability. In the tropics, there have been increases in the frequency of high flow events. Testing the robustness of the historical trends to the assumptions made in the analysis, we find that the rarer the event, the more likely it is to be increasing in frequency. These results provide some evidence that climate change is impacting both streamflow magnitude and frequency, which has significant implications for water supply, as well as the health of our ecological and environmental systems.

title: Land-use controls on soil hydraulic functioning: the role of pore organization and gravel distribution in an agricultural catchment
abstract: Soil hydraulic functioning in headwater catchments reflects interactions among pore organization, land use, and coarse-fragment distribution, but the relative importance of these controls remains uncertain when point measurements are interpreted at broader spatial scales. This study evaluated how near-surface soil permeability and water storage varied among land-use and tillage systems and whether those variations were associated with soil structure and gravel distribution in a 1.19 km 2 agricultural headwater catchment in southern Brazil. Physical and hydraulic properties were measured in the 0–0.05 m layer at 69 sampling points (414 undisturbed cores), including bulk density, pore-size distribution, saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ksat), air permeability (Ka), water retention across matric potentials, gravel content, texture, and soil organic carbon (SOC). Planned contrasts, Pearson correlations, and principal component analysis (PCA) were used to evaluate group differences and multivariate associations. Natural forest had lower bulk density and greater permeability-related attributes than grazed grassland, whereas conservation tillage increased water retention and plant-available water relative to conventional tillage without a consistent increase in Ksat. Gravel abundance was positively associated with macroporosity, Ka, and Ksat and negatively associated with water retention near field capacity, but these correlations do not establish a causal pathway. Land-use differences in water retention were strongest near saturation and diminished at higher suctions. The first two PCA axes explained 49.3% of total variance and separated transmission-related attributes (Ksat, Ka, macroporosity, total porosity, and saturated water content) from denser, storage-related conditions, while substantial variability remained in higher components. Overall, near-surface hydraulic functioning was more closely associated with pore organization and coarse-fragment abundance than with texture or SOC. Because the study represents only the surface layer of one catchment and did not explicitly model spatial autocorrelation or deeper pedogenetic discontinuities, extrapolation to profile- and catchment-scale flow should be made cautiously.

title: From end-of-pipe detention to source–process regulation: multi-objective optimization of gray–green infrastructure for urban flood mitigation
