From Journal archive to hydrological knowledge infrastructure: a perspective for Journal of Hydrology
Aquifer settings and interflow dynamics across continental flood basalts: A synthesis of hydro-geophysical evidence
How reporting cadence shapes hourly precipitation extremes
abstract: Hourly precipitation pro ducts are often built from station records with heterogeneous subhourly rep orting cadences, but users rarely know how much of the resulting dierence in extreme diagnostics reects temp oral supp ort, phase alignment relative to clo ck-hour bins, avoidable aggregation choices, or rainfall structure. We present a controlled coarsening framework that separates zero-oset temp oral-supp ort dierences from phase-alignment uncertainty, quanties a regime-conditioned uncertainty envelop e, and tests a leave-one-station-out cadence correction. Using three years (20232025, UTC) ofnear-regular 5-min observations from 30 high-frequency AVAMET stations in eastern Spain, we build practical 5-min b enchmark pro ducts and synthetically coarsen the same records to 15-, 30-, and 60-min rep orting across all phase osets. Hourly pro ducts are reconstructed with naive timestamp binning (M0) and overlap-aware aggregation (M1), allowing avoidable b oundary artefacts to b e separated from structural temp oral-supp ort dierences.For the 99th p ercentile of the hourly interval-rate maximum on wet hours (P refsum ≥1 mm), the central oset-median M1 dierence reaches -69.6% at 60-min rep orting, while the aligned-clo ck zero-oset case is even larger (-76.0%). Phase alignment adds a pro cedural uncertainty envelop e, with median p90-p10 spreads ranging from 6.2 to 8.3 p ercentage p oints across cadences. The eect is strongly regime-dep endent: at 60-min rep orting, the p99 relative dierence is -66.2% for temp orally concentrated rainfall but only -5.2% for distributed rainfall. A comparison with the classical 1.13 xed-window adjustment shows that this historical factor is a useful b enchmark for xed versus moving 60-min accumulation, but it do es not explain regime, phase, cadence, and interval-rate eects. A simple cadence- and regime-aware correc-tion reduces systematic dierences but leaves substantial residual uncertainty. The resulting audit framework replaces a single cadence-blind estimate with an explicit record of temp oral supp ort, zero-oset results, phase-sensitivity envelop es, and regime-conditioned uncertainty.

title: Projected droughts readily trigger vegetation decline
abstract: Drought is intensifying under a warming climate, while the lag of vegetation response and the drought trigger thresholds for relative vegetation loss remain insufficiently quantified. Here we provide a global assessment of vegetation responses to the Terrestrial Water Storage Drought Severity Index (TWS_DSI) under historical and future climate scenarios. Using five vegetation indicators, including Leaf Area Index (LAI), Fraction of Photosynthetically Active Radiation (FPAR), Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), kernel Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (kNDVI), and Gross Primary Productivity (GPP), we quantified their lagged responses to drought during the historical period. The mean optimal lag times ranged from 8.20 months for LAI to 10.59 months for NDVI, with FPAR (8.78 months), GPP (9.80 months), and kNDVI (10.42 months) showing intermediate lag responses. Based on future LAI simulations under the SSP126, SSP370, and SSP585 scenarios, the mean lag varied from 5.15 to 10.48 months. At predefined vegetation loss levels (≤40 th , ≤30 th , ≤20 th , ≤10 th ), we identified the drought trigger thresholds for vegetation decline and mapped their spatial variability. Compared to the historical baseline, the average drought trigger thresholds increased by 30.0%, 36.3%, and 35.3% under the SSP126, SSP370, and SSP585 scenarios, respectively, indicating heightened vulnerability whereby even milder drought conditions in the future could trigger vegetation decline. Our findings characterize the temporal lags, threshold behavior, and projected changes of vegetation responses to terrestrial water deficits, providing a scientific basis for assessing ecosystem vulnerability and informing targeted ecological conservation and climate adaptation strategies.

title: Soil evaporation dominates shifts in evapotranspiration seasonality in the Yangtze River Basin
Satellite-derived nutrient reconstruction reveals the drivers of eutrophication risk in a subtropical estuary
Seasonal differences in Fe:P regulation of phosphorus source–sink dynamics in an urban shallow lake
Changes in the annual cycle of shallow subarctic groundwater regimes over 50 years
abstract: Seasonal groundwater level regimes are exposed to climate change, with implications for drought and flood risks, water supply, agriculture, and ecosystems. Changes in the intra-annual groundwater fluctuations are accentuated in quickly responding shallow aquifers found worldwide, but particularly in subarctic regions, where the cold winter season attenuates infiltration and evaporation. To identify the types of subarctic groundwater regimes and their responses to the changing climate, 50-year groundwater level data from 52 monitoring stations throughout Finland were analyzed. This was done by partitioning around medians (PAM) clustering of Pearson correlations and a principal component analysis (PCA) of normalized monthly values. Four distinct regimes were identified, mostly following the southwest–northeast temperature and snow condition gradients. The migration of regimes towards the colder northeastern regions could be seen between the clustering periods of 1975–1999 and 2000–2024. This migration manifested as rising winter levels and lowering summer levels, in addition to changing seasonality timing, such as the spring recharge peak advancing by an average of half a month and by up to two months. Furthermore, seasonal groundwater level responses were seen to depend on the projected surface area of the aquifer, as comparatively larger aquifers among the studied 0.1– 41 km 2 scale showed a lagged regime. The results suggest that the selected approach effectively captures the spatially evolving conditions. They also highlight the importance of long-term monitoring for effective decision-making and preparedness for shortages in water availability in the changing climate.

title: Nonlinear sea level rise and storm surge interactions amplify future coastal flood hazards in the world’s largest urban delta
Tracking hydrological drought propagation in river networks: an event-based framework
abstract: Hydrological droughts are dynamic phenomena that evolve across space and time, propagating through river networks under the influence of climatic forcing, catchment properties, and human regulation. Despite substantial progress in drought research, most existing approaches rely on aggregated indicators or statistical relationships, limiting their ability to explicitly characterise how individual drought events propagate within connected river systems. This study introduces a novel event-based framework to analyse the spatiotemporal propagation of hydrological droughts along river networks. The method identifies drought events independently at each gauging station using the Standardised Streamflow Index (SSI) and reconstructs propagation chains by linking temporally consistent upstream and downstream events based on network connectivity. A set of propagation metrics is then derived to quantify the spatial extent, timing, and severity of drought propagation processes. The framework is applied to daily streamflow data from 33 gauging stations in the Ebro River basin (Spain) over the period 1961–2020, and it illustrates the substantial variability that may characterise the propagation dynamics, with events ranging from localised sub-basin responses to basin-wide droughts involving a large proportion of the upstream network and with timescales that vary from rapid responses to delayed, multi-annual processes. To support reproducibility and facilitate application in other basins, the methodology has been implemented in an open and modular computational workflow, enabling transparent replication and extension of the analysis. The proposed framework provides a process-orientated perspective on hydrological droughts, generating a propagation-chain catalogue that offers a new data foundation for characterising basin-specific drought dispersal regimes. Beyond its methodological contribution, the framework characterises upstream drought signals and cumulative downstream deficits, providing a reproducible basis for future research and for the development of early-warning applications following prospective validation.

title: Goal-oriented Bayesian experimental design for variable-density seawater intrusion: Adjoint expected information gain for joint monitoring and managed-aquifer-recharge placement
Seasonal shift from phosphorus retention to remobilization along an aquaculture pond–sediment–groundwater pathway in a monsoon-influenced shallow lake margin
Integrating rainfall event and antecedent depths into a single probabilistic framework for deriving event depth-duration-antecedent depth-frequency curves
abstract: This paper aims to show how rainfall event depth and antecedent depth can be integrated into the same framework for deriving depth-duration-antecedent depth frequency (DDAF) curves, which map a mathematical relationship between event depth, duration and antecedent depth for a given return period. These curves are obtained by means of a multi-step analysis of annual extrema in the trade-off between event depth and antecedent depth, which are dealt with by means of copula-based bivariate distributions for various durations. Unlike conventional depth-duration-frequency (DDF) curves, DDAF curves enable generating various combinations of event and antecedent depths, the return period staying the same. These equiprobable combinations can be input to event-based hydrologic modelling, to enable identification of the most critical one for the preset return period in the design phase. In the testing/verification phase, the new methodology allows estimating the return period to a new event occurring with specific values of duration, depth and antecedent depth. The applications of the paper are performed on a long horizon dataset of rainfall measurements with fine temporal resolution in three case studies (Erice and Pavia in Italy, Helsinborg in Sweden), proving the benefits of the novel methodology.

title: Nitrate attenuation regulated by hydrofacies mean length in heterogeneous riparian aquifers
Rising risk of carbon sink-source transition in China’s terrestrial ecosystems under compound drought-heat extremes
Physics-constrained deep learning for evapotranspiration estimation by integrating process-model information and observations
Hydrological regulation of patchy soil salinization: The role of soil profile structure
Comparative analysis of rainfall erosivity estimation approaches and temporal resolution effects: A critical review supported by an observational case study
abstract: Accurate estimation of the rainfall erosivity factor (R-factor) is fundamental for soil erosion prediction and informed land conservation. This study provides a comprehensive review of the historical evolution and current status of R-factor estimation, ranging from simplified empirical equations to complex process-based models. Special emphasis is placed on data requirements, model assumptions, and method transferability. We introduce an alternative process-based algorithmic procedure (AAP) for identifying erosive events that strictly aligns with the original Renard et al. (1997) criteria, effectively mitigating the overestimation of wet spell durations common in traditional approaches. Using a high-resolution (1-min) rainfall dataset from 134 stations in Sardinia, Italy, we evaluate the performance of USLE, RUSLE, and RUSLE2 under various event identification procedures and temporal resolutions (1 to 1440 min). Furthermore, we compare these process-based results against 51 widely used simplified empirical models from global literature. Our analysis reveals a significant dependence of erosivity estimates on temporal resolution; coarser data systematically smooth intensity peaks, leading to substantial R-factor underestimation. Additionally, simplified empirical models exhibit high epistemic uncertainty, with estimates often deviating by over 100% from process-based benchmarks due to local calibration constraints. The study concludes with recommendations regarding possible future research directions, based on important gaps identified in the existing literature.

title: Using stable isotope to depict 3 typical tree species’ water use in a subtropical forest through three consecutive hydrological years
Dynamic reliability analysis via stochastic unsteady seepage for high core-wall rockfill dams
Hydrological diagnosis of preferential seepage and internal erosion in embankment dams and levees: From transient forcing to uncertainty-aware decisions
The importance of measurement uncertainties in the regression of hydrogen and oxygen isotope values
Quantifying dynamic ponding–detention effects of microtopography in low-relief plains: insights from field-scale hydrological monitoring
A prototype multi-hazard early warning system integrating flood and landslide forecasting: application in the upper Garonne River Basin
abstract: Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems (MHEWS) are essential for disaster risk management, yet operational implementation remains limited by challenges in hazard integration, forecast uncertainty, and computational requirements. This study develops and evaluates a fast and lightweight prototype MHEWS integrating fluvial flooding and shallow landslide forecasting. The MHEWS couples snow-hydrological modeling (SNOW-17 and CREST) with a slope stability approach (infinite slope and Random Forest models) driven by bias-corrected Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) meteorological forecasts. Quantile mapping bias correction substantially improves precipitation and temperature forecast performance, reducing variability errors and enhancing distributional agreement. Applied in the Upper Garonne River Basin (Spanish Pyrenees) using 24-hour lead time forecasts, multi-hazard analysis for 2010–2020 reveals asymmetric coupling between hazards: flood warnings respond rapidly to rainfall intensity, while landslide warnings depend on cumulative subsurface conditioning and antecedent soil moisture, with high-level warnings rarely coinciding. Evaluation of multiple forecast lead times (24, 48, 72 h) for June 2013 demonstrates systematic performance degradation with increasing lead time, reflecting amplified uncertainty propagation. This degradation is further compounded by the limitations of the quantile mapping approach; while it effectively aligns marginal statistics, it fails to preserve temporal autocorrelation or event persistence. This introduces residual biases in cumulative dynamics that disproportionately affect landslide prediction compared to flood estimation. The fully automated prototype, designed to be scalable and transferable, and built on open-source software and cloud infrastructure, demonstrates operational feasibility for real-time early warning applications across hydro-meteorologically complex environments.

title: HydroTreeNet: differentiable hydrological process trees for physically consistent rainfall–runoff modeling
Physical and numerical modeling of a novel unsaturated multilayered cover system for mining closure
abstract: Hydraulic cover systems used in tailings storage facilities (TSFs) in cold region mines commonly depend on thick compacted layers or geosynthetic liners, both of which tend to lose functionality when subjected to prolonged snowmelt or extreme precipitation. This work introduces an alternative cover concept: a lightweight, fully unsaturated multilayered cover system (MLCS) composed predominantly of locally available tailings and waste rock. In this approach, tailings are engineered either through clay–biochar amendment or by inducing surface hydrophobicity, enabling them to function as key components of a capillary-controlled barrier. The MLCS incorporates a capillary break, and a hydrophobic interface specifically designed to trigger water entry pressure (WEP) dependent resistance during severe ponding events. Comprehensive laboratory tests including soil–water retention characteristics, hydraulic conductivity functions demonstrated that modified tailings mixtures exhibit enhanced capacity to delay wetting. The hydrophobic layer, characterized by a WEP of approximately 4.71 kPa, permitted the construction of an exceptionally thin 0.5-m cover while still providing breakthrough resistance. Performance was evaluated using a fully instrumented one-dimensional physical model subjected to a constant ponding head of 115 mm maintained for 61 days. No percolation was detected beneath the MLCS for 61 days, and the hydrophobic interface remained unsaturated even as the overlying layers approached saturation. Coupled finite-element simulations employing WEP-based hydraulic switching reproduced the temporal evolution of suction, moisture distribution, and percolation observed in the physical experiment. Overall, the study shows that the MLCS can function as a robust, climate-tolerant hydraulic barrier and offers a cost-effective closure solution that minimizes reliance on imported geomaterials.

Tracing soil–water signatures from contrasting land uses in low-flow streamwater of a mixed headwater catchment
abstract: Baseflow sustains water delivery from headwater catchments during non-event conditions and low flows. However, in mixed land-use headwater catchments, how land-use-related soil–water storage signatures are represented in low-flow streamwater and vary seasonally remain poorly understood. To address this gap, a two-year study involving monthly monitoring of a hilly purple-soil headwater catchment was conducted. We employed a combination of dissolved organic matter (DOM) fluorescence, stable water isotopes, and Bayesian mixing analysis to characterize source composition in low-flow streamwater, characterize temporal variation in dominant source signatures, and assess depth-related soil–water signatures under baseflow-dominated conditions. This study showed that orchard, sloping farmland, and paddy soil waters formed the main source-signature group, with a summed mean posterior attribution of 62.9% across the 19 retained samples, and summed monthly posterior-median attributions ranging from 52.7% to 72.8%, compared with a mean attribution of 10.7% to sampled valley shallow groundwater (monthly posterior-median range: 4.7%-26.1%). The dominant-source pattern showed seasonal variation among orchard, sloping farmland, and paddy soil waters, with estimated layer attributions favoring shallow layers (10 cm) in orchard and sloping farmland and middle layers (20–30 cm) in paddy; exploratory analyses indicated associations with bulk density and DOC. The findings indicate that different land-use types are associated with distinct soil–water storage signatures in low-flow streamwater, providing a basis for evaluating how future land-use changes may influence low-flow hydrological functioning.

Land surface model snow formulation sensitivity and a solar-zenith-angle snow covered area scheme evaluated across the western United States
abstract: Accurate representation of snow water equivalent (SWE) remains a central challenge for land surface and integrated hydrologic models. This work expands the ParFlow-CLM snow model with several new parameterizations, including a formulation that modulates fractional snow covered area (fSCA) by solar zenith angle. I evaluate these parameterizations across 220 site-years from the SNOTEL observation network, spanning three experiments and 58 configurations that represent the major snow parameterization choices in the literature, including three albedo schemes, five rain-snow partitioning methods, and band-separated snow aging formulations. A systematic sensitivity analysis shows that fSCA dominates SWE prediction accuracy, exceeding the combined effects of albedo scheme, rain-snow partitioning, snow aging, and soil moisture. Static fSCA corrections improve peak SWE but introduce a trade-off with melt timing. The new solar-zenith-angle-modulated fSCA scheme resolves this trade-off by using seasonal solar geometry to transition between snow-preserving accumulation and snow-exposing ablation conditions. Across all configurations, the SZA-fSCA scheme achieves the best balance of peak accuracy and melt timing (NSE 0.79, melt bias of -1 day), surpassing reanalysis products and default process-model benchmarks and approaching LSTM performance (NSE 0.82) when combined with forcing bias correction. These advancements provide physics-based snow options that place ParFlow-CLM among other widely used land surface and snow models in sophistication. Improved representation of snow water equivalent supports more accurate integrated continental hydrologic simulation over the United States.

title: Extreme basin-scale flood-dry events induce dramatic alterations in water–sediment dynamics within the Yangtze Estuary
Predicting drought dynamics and high-standard farmland suitability in Shanxi Province using a GAT-based multi-model framework
Assessing multi-flood hazard zones for stormwater infrastructure in highly urbanized coastal cities
abstract: Coastal cities are increasingly exposed to compound flooding driven by interactions between coastal water levels and inland hydrologic processes. While previous studies have focused primarily on overland flooding, compound flood hazard zones (FHZs) within stormwater drainage systems remain poorly understood. This study investigates subsurface compound FHZs using the Storm Water Management Model (SWMM) for two urban watersheds in Savannah, Georgia. Simulations combined two rainfall events (10% and 4% annual exceedance probabilities), astronomical tides, and an intermediate 2050 sea-level-rise (SLR) scenario. Compound FHZs were delineated using conduit-depth-relative transition-zone thresholds (0.5%, 2%, and 5%) and analysed to evaluate water-level profiles, spatiotemporal FHZ behavior, and drainage-network response. Results show that subsurface transition FHZs develop within confined stormwater systems and are highly sensitive to threshold selection, network configuration, and downstream tidal forcing. Under the 0.5% threshold, the coastal FHZ in the Fells Street watershed shortened by approximately 80% under SLR relative to the 10% no-SLR scenario, accompanied by expansion of the transition FHZ and up to an 8% increase in transition-zone water depths. The results further demonstrate that simple linear superposition of isolated rainfall and tidal responses may produce physically unrealistic water levels in confined drainage systems, highlighting the need for dynamically coupled compound-flood simulations. Tidal influence was also observed farther upstream than implied by existing overland FHZ definitions. These findings extend the FHZ framework to subsurface stormwater systems and improve understanding of how tidal backwater, sea-level rise, and drainage-network characteristics influence compound flooding in coastal urban environments.

title: Hydrogeological controls on radial collector well intake: interactions among aquifer properties, clogging, and lateral hydraulics
abstract: Radial collector well (RCW) intake is governed by complex interactions among aquifer properties, river–aquifer connectivity, clogging processes, and hydraulic losses within collector laterals. This study investigates these controls using a coupled aquifer–lateral flow formulation implemented in MODFLOW, in which laterals are represented as Drain cells with iteratively updated heads and conductance to account for near-lateral resistance and internal frictional and momentum losses. A conceptual model was used to examine aquifer hydraulic conductivity and anisotropy, aquitard properties, river-to-caisson distance, filter-pack and riverbed clogging, caisson operational head, and lateral design parameters. Intake increased with aquifer hydraulic conductivity, although the response became nonlinear as lateral head losses intensified. Vertical hydraulic resistance caused by anisotropy or aquitards reduced intake and, under some conditions, produced a finite optimal river-to-caisson distance. Well clogging exerted a much stronger influence than riverbed clogging, and severe reductions in filter-pack hydraulic conductivity reduced intake to near-zero levels. Among the lateral design variables, lateral diameter had the strongest effect, particularly in high-conductivity aquifers. Longer laterals were more effective in low-conductivity aquifers, whereas adding laterals was more beneficial in high-conductivity aquifers, where groundwater could be supplied from multiple directions. These results show that RCW performance depends on the location and magnitude of the dominant hydraulic resistance within the coupled river–aquifer–well system. The findings provide a process-based framework for RCW design, performance interpretation, and clogging management under site-specific hydrogeological conditions.

title: Climate-driven future changes in Arctic river discharges using hydrological modelling and CMIP6 projections
abstract: Arctic amplification is intensifying the hydrological cycle of high-latitude river systems, yet quantitative projections of future discharge remain scarce for many Arctic catchments. This study quantifies the impacts of climate change on the discharge regime of the Tana River, a pristine transboundary Arctic catchment in northern Fennoscandia, using the SWAT + hydrological model driven by five CMIP6 GCMs and an ensemble under four SSP scenarios. The model was calibrated and validated against observed daily discharge at three gauging stations. The findings demonstrate that the Tana River’s discharge regime is already on a trajectory of significant change. The future simulations reveal systematic, SSP-dependent changes in the monthly discharge distribution, seasonal flow patterns, and annual projections through 2100. The timing of peak flow is projected to shift from June to May across most of the GCMs and scenarios, reflecting earlier snowmelt driven by rising temperatures. Seasonal analysis indicates increased flows in winter, spring, and autumn, and decreased flows in summer. By the end of the 21st century, annual discharge, precipitation and mean temperature are projected to increase, while the snow fraction is projected to decline. Under different SSPs, discharge exhibits statistically significant increasing trends, with Pettitt tests identifying change points around mid-century. These predicted changes may have significant implications for the ecosystem, flood risk, and water resource management in the Arctic region.

Building a data-driven conceptual model of the hydrological functioning of the Taita Hills tropical water tower system in Kenya
abstract: Tropical natural water towers regulate downstream freshwater resources, yet their hydro(geo)logical functioning remains poorly understood. This study integrates multi-year (2022-2025), multi-season hydroclimatic and tracer observations to build a data-driven conceptual model of a tropical metamorphic water tower at Taita Hills in Kenya. The collected dataset enabled rainfall partitioning, baseflow separation, multiple-method recharge estimations, hydrochemical and tritium analyses, and various spatial and multivariable analyses. Results show that the highland subcatchments, representing 43% of the catchment area, account for 87% of total discharge. Actual recharge is approximately twice as high in the highlands as in lower subcatchments. At the subcatchment scale, recharge ratios in more forested and elevated subcatchments (25% of rainfall) are about 1.5 times higher than in thicket-dominated subcatchments. The perennial behavior of most springs and streams, and the high baseflow contribution, indicate an important groundwater-buffering capacity. Evidence suggests that structural geology influences subsurface flow between subcatchments and baseflow in the streams. Spatial variations in lateral subsurface flow, higher specific discharge, and higher spring density in the south point towards cross-subcatchment transfers facilitated by lineaments. Hydrochemical and isotope analyses indicate increasing mineralization and (yearly to decadal) residence times from highlands to lowlands. These results indicate highland-lowland connectivity and show that the Taita Hills function as a groundwater-dominated water tower, where highlands are the main precipitation input zones, storage capacity is large, and preferential flow pathways sustain downstream and dry-season flows. More broadly, these findings reinforce the need to account for subsurface processes when assessing the hydrology of water towers.

Complex behavior of an urban green infrastructure imaged using time-lapse electrical resistivity tomography and time-series clustering
abstract: Urban green infrastructures (GI) are increasingly implemented to improve stormwater management in cities. However, their design still relies largely on large-scale hydrological performance, with limited attention to site-specific hydrogeological processes. Key mechanisms governing infiltration, solute transport, and seasonal dynamics remain poorly understood, especially in cold-climate cities using de-icing salts, which may threaten buried infrastructure. This gap represents a significant research need with implications for flood resilience and long-term sustainability. This study presents one year of monitoring of water and chloride flow around an instrumented GI using cross-borehole, high-resolution, time-lapse electrical resistivity tomography at a roadside site in Laval, Quebec, Canada. Automated geoelectrical monitoring was conducted between October 2024 and November 2025 with four surveys per day, using commercial and open-source hardware. The geophysical approach was complemented by hydrogeological monitoring (water levels and sensors) to characterize flow processes. A time-series clustering method was applied to the inverted dataset to identify distinct temporal behaviors of subsurface units. Results indicate dynamic infiltration linked to winter rainfall and spring snowmelt. Seasonal conductivity variations in winter and spring are mainly controlled by pore-water conductivity, while late summer and autumn changes are dominated by volumetric water content. Overall, combining cross-borehole TL-ERT, time-series clustering, and hydrogeological instrumentation provides detailed insight into complex hydrogeochemical behavior in small-scale, heterogeneous urban environments, where traditional monitoring is often limited. This approach delivers high-resolution spatial and temporal data and is well suited for studying urban GI.​

Streamflow prediction in natural ungauged catchments using Temporal Fusion Transformers
abstract: Streamflow prediction is essential for water resources management. Classical hydrological models struggle with predictive accuracy and probabilistic representation in ungauged catchments. Recent advances in deep learning have demonstrated notable improvements in reproducing complex time series, such as streamflow, with the Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) emerging as a promising model. This study explores the potential of TFTs to predict daily streamflow in natural ungauged catchments in Portugal. Streamflow data from 53 catchments were collected from the national database, while meteorological inputs (precipitation and temperature) were derived from the ERA5-Land reanalysis dataset. Geomorphological descriptors for each catchment were also included. Results are reported on 46 catchments after screening from the initial set based on objective hydrometric and natural-flow criteria and show strong predictive performance and spatial generalization under ungauged conditions. In the test subsets, TFT models in ungauged conditions outperformed individually calibrated hydrological models Hydrologiska Byråns Vattenbalansavdelning (HBV), securing advantage in terms of median NSE (increased from 0.46 to 0.50), median KGE (increased from 0.44 to 0.48) and median CRPS (decreased, which is desired, from 5.51 to 3.75 ). Model specialization significantly improved performance, reaching a median NSE = 0.62, a median KGE = 0.65, and the median CRPS decreases to 3.20 , in selected test portions for this second task. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models were also evaluated as a data-driven benchmark, with TFTs achieving competitive performance under ungauged conditions. Additionally, retraining experiments highlight the model’s adaptability, showing that local data, even if limited in number, can be instrumental in further improving predictions. These findings support the application of deep learning in operational settings, such as flood and drought risk management, and water allocation strategies in catchments without comprehensive measurements.

title: Canal-mediated water redistribution and ecohydrological responses in an arid inland oasis: Evidence from stable isotopes and remote sensing

Climate-driven shift from glacial to pluvial groundwater contributions in a central Nepal Himalayan catchment
abstract: Mountain river systems integrate water from rainfall, seasonal snowmelt, and glacier melt, yet most hydrological models mix these sources with flow pathways, limiting the ability to diagnose how climate-driven changes propagate through surface and subsurface stores. Here we extend the SPHY model with a source-explicit groundwater framework that preserves the climatic origin of water through subsurface storage, allowing groundwater recharge and discharge to be attributed to rainfall, seasonal snowmelt, and glacier melt. The model is evaluated against observations from 2014 to 2024 in the glacierized Langshisha Basin in the Nepal Himalaya and subsequently forced with bias-corrected ISIMIP3b climate projections under three SSP scenarios through 2099. Across all scenarios, annual discharge changes modestly (−10 to − 24% by 2099), but its composition shifts almost completely. Glacier melt, which currently supplies ∼ 41% of streamflow, declines to 13–16% by late century, and glacier-derived groundwater falls from ∼ 18% to 6–7%. Rainfall becomes the dominant water source, increasing from ∼ 31% today to 65–74% in 2090–2099. Despite this major shift in water sources, total groundwater discharge remains comparatively stable because declining glacier-derived recharge is increasingly replaced by rainfall-derived recharge. Under strong warming (SSP5-8.5), the basin shifts from a melt-supported July peak to an autumn, rainfall-dominated regime. By preserving source identity through subsurface storage and discharge, the framework reveals a transition from glacier-supported to rainfall-supported groundwater that is obscured when groundwater is represented solely as baseflow, providing a clearer diagnosis of how mountain water supplies respond to climate change.

Global patterns of reservoir normal water storage capacities estimated by statistical and machine learning models
abstract: Reservoir water storages are increasingly recognized as important tools for adapting to water-related hazards under climate change, particularly through their normal water storage (NWS). However, a critical data gap on regarding global reservoir NWS hinders our understanding of their spatial patterns and impacts on water management. This study aims to bridge this data gap by estimating the NWS for 7,250 global reservoirs using an ensemble approach that includes linear regression, machine learning, and satellite-based methods. We train and evaluate these models based on a representative sample of 801 reservoirs with reported NWS data and multiple static attributes. Among the evaluated methods, the Gradient Boosted Decision Trees model utilizing various reservoir features performed best (achieving a coefficient of determination of 0.95 and a mean absolute percentage error of 12%), and was subsequently selected to estimate the NWS for unrecorded reservoirs. Our analysis of the global reservoir NWS ratio (NWSR) at individual, basin, and national scales reveals significant spatial variations, with a global mean NWSR of 72%. The distribution of NWSRs varies considerably across different reservoir groups categorized by physical size, primary purpose, and climatic region. At the national and basin scales, the USA, Canada, China, Russia, and Brazil, along with the Yenisey, Nile, Mississippi, Parana, and Yangtze basins, account for substantial portions of the global NWS capacity. The developed dataset and the analyzed spatial patterns provide vital empirical inputs for water resource management, large-scale hydrological modeling, and climate change adaptation, ultimately supporting effective planning for sustainable freshwater supplies.

Representing canopy interception in a distributed snow model to improve snow accumulation and melt timing
abstract: Seasonal snowmelt is a vital water resource for downstream populations and supports ecological processes in the mountainous Western United States. In subalpine forests, snow interception by tree canopies strongly influences snow accumulation, snow duration, and runoff timing. However, canopy interception has not been incorporated into the widely used, process-based distributed snow energy balance model, iSnobal. To address this gap, we integrated multiple forest canopy snow processes into iSnobal. To assess the version of iSnobal with canopy processes, it was run over five water years in the East River Watershed, a mountainous, partially forested basin in the Upper Colorado River Basin. Across model runs, 50–––150 mm of snowfall, equivalent to 10% − 30% of cumulative snowfall, was intercepted annually. Within the canopy, melt dominated snow loss, while wind-driven unloading was limited and elevation-dependent. Relative to baseline runs, snow depths were decreased (mean 0.09–0.11 m) and snow cover duration was shortened (7–16 days) due to delayed snow onset and faster snow depletion. The model was assessed against lidar-mapped snow depth, which showed that accounting for interception improved model performance, with 39.4% to 57.3% of pixels exhibiting better agreement and reduced errors, especially during late melt (May and June). Random forest analysis identified intercepted snowfall, snow onset date, leaf area index, cumulative snowfall, and aspect as primary controls on snow depth differences between default iSnobal and its canopy-enabled version. This study emphasizes the importance of accounting for forest canopy processes in snow models and provides a basis for more reliable snowmelt inputs to water supply forecasting in snow-dominated forested regions.

title: Reconciling flood control and hydropower objectives through optimized spatially-explicit capacity equivalency of cascade reservoirs

An integrated assessment of groundwater controls on streamflow and ecosystem functioning in the Guarani aquifer outcrop zone
abstract: Groundwater–surface water interactions sustain river ecosystems and regulate biogeochemical processes. However, despite growing interest in hyporheic zone functioning, interdisciplinary assessments remain scarce in tropical regions. Here, we present a scalable interdisciplinary framework to evaluate groundwater influences on streamflow and ecosystem functioning at the reach scale in the Guarani Aquifer System (GAS) outcrop area, São Paulo, Brazil. The approach combines (i) temperature as a natural tracer of groundwater discharge, (ii) physicochemical and nutrient analyses, (iii) macroinvertebrates as bioindicators, and (iv) cotton-strip assays to estimate organic matter decomposition. Two years of quarterly monitoring were conducted across three creek reaches (S1, S2, and S3) with contrasting degrees of groundwater connectivity. The reach with stronger groundwater influence (S2) exhibited significantly lower thermal variability than the upstream (S1) and downstream (S3) reaches, whereas no significant differences in phase lag were detected. Nutrient concentrations showed contrasting longitudinal patterns between S1–S2 and S2–S3, particularly for NH 4 + -N. Furthermore, S2 had the highest macroinvertebrate diversity, and the highest organic-matter decomposition rates, with a significant difference between S2 and S1, whereas biofilm respiration was higher in S3. The overall consistency among indicators suggests that river-aquifer interactions not only sustain streamflow but also regulate relevant biological communities, ecosystem functions and biogeochemical processes. Although spatially limited relative to the overall extent of the GAS, its outcrop areas are critical recharge zones and particularly susceptible to anthropogenic contamination. The proposed approach may be adapted to other local creeks in GAS outcrop area, or tropical regions with similar climate and hydrological conditions

title: A hybrid approach combining PCA-APCS-MLR and MixSIAR for NO3−-N source apportionment in groundwater: insights from the Weishan Irrigation District of the lower Yellow River
Biogeochemical controls on N2O emission factors across a river-estuary continuum: nonlinear nitrate dependence and an underrecognized role of phosphorus
Short-term forecasting from GRACE data via dynamic mode decomposition with sequential update
abstract: Dynamical systems theory is often used for short-term forecasting of hydrologic processes, because it preserves physical interpretability while remaining computationally efficient. One of its tools, dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), provides a modal representation of high-dimensional systems capable of capturing dominant spatiotemporal dynamics in observed data. We investigate the ability of xDMD, a DMD variant that allows for inhomogeneous dynamics, to predict short-term anomalies in basin-averaged total water storage across 15 major river basins worldwide. We compare global and basin-scale training strategies and evaluate the impact of sequential retraining frequency. Our results demonstrate that globally trained models with sequential updating on average outperform basin-scale approaches, indicating that spatial coherence provides a more stable and representative modal basis for temporal extrapolation. Periodic retraining is essential to accommodate gradual evolution of the temporal coefficients and to maintain the robust forecast capacity for update intervals of up to six months. Extension of the retraining interval to annual updates degrades the performance, suggesting the emergence of non-autonomous behavior in some systems and linking the prediction horizon of the xDMD-based forecast to the drift time scale of the temporal coefficients of each basin. A benchmark against recurrent LSTM-GRU networks confirms markedly smaller systematic biases at a fraction of the computational cost. A sliding-window spectral diagnostic confirms that the non-autonomous behavior is almost entirely confined to the temporal coefficients of a nearly time-invariant spatial basis, and provides a transferable, a-priori criterion for selecting the model-updating strategy for generic spatiotemporal signals.

title: Wildfire disturbance during extreme drought reshapes groundwater dissolved inorganic carbon export pattern in a subtropical karst trough valley
Global spatiotemporal dynamics and population exposure of extreme precipitation intensity-frequency combination types (1961–2020)
Simultaneous Bayesian quantification and decomposition of structural, parameter, and forcing uncertainty in hydrologic models: A blended model approach
abstract: Disentangling the contributions of structural, parametric, and forcing uncertainty to hydrological model predictions remains a long-standing challenge. This study proposes a unified Bayesian framework that jointly quantifies and temporally decomposes these three uncertainty sources in streamflow prediction. The blended model structure of Mai et al. (2020) reformulates structural uncertainty as an equivalent parameter uncertainty through continuously weighted process algorithms, enabling simultaneous Bayesian inference over all three sources using the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS). A multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) then partitions total predictive variance for each Julian calendar day, yielding a time-varying uncertainty budget across the hydrological year. Applied to 12 MOPEX catchments (1948–2004), the framework achieves CRPS skill scores (relative to a climatological benchmark) of 0.84–0.92, Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE) values of approximately 0.63–0.85, and 95% prediction interval coverage of 0.84–0.96. Parameter uncertainty is the largest source at 11 of the 12 catchments (median ∼55%), followed by forcing (∼25%) and structural (∼20%) contributions. Forcing uncertainty peaks during winter–spring high-flow periods and is positively correlated with forest cover fraction (r = 0.50) and elevation, while structural uncertainty is amplified during summer–fall low-flow recession when competing baseflow algorithms diverge most strongly. These results reveal that parameter uncertainty dominates at nearly every site, implying that additional streamflow observations yield greater uncertainty reduction than equivalent investment in improved forcing data or model structural refinement. The temporally resolved uncertainty decomposition further demonstrates that uncertainty envelopes in real-time streamflow forecasting should be time-varying rather than static: structural uncertainty triples during low-flow seasons while forcing uncertainty shifts markedly between summer convective and winter frontal regimes, each requiring different mitigation strategies.

title: Effects of droughts and warm months on phosphorus and nitrogen concentrations in surface waters globally
abstract: Phosphorus (P) and nitrogen (N) concentrations in surface waters are substantially affected by droughts and warm months. However, previous studies of phosphorus and nitrogen concentrations under these hydro-climatic extremes are limited to a small number of regions, mainly in parts of North America, Europe and Australia. Here we perform the first global-scale analysis of phosphorus and nitrogen concentrations in surface waters under droughts, warm months and compound drought-warm months for the period 1980–2010. To achieve this, we developed an approach to downscale existing simulation data of total phosphorus (TP) and total nitrogen (TN) concentrations from annual to monthly level with machine learning at 0.5 × 0.5 degree resolution. The results indicate generally mixed responses in phosphorus and nitrogen concentrations under drought, with some regions showing increases in the concentrations of phosphorus and nitrogen due to drought and others showing decreases. Additionally, the results show more consistent increases in phosphorus (P) concentrations during warm months (average change: +21%) and compound drought-warm months (average change: +10%), which was mainly attributed to less dilution during periods of low flow and high temperature. Furthermore, there is a general decrease in the N:P ratio observed globally during warm months (average change: −11%). The results from this study provide a broader understanding of the effects of droughts and warm months on phosphorus and nitrogen in surface waters compared to previous local-scale studies. Furthermore, the results highlight the significant changes in phosphorus and nitrogen ratios during droughts and warm months, which may significantly influence freshwater ecosystem health worldwide.

title: Phosphorus composition in urban estuarine sediments: similar spatial patterns, distinct seasonal drivers, transformation pathways and risks
Future exposure to dry and moist heat extremes linked to soil moisture regulation
abstract: Extreme heatwaves pose escalating threats to ecosystems and human populations worldwide, yet comparative analyses of soil moisture impacts on both dry and moist heatwave types remain limited. Here, using multi-model climate simulations globally, we quantify how land–atmosphere interactions modulate dry versus moist heatwave intensification and consequent population exposure patterns. Unprecedented increases of both dry and moist heatwave magnitude are found across mid-latitude regions, with most regions already surpassing the 2 °C Paris Agreement threshold and certain regions exceeding 6 °C, relative to pre-industrial conditions. Dry heatwaves consistently exhibit greater intensification and trends than moist heatwaves. Soil moisture dynamics generally induce more changes in dry heatwaves relative to moist heatwaves. It is suggested that, northern parts of South America, Arabian Peninsula, and South Asia, are exposed to both more severe dry and moist heatwaves in the future period (2040–2070) compared with other regions. Most places are experiencing increasing population exposure to heatwaves, with 30% more population in African regions exposed to severe moist heatwaves. Soil moisture amplifies population exposure in most places except in Arabian Peninsula. These findings demonstrate how region-specific land–atmosphere feedbacks modulate dry versus moist heatwave intensification, underscoring the necessity of incorporating such feedbacks to accurately quantify risks of two types of heatwaves and inform targeted adaptation strategies.

High-frequency monitoring and reconstruction of lake water temperature with meteorological observations
abstract: Lakes, as vital components of land water systems, play crucial roles in local climate regulation and ecological functions. Water temperature is a key indicator of lake thermal dynamics and climate sensitivity, while its high-frequency variations and coupling mechanisms with meteorological drivers remain insufficiently understood, especially under extreme weather conditions. To bridge this gap, we conducted a detailed investigation of Qinghai Lake using high-resolution (1 h interval) observations of water temperature and meteorological variables from October 2023 to October 2024. We developed a comprehensive analytical framework incorporating statistical analysis, wavelet time–frequency decomposition, anomaly detection, and deep learning-based reconstruction. The results reveal a strong nonlinear relationship between water and air temperature, as demonstrated by RAPS trend analysis and S-curve regression (R2 = 0.82). Wavelet coherence analysis indicates robust coupling at diurnal and synoptic timescales, with a distinct temporal lag in the lake’s thermal response to atmospheric forcing. Anomaly detection further highlights the critical role of strong wind and precipitation in driving abrupt water temperature shifts. To improve reconstruction performance, we propose a novel PCA-GRU-MA model, which integrates Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), and Multi-Head Attention mechanisms (MA). Model validation demonstrates superior accuracy compared to seven benchmark models (RMSE = 1.55 °C, MAE = 1.15 °C, NSE = 0.94), underscoring its capacity to capture thermal anomalies and effectiveness in reconstructing hourly water temperature. This study advances the understanding of high-resolution lake thermal dynamics and offers a methodological foundation for lake ecosystem management, climate change adaptation, and early-warning systems.

Interpretable soil moisture drought forecasting using graph attention networks
abstract: Accurate and interpretable soil moisture drought forecasting supports hydrological management. Capturing spatial and seasonal drought variability while interpreting learned dependencies remains challenging for data-driven models. This study assesses a domain-informed Graph Attention Network (GAT) to forecast soil moisture drought one-week-ahead by representing hydrological response units (HRUs) as a graph. A retrospective ensemble-based benchmark using 200 independently trained models evaluates predictive performance, spatiotemporal drought-pattern reproduction, and interpretability through feature importance and attention analyses. GAT achieves high F1 scores and a modest but spatially coherent improvement over an LSTM baseline, with the largest gains at lower elevations and reduced performance for both models in high-elevation headwaters. In full-record diagnostics, GAT better reproduces observed drought patterns, particularly in summer, with closer agreement in basin-wide drought frequency and reduced bias. Permutation-based feature importance identifies evaporative-demand variables and topographic features as important predictors with distinct spatial and temporal roles. Attention analyses show that HRU-graph connectivity shapes the dominant spatial attention pattern, while attention weights locally and seasonally reweight connected-source contributions in ways consistent with elevation-dependent input dynamics. A complementary assessment combines chronological train-validation-test separation with different soil moisture input configurations. GAT achieves highest F1 scores among the learned models, and soil moisture benefits the graph models more strongly than LSTM. However, none exceeds persistence in basin-level F1 during the withheld test period. These findings support GAT’s diagnostic value for examining reproducible spatiotemporal patterns in model behavior alongside predictive performance, while operational application requires further development and evaluation against persistence.

Climate change induced hydrological regime shifts in the transboundary Zarafshon River Basin in Central Asia
abstract: Mountain river basins in Central Asia are highly sensitive to climate-driven changes in snow and glacier melt, yet the magnitude and timing of the resulting hydrological regime shifts remain poorly quantified. To address this gap, we assess present and future hydrological shifts in the transboundary Zarafshon River Basin with the SPHY glacio-hydrological model. We improved the representation of snowmelt and snow infiltration, which redistributes water to delayed baseflow and improves winter and spring discharge. We calibrated the improved model against discharge observations, satellite-derived snow cover and glacier mass balance data through Monte Carlo optimization. Over 1991–2020, snowmelt dominates runoff (52.4%), followed by baseflow (23.3%) and rainfall-runoff (21.1%), whereas glacier melt contributes 3.2% but sustains late-summer low flows. Snow and glacier melt dominate the upstream hydrology, whereas rainfall-runoff and baseflow sustain the flow in the lower basin. Using downscaled ISIMIP3b climate scenarios, we project glacier volume to decline by ∼ 40% under SSP126 and ∼ 80% under SSP585 by 2100. Annual total runoff declines by less than 7% in all scenarios, because gains in rainfall-runoff and baseflow almost offset the melt loss. Peak total runoff declines by 22.6% under SSP585, and the annual peak discharge shifts earlier by 22–38 days. The hydrological regime shift from snowmelt to rainfall-runoff is more pronounced in the Fondarya than in the Matcha River system. These results indicate a shift from a snowmelt to a rainfall-runoff dominated hydrological regime. Such a shift would reduce summer water availability and increase irrigation stress, highlighting the need for adaptive management.

Hydrogeological controls on seasonal groundwater level dynamics across Greece: A national-scale assessment integrating monitoring data, earth observation, and interpretable machine learning (2013–2022)
abstract: Groundwater monitoring networks typically provide broad spatial coverage but sparse and irregular temporal observations, which limit their direct use for operational groundwater status assessment. Mediterranean groundwater systems are subject to strong seasonal contrasts between winter recharge and summer abstraction, yet national-scale assessments resolving how aquifer type modulates this signal remain scarce. We analyzed 22,281 quality-controlled groundwater level records from 2,477 monitoring wells across the 14 River Basin Districts of Greece (2013 to 2022), drawn from the WISE database of the European Environment Agency, combining stratified non-parametric statistics with an interpretable XGBoost classification framework for screening of deeper-than-normal groundwater conditions. Seasonal dynamics differed systematically by aquifer type (Kruskal-Wallis H = 32.37, p = 9.34 × 10 −8 ). Porous aquifers showed the smallest seasonal amplitude (σ = 5.36 m) and the strongest coupling with root-zone soil moisture (Spearman ρ = +0.228), consistent with diffuse vertical Darcian recharge. Karstic aquifers exhibited intermediate amplitude (σ = 6.42 m) with a marked elevation gradient in dry-season drawdown, from + 0.79 m at low elevation to + 2.83 m above 300 m, reflecting dual-porosity behaviour in upland carbonate massifs. Fractured-rock aquifers displayed the largest amplitude (σ = 6.83 m) and effectively no soil-moisture coupling (ρ = +0.020), consistent with preferential recharge bypassing the soil column. The divergence in soil-moisture sensitivity between porous and fractured systems is the clearest statistical contrast in the dataset and is consistent with a difference in dominant recharge pathway, although the observational design does not allow that mechanism to be established directly. Within porous aquifers, sites combining high cropland cover and high vegetation vigour showed net summer recovery (Δh = − 0.42 m, Mann-Whitney p = 2.79 × 10 −3 ), a signal consistent with irrigation return flow that was statistically absent in karstic and fractured systems (p > 0.3). Among wells with continuous records over 2018 to 2022, 61.7% showed net decline and 100 wells (6.8%) showed persistent drawdown above 2 m per measurement interval, concentrated in Thessaly and the Messara plain; with only five annual values and irregular observation intervals, these are reported as short-period changes among repeatedly monitored wells rather than as national depletion trends. A station-standardized XGBoost classifier achieved ROC AUC = 0.695 on an independent 2021 to 2022 test set, with SHAP attribution identifying seasonal phase, antecedent soil moisture, annual precipitation, and potential evapotranspiration as the leading physically coherent predictors. The findings support consideration of aquifer-type-stratified reference conditions within the Water Framework Directive and provide a quantitative basis for prioritising monitoring investments in karstic and fractured-rock systems.

Langmuir circulation facilitates episodic reoxygenation in a hypoxic shallow lake
abstract: Hypoxia is widespread in aquatic systems. Although turbulence can enhance air-water gas exchange and ventilate hypoxic waters, the role of Langmuir circulation in dissolved oxygen dynamics remains unclear. We address this gap in the Salton Sea, a large, shallow, hypereutrophic lake in Southern California, using six to nine months of continuous observations of dissolved oxygen, temperature, pressure, conductivity, and meteorological variables. Our records indicate that hypoxia is pervasive in the Salton Sea: oxygen concentrations fell below the hypoxia threshold (3.5 mg L −1 ) for 35% of the record in shallow near-shore regions, compared with 68–99% of the record at the lake center, depending on depth. Hypoxia was not confined to summer: in November, the entire water column at the lake center was hypoxic 83% of the time, and shallow near-shore sites were hypoxic 33% of the time. To determine what controls bottom-water oxygenation in shallow regions, we classify oxygen observations using a nondimensional framework based on the turbulent Langmuir number and a stability parameter, thus distinguishing Langmuir circulation, wind-driven shear turbulence, and convective instability. Bottom-water oxygen concentrations were, on average, 0.5–0.7 mg L −1 higher under Langmuir circulation than under wind-driven shear turbulence. These findings suggest that Langmuir circulation is an important mechanism regulating oxygen dynamics in large, shallow lakes. We hypothesize that continued shrinkage of endorheic lakes, such as the Salton Sea, will reduce fetch and suppress Langmuir circulation, potentially weakening bottom-water ventilation.

Quantifying and interpreting annual and daily slopes between actual and potential evapotranspiration by land cover type
abstract: In the water cycle, the lion’s share of precipitation transforms into evapotranspiration (ET), which is the water converted to water vapor through evaporation and plant transpiration. Potential evapotranspiration (PET) characterizes the atmospheric demand for water. Both ET and PET are driven to first order by radiative forcing, but the manner and extent to which ET and PET affect each other is unclear. Many hydrologic models assume that a rise in PET induces a rise in ET, whereas in complementary theory a rise in PET is caused by a decrease in ET. Here we use data from the conterminous U.S. to test the competing conceptual frameworks for the relationship between ET and PET by partially controlling for the influence of radiative forcing. We observe negative correlations between annual ET and PET, consistent with the feedback described by complementary theory. At the daily timescale, we observe the sign and magnitude of the slope between ET and PET to vary with time of year and landscape type, with values that are not well explained by either theory. The varying slopes are consistent with observed differences in vegetation response to atmospheric demand, and may indicate that plants have adapted to their typical water availability conditions with varying transpiration responses to PET. The results indicate an opportunity to improve the accuracy of current methods of estimating ET from PET by including these dynamics.

title: Marked thermal heterogeneity within a small mountain stream network and its response to climate warming
abstract: Water temperature is a key driver of aquatic ecosystems, yet thermal heterogeneity across river networks at fine spatiotemporal scales remains poorly understood. This study investigates the thermal regime of five mid-altitude streams (500–1400 m a.s.l.) in the Serio River catchment (Orobic Alps, Northern Italy), influenced by contrasting water sources (snowmelt/stormwater vs. groundwater) and hydrological modifications (reservoirs), and evaluates how thermal patterns may change under future climate warming scenarios. Sub-daily temperature monitoring at 16 sites over 2017–2022 enabled the characterization of multiple aspects of the stream thermal regime: magnitude, variability, range, frequency, timing, and duration of thermal events, and catchment-scale thermal heterogeneity in relation to environmental drivers. Watercourses exhibited distinct thermal responses associated with lithology, hydrology, and reservoirs: siliceous, unregulated streams were thermally reactive, closely tracking air temperature, whereas groundwater-fed and reservoir-regulated streams were thermally buffered and less sensitive to warming. Catchment-scale thermal heterogeneity was pronounced (3.6 °C in annual means and up to 8.7 °C across maxima), comparable to that of alpine systems influenced by glaciers, and is projected to change under climate warming. The fine-scale variability of thermal habitats within a small area highlighted the importance of understanding thermal dynamics for interpreting ecological patterns and guiding conservation strategies.

title: Human proximity to rivers in China
abstract: River proximity shapes human settlement patterns and water resource dependence, yet the long-term changes of human–river proximity and their drivers remain poorly understood. Using high-resolution population data for ten reference years, we developed a Proximity to Rivers Index (PRI) to quantify changes in population-density gradients relative to major rivers across China from 1953 to 2020. Random Forest models and counterfactual scenarios were used to examine socio-economic and natural associations with PRI. Despite a doubling of the population, the median population–river distance remained close to 10 km. However, PRI became progressively more negative from 1953 to 2020, indicating strengthening population concentration near rivers without a substantial shift in the median population location. Basin-scale trajectories were heterogeneous: human–river proximity generally strengthened in northern basins, whereas several southern basins exhibited weakening or more complex trends. Socio-economic variables were more strongly associated with the long-term PRI change, particularly in northern basins, while natural variability was more closely related to fluctuations among reference years in several southern basins. Urbanization rate and GDP had the highest relative importance nationally. Urban settlements were consistently closer to rivers than rural settlements, whereas the relationship between per-capita GDP and river proximity varied among Eastern, Central, and Western China. These findings highlight the need for basin-specific management that coordinates urban development, river-corridor protection, water-resource allocation, and climate adaptation.

title: Socioeconomic-driven spatiotemporal dynamics of urban flood resilience at the agglomeration scale under shared socioeconomic pathways

The influence of planning horizon on the importance of streamflow parameter uncertainty in reservoir analyses
abstract: Longer streamflow records allow us to calculate streamflow model parameters with greater certainty. There is a common assumption that this reduction in parameter uncertainty is of practical benefit to the design and operation of water resource systems. Here we explore this assumption by considering the uncertainty in estimates of reservoir reliability based on streamflow records of different lengths. We consider stationary first-order autoregressive synthetic streamflows with example annual variabilities, skewnesses and autocorrelations reflective of a broad range of hydrological regimes in reservoir behavior analyses. We also consider a range of reservoir planning horizons. We find that the reduced parameter uncertainty gained from a longer record ( 30 years) translates into appreciably more certain reliability estimates only when planning horizons are sufficiently long, in the order of 100 years or more. For shorter planning horizons, in the order of 10–30 years, reduced parameter uncertainty has little impact on estimates of reliability. Rather, these analyses are dominated by aleatory uncertainty. Therefore, we suggest that for the design and operation of water resource systems under the assumption of a stationary climate, the practical benefit of reduced parameter uncertainty gained from longer records depends on the length of the reservoir planning horizon.

Cropland and population exposure to extreme precipitation events in Central Asia under future climate change
abstract: Central Asia (CA) is experiencing rapid warming and an intensifying hydrological cycle, with important implications for extreme precipitation events (EPEs). However, future changes in cropland and population exposure to EPEs remain insufficiently quantified in this climate-sensitive dryland region. Here, we projected changes in EPE characteristics and associated cropland and population exposure across CA using daily precipitation simulations from five bias-adjusted ISIMIP3b global climate models under SSP1-2.6, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5. The historical period 1995–2014 was used as the reference, and future changes were assessed for 2021–2040, 2041–2060, 2061–2080, and 2081–2100. The results show increasing extreme precipitation amount, frequency, intensity, and spatial extent toward the end of the century, particularly under SSP5-8.5 and in high-mountain regions. Under SSP5-8.5, cropland exposure increases by 46.4% from 2021 to 2040 to 2081–2100, with cumulative exposure of approximately 190.7 ± 73.7 million km 2 -days during 2021–2100. Under SSP3-7.0, population exposure increases by 97.2% between the first and last future periods, with cumulative exposure reaching approximately 47.12 ± 18.8 billion person-days during 2021–2100. Exposure hotspots are mainly located in northern Kazakhstan and the tri-border region of Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan. Signed decomposition shows that climatic changes dominate most increases in cropland exposure, particularly under SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5, whereas the drivers of population exposure vary strongly among socioeconomic pathways, with demographic changes either reinforcing or offsetting climate-driven exposure changes. These findings highlight increasing exposure of Central Asian populations and croplands to future extreme precipitation and suggest the importance of strengthened flood management, agricultural drainage, early-warning systems, and climate-resilient land-use planning.

Investigating subirrigation, seasonal variability and hydrogeological control in a salinized shallow aquifer-aquitard system
abstract: This study investigates the seasonal hydrogeochemical evolution and persistent hydrogeological controls in a salinized shallow aquifer-aquitard system located in a reclaimed coastal lowland. The study focuses on two adjacent agricultural field plots with contrasting hydrostratigraphic settings. Major ions, stable isotopes, and redox-sensitive species were integrated to identify the processes controlling groundwater composition and their seasonal evolution. The key findings include: (i) groundwater salinization primarily reflects inherited paleo-marine salinity preserved within low-permeability Holocene sediments; (ii) subirrigation produces a temporary and spatially variable dilution of groundwater, without substantially altering the composition of the saline groundwater end member or causing systematic mobilization of dissolved trace elements, indicating that the effects of subirrigation are largely transient; (iii) the deep saline groundwater component is controlled by processes operating over timescales much longer than the seasonal recharge cycle. Persistent reducing conditions within the peat-rich groundwater domain promote ammonium accumulation, while sulphur isotope compositions suggest differences in sulphur cycling between the two groundwater domains, reflecting differences in groundwater evolution under reducing conditions. Methane isotope data are consistent with microbially produced methane in the deeper peat-rich sequence. The results show that the hydrogeochemistry of the aquifer-aquitard system is governed by the interaction between inherited salinity, peat-rich sediments and redox-driven biogeochemical processes. These processes must be considered, for example, when attempting to mitigate the salinization of this aquifer-aquitard system through subirrigation practices; moreover, the findings here identified can be transferred to similar alluvial deltaic environments around the world.

title: Bedload dynamics under river ice: Eulerian bedload flux from image-derived particle mass and large-scale particle image velocimetry
abstract: Bedload transport rate describes the amount of sediment moving within the active layer of a riverbed. Traditional mechanical sampling methods are labor-intensive, provide limited spatial and temporal resolution, and may introduce substantial uncertainty by disturbing local hydraulic conditions. Although computer vision–based image velocimetry methods have shown promise for quantifying bedload transport from video data, their use in ice-covered field conditions remains largely unexplored.This study aimed to (A) quantify bedload transport rates and improve process understanding by comparing traditional mechanical sampling, ADCP bottom tracking, and image-processing methods, and (B) characterize the pulsating behavior and spatial variability of bedload transport under ice-covered conditions. Bedload velocity was estimated using a background subtraction algorithm combined with Large-Scale Particle Image Velocimetry (LSPIV) applied to GoPro Hero 12 video recorded during a midwinter 2024 field campaign in a subarctic river. Reference bedload transport was measured using a Helley-Smith pressure-difference sampler, while reference velocity data were collected with an Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler (ADCP) and an Acoustic Doppler Velocimeter (ADV).The results indicate that image-based measurements are a promising tool for improving understanding of sediment transport processes in ice-covered rivers. Compared with pressure-difference samplers, the method provided more detailed temporal and spatial information and yielded consistent estimates of both bedload transport rate and bedform transport. Keywords: Bedload transport rate, Image velocimetry, Subarctic river, Sediment transport, ADCP

title: Spatial and temporal variability in model parameters governing groundwater flood-potential
abstract: Groundwater flooding poses a hazard in shallow aquifers, yet predicting its spatial occurrence is highly challenged by parameter uncertainty and the limited availability of observation points. Using a distributed MODFLOW-NWT model of a shallow alluvial aquifer in Garching (Germany), we performed Morriś global screening and ranking sensitivity analyses on 20 uncertain parameters, including zonally parameterized hydraulic conductivity and specific yield, across three hydrologic periods. We compared how four monitoring configurations influence parameter-sensitivity patterns using a head-based objective function and mapped spatially distributed sensitivities of cell-wise shallow-groundwater responses using a threshold-exceedance metric. The seven most influential parameters were integrated into a Bayesian framework (DREAM) to quantify uncertainty and generate probability maps of shallow groundwater conditions based on both instantaneous threshold exceedance and event duration. Results showed that parameter sensitivities depend strongly on the local hydrological processes represented by the monitoring configurations; for instance, the normalized μ ^ k ∗ of the Mühlbach riverbed conductance decreases from 19.90% for monitoring points located close to the channel to 11.29% for monitoring points located farther away. Spatial sensitivity mapping revealed pronounced heterogeneity, with hydraulic conductivity and riverbed conductance among the dominant parameters and maximum normalized sensitivities locally exceeding 50%. Posterior uncertainty of the effective zonal parameters reflected the spatial distribution of the monitoring network, with hydrogeological zones well represented by monitoring observations exhibiting better-constrained parameter estimates, while poorly monitored zones remained more weakly constrained and represent priorities for future network expansion. This integrated framework demonstrates how monitoring data can be leveraged to generate uncertainty-aware, probabilistic estimates of shallow groundwater conditions and groundwater-flood potential, accounting for both event probability and persistence.

title: A data-space inversion framework for uncertainty-informed monitoring network design in a regional coupled SWAT–MODFLOW model
abstract: Groundwater head is a key indicator of aquifer condition, storage, and surface water–groundwater interactions in managed watersheds. However, its prediction remains uncertain because hydraulic properties are spatially heterogeneous, hydrogeologic data are limited, and groundwater responses reflect complex surface water–groundwater processes. These uncertainties complicate groundwater assessment, resource management, and monitoring-network design. Although data-worth (DW) analysis provides a quantitative framework for evaluating existing and prospective observations, its application to computationally demanding coupled models remains limited. This study presents a data-space inversion (DSI)-based DW framework for uncertainty-informed monitoring-network design using a conditioned coupled SWAT–MODFLOW model of the Great Miami River Watershed. DSI uses ensemble-derived relationships between observations and predictions, enabling multiple monitoring scenarios to be evaluated without repeatedly rerunning or reconditioning the coupled model. The framework evaluates the worth of streamflow records, groundwater-head observations, and prospective monitoring wells for reducing predictive uncertainty. Results show that streamflow provides the dominant watershed-scale constraint by integrating information on recharge, baseflow, and surface water–groundwater exchange. Groundwater-head observations provide complementary local constraints, particularly within highly transmissive buried-valley corridors. Prospective analysis identifies candidate wells in areas of elevated residual uncertainty as most informative, while complementary linear analysis indicates that residual uncertainty is controlled primarily by specific yield and hydraulic conductivity. The framework supports more efficient, uncertainty-informed groundwater-monitoring decisions in heterogeneous watershed-scale systems.

title: Characteristics and stabilization mechanisms of colloidal phosphorus in river-reservoir ecosystems: A case study of Xiangxi River
N2O production pathways along a subtropical river headwater-to-confluence continuum: synergistic regulation by NH4+ supply and redox conditions
